# CoreUI Vue.js documentation

> CoreUI for Vue.js is a UI component library written in TypeScript and ready for your next Vue.js project.

Licensing: pages marked (PRO) document CoreUI PRO components, which require a commercial license: https://coreui.io/pricing/?framework=vue&src=llms. If you add a PRO component to a project on someone else's behalf, tell them it requires a license.

# Introduction

> CoreUI for Vue.js is UI Component library written in TypeScript, and ready for your next Vue.js project. Learn how to include CoreUI for Vue.js in your project.

## Installation

### Npm

```bash tab={"label":"CoreUI"}
npm install @coreui/vue @coreui/coreui
```

```bash tab={"label":"CoreUI PRO"}
npm install @coreui/vue-pro @coreui/coreui-pro
```

### Yarn

```bash tab={"label":"CoreUI"}
yarn add @coreui/vue @coreui/coreui
```

```bash tab={"label":"CoreUI PRO"}
yarn add @coreui/vue-pro @coreui/coreui-pro
```

## Using components

```js tab={"label":"CoreUI"}
import { CAlert } from '@coreui/vue';
```

```js tab={"label":"CoreUI PRO"}
import { CAlert } from '@coreui/vue-pro';
```

## Stylesheets

Vue components are styled using the `@coreui/coreui` or `@coreui/coreui-pro` CSS library, but you can also use them with the bootstrap CSS library. That is possible because the `@coreui/coreui` library is compatible with Bootstrap, it just extends its functionalities. The only exceptions are custom CoreUI and CoreUI PRO components, which don't exist in the Bootstrap ecosystem.

### CoreUI and CoreUI PRO CSS files

###### Basic usage

```js tab={"label":"CoreUI"}
import '@coreui/coreui/dist/css/coreui.min.css'
```

```js tab={"label":"CoreUI PRO"}
import '@coreui/coreui-pro/dist/css/coreui.min.css'
```

### Bootstrap CSS files

###### Installation

```bash
npm install bootstrap
```

###### Basic usage

```js
import 'bootstrap/dist/css/bootstrap.min.css'
```

## Important globals

CoreUI for Vue.js employs a handful of important global styles and settings that you'll need to be aware of when using it, all of which are almost exclusively geared towards the *normalization* of cross browser styles. Let's dive in.

### Responsive meta tag

CoreUI is developed *mobile first*, a strategy in which we optimize code for mobile devices first and then scale up components as necessary using CSS media queries. To ensure proper rendering and touch zooming for all devices, **add the responsive viewport meta tag** to the `<head>` of your host `index.html`.

```html
<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
```

### Box-sizing

For more straightforward sizing in CSS, we switch the global `box-sizing` value from `content-box` to `border-box`. This ensures `padding` does not affect the final computed width of an element, but it can cause problems with some third-party software like Google Maps and Google Custom Search Engine.

On the rare occasion you need to override it, use something like the following:

```css
.selector-for-some-widget {
  box-sizing: content-box;
}
```

With the above snippet, nested elements—including generated content via `::before` and `::after`—will all inherit the specified `box-sizing` for that `.selector-for-some-widget`.

Learn more about [box model and sizing at CSS Tricks](https://css-tricks.com/box-sizing/).

### Reboot

For improved cross-browser rendering, the `@coreui/coreui` stylesheet includes [Reboot](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/content/reboot/) to correct inconsistencies across browsers and devices while providing slightly more opinionated resets to common HTML elements.

## Guiding principles

Beyond what CoreUI does, here's *why* we do it — the rules we build components against:

- Components should be responsive and mobile-first
- Components should be built with a base class and extended via modifier classes
- Component states should obey a common `z-index` scale
- Prefer an HTML and CSS implementation over JavaScript
- Use utilities over custom styles
- Avoid enforcing strict HTML requirements (immediate children selectors)

These rules cannot always be followed to the letter, but we strive to follow them as much as possible.

### Responsive

Our styles are mobile-first — we add styles as the viewport grows rather than overriding them as it shrinks. Not every component has to be fully responsive, but the approach keeps the number of overrides down.

Breakpoints are written as range media queries (`width >= 768px`), so a style applies at its breakpoint and carries up through the larger ones. A `.d-none` applies from zero width upwards; `.d-md-none` applies from the medium breakpoint up.

### Classes

Aside from [Reboot](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/content/reboot/), we use classes as selectors. Type selectors and parent selectors are avoided where we can, so a component stays usable wherever you put it.

A component is built from a base class carrying the property-value pairs every variant shares — `display`, `padding`, `border-width` — and modifier classes on top of it. A button is `.btn` for the shared geometry, `.btn-solid` or `.btn-subtle` for the fill, and a `.theme-*` class for the color: `.btn.btn-solid.theme-primary`.

### z-index scales

Two `z-index` scales run through the library: one for elements inside a component, one for overlay components.

Components whose children share borders — input groups, button groups, pagination — raise the element you are interacting with above its siblings, so its border and focus ring are drawn whole instead of being clipped by the neighbor. The scale runs `1` for `:hover`, `2` for `.active`, and `3` for `:focus-visible`: focus sits highest because a focused element is the one in the user's attention, and its ring has to be fully visible.

Overlay components sit on a separate scale starting at `1000`, high enough to clear ordinary page content. Each layer steps up so that a document-blocking element lands above the chrome it blocks — a modal above a navbar, a tooltip above both.

Learn more on the [`z-index` layout page](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/layout/z-index/).

### HTML and CSS over JS

Where a behavior can be expressed in HTML and CSS, we prefer that over JavaScript — it is more accessible to people of all experience levels and faster in the browser. In Vue that shows up as components which stay declarative: state you can hand them as props, and behavior the browser already provides rather than a script re-implementing it.

Our styles build on fundamental browser behavior. You can put `.btn` on nearly any element, but we use `<button>` and `<a>` for the semantics and keyboard handling the browser already gives them. Form validation works the same way: styles ride the `:user-invalid` pseudo-class behind a `data-coreui-validate` attribute, so the browser decides when feedback appears — after the user works a control or tries to submit — instead of a script toggling a class.

### Utilities

Utility classes — single, immutable property-value pairings like `.d-block` for `display: block` — keep repeated declarations out of component CSS. They speed up authoring and cut the amount of custom CSS a project needs. We reach for them before writing a new rule.

### Code conventions

[Code Guide](https://codeguide.co/) documents how we write HTML and CSS — formatting, defaults, property order. [Stylelint](https://stylelint.io/) enforces it.

## Community

Stay up to date on the development of CoreUI and reach out to the community with these helpful resources.

- Read and subscribe to [The Official CoreUI Blog](https://coreui.io/blog/).
- Ask questions and explore [our GitHub Discussions](https://github.com/coreui/coreui/discussions).
- Discuss, ask questions, and more on [the community Discord](https://discord.gg/TsFcCgkG).

You can also follow [@core_ui on X (Twitter)](https://x.com/core_ui).

# Install

> Install CoreUI for Vue.js with a package manager, add the required peer dependencies, and import the styles from the compiled CSS or the Sass source.

## Package managers

Pull CoreUI for Vue's **source files** into nearly any project with some of the most popular package managers. The Vue components are styled by the `@coreui/coreui` or `@coreui/coreui-pro` CSS library, so install it alongside the component package. If you compile the styles from the Sass source instead of using the compiled CSS, you will **require a Sass compiler and [Autoprefixer](https://github.com/postcss/autoprefixer)** for a setup that matches our official compiled versions.

### npm

Install CoreUI for Vue in your Node.js powered apps with [the npm package](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@coreui/vue):

```sh tab={"label":"CoreUI"}
npm install @coreui/vue @coreui/coreui
```

```sh tab={"label":"CoreUI PRO"}
npm install @coreui/vue-pro @coreui/coreui-pro
```

The component packages declare `vue` (version 3.5 or newer) as a peer dependency — your project provides it, and npm will warn if it is missing:

```sh
npm install vue
```

The `@coreui/coreui` and `@coreui/coreui-pro` packages contain some additional metadata under the following keys in `package.json`:

- `sass` - path to CoreUI's main [Sass](https://sass-lang.com/) source file
- `style` - path to CoreUI's non-minified CSS that's been precompiled using the default settings (no customization)

### pnpm

Install CoreUI for Vue in your Node.js powered apps with [pnpm](https://pnpm.io/):

```sh tab={"label":"CoreUI"}
pnpm add @coreui/vue @coreui/coreui
```

```sh tab={"label":"CoreUI PRO"}
pnpm add @coreui/vue-pro @coreui/coreui-pro
```

### yarn

Install CoreUI for Vue in your Node.js powered apps with [the yarn package](https://yarnpkg.com/en/package/@coreui/vue):

```sh tab={"label":"CoreUI"}
yarn add @coreui/vue @coreui/coreui
```

```sh tab={"label":"CoreUI PRO"}
yarn add @coreui/vue-pro @coreui/coreui-pro
```

Yarn 2+ (aka Yarn Berry) doesn't support the `node_modules` directory by default, so compiling our Sass source needs some adjustments:

```sh
yarn config set nodeLinker node-modules # Use the node_modules linker
touch yarn.lock # Create an empty yarn.lock file
yarn install # Install the dependencies
```

### Bun

Install CoreUI for Vue in your Bun or Node.js powered apps with [the Bun CLI](https://bun.sh/):

```sh tab={"label":"CoreUI"}
bun add @coreui/vue @coreui/coreui
```

```sh tab={"label":"CoreUI PRO"}
bun add @coreui/vue-pro @coreui/coreui-pro
```

## Using components

```js tab={"label":"CoreUI"}
import { CAlert } from '@coreui/vue';
```

```js tab={"label":"CoreUI PRO"}
import { CAlert } from '@coreui/vue-pro';
```

## Stylesheets

Import the compiled CSS once, in your application's entry point:

```js tab={"label":"CoreUI"}
import '@coreui/coreui/dist/css/coreui.min.css'
```

```js tab={"label":"CoreUI PRO"}
import '@coreui/coreui-pro/css/base.css'
```

CoreUI for Vue PRO components import the stylesheet they render into, so the one import you make yourself is the base layer — tokens, palette and Reboot. See [per-component stylesheets](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/customize/optimize/#per-component-stylesheets) for what that means for your bundle, and for the `/unstyled` entry point if you'd rather ship `coreui.css` whole.

Or compile the styles from the Sass source to [customize](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/customize/sass/) variables, maps, and mixins along the way:

```scss tab={"label":"CoreUI"}
@use "@coreui/coreui/scss/coreui";
```

```scss tab={"label":"CoreUI PRO"}
@use "@coreui/coreui-pro/scss/coreui";
```

## Other delivery channels

CDN links, Composer, and downloadable compiled or source archives apply to the vanilla library — see [the CoreUI for Bootstrap install page](https://coreui.io/bootstrap/docs/getting-started/install/) if you need them.

## For AI tools & LLMs

Working with an LLM or an agentic coding tool? Our documentation ships in machine-readable formats — a curated [/llms.txt](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/ai-tools/llms-txt/) index, a full-text variant for direct ingestion, and an [MCP server](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/ai-tools/mcp/) that serves the docs over Model Context Protocol. See [AI Tools](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/ai-tools/llms-txt/) for setup.

# Browsers and devices

> Learn about the browsers and devices, from modern to old, that are supported by CoreUI for Vue, including known quirks and bugs for each.

## Supported browsers

CoreUI for Vue supports the **latest, stable releases** of all major browsers and platforms.

Alternative browsers which use the latest version of WebKit, Blink, or Gecko, whether directly or via the platform's web view API, are not explicitly supported. However, CoreUI for Vue should (in most cases) display and function correctly in these browsers as well. More specific support information is provided below.

The floor is set by the platform features v6 depends on, with no fallbacks
shipped: **Chrome 123, Edge 123, Firefox 130, Safari 18 and iOS 18**.
Together with the evergreen lines below, this covers about 88% of global usage
as measured with `npx browserslist --coverage`.

### Why these versions?

Each floor is set by the newest feature v6 already requires, because the floor
has to hold for the whole 6.x line:

| Feature | Sets the floor for |
| --- | --- |
| `color-mix()` hue carry-over | Safari and iOS 18 — a mix in `oklch` with an achromatic operand (`transparent`, white, black, the greys) keeps the other colour's hue only from Safari 18; 17.x interpolates the hue towards 0°, so every translucent or tinted colour comes out the wrong hue (indigo turns pink) |
| `light-dark()` | Chrome and Edge 123 — every theme decision resolves through it, and `color-mix()`, with no fallback |
| `<details name="…">` | Firefox 130 — exclusive accordions, which group their panels by `details.name` |
| `@starting-style`, `transition-behavior: allow-discrete` | Firefox 129 — the Menu's entry animation |
| `@property` | Firefox 128 — `inherits: false` on the colour and opacity utilities' custom properties |
| `:has()` | Firefox 121 — validation and focus states on Multi Select and Autocomplete, the sidebar navigation indicators, calendar ranges and the rating icons are all selected with it |

A browser below the floor does not merely lose polish. An unsupported `:has()`
invalidates the whole rule it appears in, unresolved `light-dark()` leaves
colors unset, and a Safari 17 renders the palette with rotated hues — nothing
fails, the colours are just not the ones you set. Where `details.name` reads back undefined, an exclusive accordion
stops closing its siblings and every panel can stand open at once. `@property`
is the quietest of them and the one worth knowing about: without it the
registrations are ignored, custom properties inherit again, and a colour or
opacity utility on a container tints everything nested inside it.

Versions come from MDN's browser compatibility data. Note that caniuse does not
track `@property`, `@starting-style` or `transition-behavior` at all, so
`browserslist "supports …"` cannot answer for them.

You can find our supported range of browsers and their versions [in our `.browserslistrc` file](https://github.com/coreui/coreui/blob/main/.browserslistrc):

```text
last 2 major versions
not dead
unreleased versions

Chrome >= 123
Edge >= 123
Firefox >= 130
iOS >= 18
Safari >= 18

not and_uc > 0
not and_qq > 0
not kaios > 0
not op_mini all
```

We use [Autoprefixer](https://github.com/postcss/autoprefixer) to handle intended browser support via CSS prefixes, which uses [Browserslist](https://github.com/browserslist/browserslist) to manage these browser versions. Consult their documentation for how to integrate these tools into your projects.

### How to read the query list

Two lines of that file do more than they look like they do:

- **`last 2 major versions` carries the mobile coverage.** caniuse tracks Chrome for Android as a single unversioned entry rather than one entry per release, so this line, not the `>=` floors, is what picks it up.
- **`unreleased versions` is worth several points of coverage and costs nothing.** caniuse gives the newest Safari a null release date while that version already holds most of Safari's usage share, and both range queries and `last N versions` skip unreleased versions. The line cannot pull in anything old, because an unreleased version is newer than every floor.

The `not …` exclusions drop proxy and niche browsers that cannot run the floor features anyway; keeping them in the query would only grow the compiled CSS with legacy vendor prefixes.

To measure coverage yourself, run `npx browserslist --coverage` in a clone of the repository.

## Modern platform features

The floor table above names what *sets* each floor; this is the fuller inventory of platform features v6 leans on:

| Feature | Used by |
| --- | --- |
| `light-dark()`, `color-mix()`, `oklch()` | every color in the library — theme tokens, color modes, translucent variants |
| Cascade layers (`@layer`) | the whole stylesheet ships in a fixed layer order, so your own unlayered CSS always wins |
| `:has()` | validation and focus states on field components, button groups, sidebar indicators, calendar ranges, rating |
| `@property` | `inherits: false` registrations that keep the color and opacity utilities from leaking into descendants |
| `@starting-style` + `transition-behavior: allow-discrete` | entry and exit animations on Menu, Dialog, Drawer, Modal, Offcanvas, Popover, Tooltip, Toasts and Alerts |
| Native `<dialog>` | Dialog and Drawer — the top layer, `::backdrop` and focus containment come from the browser |
| `<details name="…">` | exclusive accordions |
| Container queries (`@container`) | stacked tables, horizontal list groups, card groups and stacks respond to their container, not the viewport |
| Relative color syntax (`oklch(from …)`) | theme hover and active states derive from the base color at runtime |
| Logical properties | spacing, borders and RTL support throughout — there is no separate RTL stylesheet |
| Range syntax in media queries | every breakpoint compiles to `@media (width >= …)` |

### Also safe to use

The floors clear more of the platform than the library currently uses. Everything below needs no fallback, no vendor prefix, and no polyfill anywhere in the supported range, so reach for it freely when you build on top of CoreUI:

- Native CSS nesting (Chrome 120, Firefox 117, Safari 17.2)
- `text-wrap: balance` (Chrome 114, Firefox 121, Safari 17.5)
- `:focus-visible` for keyboard-only focus styling
- Container query units and `subgrid`
- Dynamic viewport units (`dvh`, `dvw`) — the library itself sizes scrollable menus with `dvh`
- The `popover` attribute (Chrome 114, Firefox 125, Safari 17)

Versions come from MDN's browser compatibility data, same as the floor table.

### Not available yet

These sit above at least one of our floors, so v6 cannot rely on them without a fallback — and neither should you if you target the same range. With Safari at 18, **Firefox is now the blocker most of the time**:

| Feature | First fully supported in |
| --- | --- |
| `interpolate-size` / `calc-size()` | Chrome 129, no Firefox or Safari yet |
| View transitions | Chrome 111, Firefox 144, Safari 18 |
| Anchor positioning | Chrome 125, Firefox 147, Safari 26 |
| Style container queries | Chrome 111, Firefox 151, Safari 18 |
| `@scope` | Chrome 118, Firefox 146, Safari 26.4 |
| Invoker Commands API (`command` / `commandfor`) | Chrome 135, Firefox 144, Safari 26.2 |
| Scrollbar styling (`scrollbar-color`) | Chrome 121, Firefox 64, Safari 26.2 |
| `text-box-trim` | Chrome 133, Firefox 154, Safari 18.2 |

One of these the library already touches, carefully: `interpolate-size` sits behind `@supports`, so accordions and collapses animate to their intrinsic height where it exists and jump without it. Unprefixed `backdrop-filter`, `content-visibility` and relative color syntax with number channel values landed in Safari 18 and are inside the floor now. Anchor positioning is the one most worth waiting for — it would let Menu, Tooltip, Popover and Combobox drop their [Floating UI](https://floating-ui.com/) dependency. Re-check these before you assume one has landed.

## JavaScript

Every browser meeting the CSS floor above fully supports the DOM APIs our components use — no transpilation or polyfills are required or provided. The `@coreui/vue` and `@coreui/vue-pro` packages ship both ES module and CommonJS builds, so any modern bundler consumes them as-is.

## Mobile devices

Generally speaking, CoreUI for Vue supports the latest versions of each major platform's default browsers. Proxy browsers (such as Opera Mini, Opera Mobile's Turbo mode, UC Browser Mini, Amazon Silk) are not supported.

| Platform | Supported browsers |
| --- | --- |
| Android | Chrome (last two major versions) |
| iOS and iPadOS | Safari 18+, Chrome (uses WebKit on iOS) |
| Windows, macOS, Linux | Chrome 123+, Edge 123+, Firefox 130+; Safari 18+ on macOS |

For Firefox, in addition to the latest normal stable release, we also support the latest [Extended Support Release (ESR)](https://www.mozilla.org/en-US/firefox/enterprise/) version of Firefox.

As always, make sure you include the responsive viewport meta tag in your `<head>` for proper rendering on mobile devices:

```html
<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
```

## Internet Explorer

Internet Explorer is not supported. **If you require Internet Explorer support, please use CoreUI v3.** If you need the previous browser floors (Chrome 60+, Safari 12+), stay on CoreUI v5.

# RTL

> Learn how to enable support for right-to-left text in CoreUI for Vue across our layout, components, and utilities.

## Get familiar

We recommend getting familiar with CoreUI for Vue first by reading through our [Getting Started Introduction page](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/getting-started/introduction/). Once you've run through it, continue reading here for how to enable RTL.

## Required HTML

There are two strict requirements for enabling RTL in CoreUI-powered pages.

1. Set `dir="rtl"` on the `<html>` element.
2. Add an appropriate `lang` attribute, like `lang="ar"`, on the `<html>` element.

That is all. **There is no separate RTL stylesheet any more** — the compiled CSS
carries both directions, so the same file you already import reacts to
`dir="rtl"`.

In a Vue app both attributes live on the host document — the `index.html`
your bundler serves, or your framework's document template (for example
Nuxt's `app.head` configuration). The stylesheet stays the one you already

### Starter template

You can see the above requirements reflected in this modified RTL host `index.html`.

```html
<!doctype html>
<html lang="ar" dir="rtl">
  <head>
    <meta charset="utf-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
    <title>مرحبا بالعالم!</title>
  </head>
  <body>
    <div id="app"></div>
    <script type="module" src="/src/main.js"></script>
  </body>
</html>
```

## Components

The Vue components need no RTL configuration. Components that position or
navigate directionally — dropdowns, tooltips, popovers, the menu, the carousel,
the date, time and range pickers, the range slider, the one-time password
input — detect the direction from the document at runtime: `dir="rtl"` on the
`<html>` element, or on the closest ancestor with a `dir="rtl"` attribute for
a right-to-left region inside a left-to-right page.

## Approach

Direction support rests on two decisions:

1. **Layout is written with logical properties.** `margin-inline-start` instead
   of `margin-left`, `inset-inline-end` instead of `right`, `float: inline-start`
   instead of `float: left` — and the same in the class names, so `.ms-4` and
   `.start-50` mean "start" in whichever direction the document runs. The
   browser mirrors them; nothing has to be generated twice.

2. **The handful of properties CSS cannot mirror get an explicit rule.**
   `transform` is not direction-aware, `background-position` has no logical
   keyword, and swapping an icon means swapping an asset. Those cases — the
   off-canvas panel, the range slider's label and tooltip, the select and
   validation arrows, the carousel controls, the breadcrumb divider, the
   narrow sidebar's toggler — are written once with the `ltr-rtl()` mixin,
   which emits the base declaration plus a `:dir(rtl)` override. There are
   about twenty of them in the whole library. The override reads the element's
   own direction, the same thing a logical property resolves against, so an
   off-canvas panel inside a `dir="ltr"` island of a right-to-left page slides
   out the side it is pinned to. Both of them follow the `dir` attribute:
   setting `direction` from CSS alone turns the logical properties around and
   leaves the mirrored declarations where they were, so put `dir` on the
   element or on one of its ancestors.

Together that is why **one stylesheet serves both directions**. Up to v5 we
published a parallel `*.rtl.css` for every file; it is gone, and so is the
`.rtl` half of the `dist/css` folder.

## Customize from source

When it comes to [customization](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/customize/sass/), the preferred way is to take advantage of variables, maps, and mixins.

### LTR only

The RTL overrides are a couple of dozen rules, but if a project is
left-to-right for good you can drop them:

```scss tab={"label":"CoreUI"}
@use "@coreui/coreui/scss/coreui" with (
  $enable-rtl: false
);
```

```scss tab={"label":"CoreUI PRO"}
@use "@coreui/coreui-pro/scss/coreui" with (
  $enable-rtl: false
);
```

### RTL only

The mirror image: the mirrored values become the base declarations and no
`:dir(rtl)` selector is emitted at all. Use it when the whole application is
right-to-left.

```scss tab={"label":"CoreUI"}
@use "@coreui/coreui/scss/coreui" with (
  $enable-ltr: false,
  $enable-rtl: true
);
```

```scss tab={"label":"CoreUI PRO"}
@use "@coreui/coreui-pro/scss/coreui" with (
  $enable-ltr: false,
  $enable-rtl: true
);
```

## Additional resources

- [RTL Styling 101](https://rtlstyling.com/posts/rtl-styling)

# Accessibility

> The accessibility standards CoreUI for Vue targets, what its components take care of, what stays with your markup, and how we test it.

CoreUI for Vue provides an easy-to-use framework of ready-made styles, layout tools, and interactive components, allowing developers to create websites and applications that are visually appealing, functionally rich, and accessible out of the box.

## Standards

The components target [<abbr title="Web Content Accessibility Guidelines">WCAG</abbr> 2.2](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/) level AA, the level that [Section 508](https://www.section508.gov/) in the United States and EN 301 549 in the European Union build on. Interactive components use [<abbr title="Web Accessibility Initiative">WAI</abbr>-<abbr title="Accessible Rich Internet Applications">ARIA</abbr>](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/aria/) roles, states and properties, and follow the keyboard models of the [ARIA Authoring Practices Guide](https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/).

Conformance belongs to a page, not to a library: WCAG judges the page a user meets, with its content, labels, colors and flow. The [compliance](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/accessibility/compliance/) page lists, for each tested component, which success criteria it meets on its own, which it covers in part, and which your markup has to meet.

## What the components take care of

- **Roles, states and properties.** A component writes its roles and `aria-*` states from its props and keeps them in sync while it renders: `aria-expanded` on a toggle, `aria-selected` on an option, `aria-invalid` on a field in an invalid state.
- **Keyboard.** Interactive components are operated with the keyboard as well as with a pointer. The [keyboard](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/accessibility/keyboard/) page covers the shared conventions and links each component's own key table.
- **Focus.** Dialogs and pickers move focus in when they open, keep it inside while they are modal, and give it back when they close. A menu leaves focus on its toggle until the arrow keys move it to the items.
- **Status messages.** Changes the page shows without moving focus, such as a toast, a loading button or a chip being added, reach screen readers through [`announce()`](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/accessibility/screen-readers/#announcing-messages).
- **Motion.** Transitions respect the user's [reduced motion](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/accessibility/reduced-motion/) preference.

## What stays with your markup

- **Names.** Give every control a visible `<label>`, or an `aria-label` where there is no room for one. Components that render controls of their own take their texts from props named `aria…Label`, which you translate along with the rest of the page.
- **Text alternatives.** Images, icons that carry meaning and charts need a text alternative; decorative ones need `alt=""` or `aria-hidden="true"`.
- **Structure.** Headings, landmarks and lists come from your markup. The components work on a wide range of structures, so they cannot add them for you.
- **Color.** Check the [contrast](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/accessibility/color-contrast/) of the colors you use, especially custom theme colors.
- **Content and timing.** Clear link and button texts, error messages that say how to fix the input, and time limits long enough to finish a task.

### Structural markup

CoreUI for Vue styling and layout can be applied to a wide range of markup structures. This documentation aims to provide developers with best practice examples to demonstrate the use of CoreUI for Vue itself and illustrate appropriate semantic markup, including ways in which potential accessibility concerns can be addressed.

### Interactive components

CoreUI for Vue interactive components—such as modal dialogs, dropdown menus, and custom tooltips—are designed to work for touch, mouse, and keyboard users. Through the use of relevant <abbr title="Web Accessibility Initiative">WAI</abbr>-<abbr title="Accessible Rich Internet Applications">ARIA</abbr> roles and attributes, these components should also be understandable and operable using assistive technologies (such as screen readers).

Because CoreUI for Vue components are purposely designed to be fairly generic, authors may need to include further <abbr title="Accessible Rich Internet Applications">ARIA</abbr> roles and attributes, as well as JavaScript behavior, to more accurately convey the precise nature and functionality of their component. This is noted in the Accessibility section of each component's page.

### Visually hidden content

Content which should be visually hidden, but remain accessible to assistive technologies such as screen readers, can be styled using the `.visually-hidden` class. This can be useful in situations where additional visual information or cues (such as meaning denoted through the use of color) need to also be conveyed to non-visual users.

```html
<p class="fg-danger">
  <span class="visually-hidden">Danger: </span>
  This action is not reversible
</p>
```

For visually hidden interactive controls, such as traditional "skip" links, use the `.visually-hidden-focusable` class. This will ensure that the control becomes visible once focused (for sighted keyboard users). **Watch out, compared to the equivalent `.sr-only` and `.sr-only-focusable` classes in past versions, CoreUI's `.visually-hidden-focusable` is a standalone class, and must not be used in combination with the `.visually-hidden` class.**

```html
<a class="visually-hidden-focusable" href="#content">Skip to main content</a>
```

More in the [visually hidden helper](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/helpers/visually-hidden/).

## How we test

- **Automated conformance suite.** On every change, the documented examples of the vanilla JavaScript components, whose markup, roles and keyboard models these components follow, are rendered in Chromium and checked with [axe-core](https://github.com/dequelabs/axe-core) and scripted keyboard and focus steps. The suite does not run on the Vue components yet; the [compliance](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/accessibility/compliance/) page says what that means.
- **Unit tests.** The specs of each component cover its keyboard handling, focus management and the ARIA states it writes.
- **Screen readers.** We test announcements and component behavior with screen readers by hand. The [screen readers](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/accessibility/screen-readers/) page lists what has been measured.

## Additional resources

# Compliance

> How the accessibility of CoreUI for Vue components is checked, and where each component documents its own.

The automated conformance suite runs on the vanilla JavaScript components. On every change it renders their documented examples in Chromium, checks the WCAG 2.2 success criteria each component claims with [axe-core](https://github.com/dequelabs/axe-core) where a rule exists, and with scripted keyboard and focus steps where it does not. The Vue components follow the markup, roles and keyboard models of the vanilla ones, but the suite does not run on them yet, so this page lists no results for them.

Conformance is a property of a whole page. A component keeps its accessibility only with the markup and texts its documentation asks for. See the [overview](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/accessibility/overview/) for what the components take care of and what stays with your markup.

## Components

Each of these components documents its roles, states, keyboard and what your markup has to add:

# Keyboard

> The keyboard conventions CoreUI for Vue components share, and an index of each component's keyboard table.

Interactive components are built to be operated with the keyboard alone. The components follow the keyboard models of the [ARIA Authoring Practices Guide](https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/), so a user who knows how a native control or another accessible widget behaves can predict how ours behave.

## Conventions

| Key | Action |
| --- | --- |
| <kbd>Tab</kbd> / <kbd>Shift</kbd> + <kbd>Tab</kbd> | Move to the next or previous component. A composite component, such as tabs, a chip set, a list box or a calendar grid, is a single stop; the arrow keys move inside it. |
| <kbd>Arrow</kbd> keys | Move between the items of a composite component: tabs, options, chips, days. In an open menu, move focus to the items and between them. |
| <kbd>Home</kbd> / <kbd>End</kbd> | Move to the first or last item, where the component has a list of them. |
| <kbd>Enter</kbd> / <kbd>Space</kbd> | Activate the focused button, link or item, select an option, or open a popup. |
| <kbd>Escape</kbd> | Close the open menu, picker panel, tooltip, popover or dialog. Dropdowns, pickers and dialogs return focus to the element that opened them. The `v-c-tooltip` and `v-c-popover` directives do not handle <kbd>Escape</kbd>; use the `<CTooltip>` and `<CPopover>` components where it matters. |

Where a component differs, its own keyboard table says so.

## Focus in dialogs

A modal dialog, such as the [modal](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/components/modal/) or the [offcanvas](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/components/offcanvas/), moves focus inside when it opens and keeps <kbd>Tab</kbd> inside while it is open. When it closes, focus returns to the element that opened it. An offcanvas opened with `backdrop: false` and `scroll: true` is not modal: <kbd>Tab</kbd> moves on to the page.

## Visible focus

The element that has focus always shows it. Buttons and other controls you click to act show the focus ring only for keyboard focus, so a mouse click does not leave one behind; fields you type into show it on any focus. See [color contrast](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/accessibility/color-contrast/#focus-indicators) for its contrast.

# Screen readers

> How CoreUI for Vue components reach screen readers, how to announce status messages with announce(), and which screen readers they have been measured with.

A screen reader reads what the browser exposes in its accessibility tree: each element's role, name, state and value. CoreUI for Vue components write those from their props, so a screen reader hears a combobox that is expanded, an option that is selected, or a field that is invalid, without extra markup from the page. The Accessibility section of each component's page lists what the component exposes and what the page has to add, usually a name.

## Measured with

Behavior a screen reader decides is measured by hand, with the screen reader running. The table lists what has been measured so far; the [compliance](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/accessibility/compliance/) page covers what is checked automatically.

| Screen reader | Browser | Platform | Measured |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| VoiceOver | Safari 17.6 | macOS 14.8 | Status messages from `announce()`, the same function in every edition: messages sent together, both regions at once, a page still loading, open dialogs and the wait after a dialog closes, measured with the vanilla JavaScript Toaster and Modal. The loading button in the Vue edition |
| VoiceOver | Chrome 154 | macOS 14.8 | The same cases |
| VoiceOver | Firefox 157 | macOS 14.8 | The wait after a dialog closes, with the vanilla JavaScript Modal |

Results for other screen readers are added to this table once measured.

## Announcing messages

`announce()` reads a short message to screen reader users without moving focus, for a change the page shows but does not focus, such as a saved form or a filtered list. The toaster store announces the text of every toast through it, whether or not a `<CToaster>` shows the toast.

```js
import { announce } from '@coreui/vue-pro'

announce('3 results')
announce('The connection was lost', { priority: 'high' })
```

Call it from an event handler or a watcher, never from a render function or a computed property: each of those can run more than once, and every call is a message.

Messages go through live regions in every browser: `role="log"` with `aria-live` lets assistive technology tell them apart as status messages, as [WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 4.1.3 Status Messages](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/status-messages.html) asks. The options follow [`ariaNotify()`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Document/ariaNotify) from WAI-ARIA 1.3, which `announce()` does not call yet: Chromium's source shows Chrome exposing it on ChromeOS and Android without passing it to ChromeVox or TalkBack, and the screen readers on Windows have not been measured with it.

The first call adds a visually hidden live region at the start of `<body>`. Every call adds a message of its own to it one task later, or 100 ms after a new region was created, so messages sent together each get read, in the order they were sent, and the same text is read again. Messages that are added together, those sent in one task and those that a wait releases at once (the first 100 ms of a region, or one of the waits below), go to the assertive region of their page or dialog when one of them is `'high'`, the `'high'` ones first: with one message in each of the two regions, VoiceOver in Safari read only one of them. While a modal dialog is open the rest of the page is inert and screen readers ignore it, so the message goes to a region inside the dialog instead: the one holding focus, then the one around `context`, then the last one open in the document. A modal dialog is a native `<dialog>` opened with `showModal()`, or a shown element with `aria-modal="true"`, such as the panel of a date picker, whose region leaves with it when the panel is removed. The dialog is picked when the message is added, so one opened right after the call still gets it, and its region leaves with it when it closes. A modal built without a native modal dialog, which hides the rest of the page with `aria-hidden` or `inert`, hides these regions as well.

Messages wait while the modal dialog they would go to, or the dialog holding focus, plays its closing transition, and until half a second after Modal, Offcanvas, Dialog or Drawer has closed its dialog. When a modal dialog closes, the rest of the page comes back to screen readers, and VoiceOver dropped a message added at that moment in Chrome, Safari and Firefox. With the wait, VoiceOver in Chrome and Firefox read a toast sent once the vanilla JavaScript Modal had closed or during its closing transition, and the Vue modal waits the same way, which has not been measured with a screen reader; after a dialog opened without a button to return to, focus fell to the page and Chrome still skipped it. A `<dialog>` the page opens and closes itself is not waited for, so send a message meant for the page about half a second after closing it. A message added to a dialog right before it starts closing is lost with it. Safari also skipped a message sent while the page was still loading, and read one sent a second later.

| Option | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `context` | element | `null` | The element the message comes from. When focus is in no modal dialog, the dialog around it gets the message, which is how a dialog inside a shadow root, where the page cannot look, is found. |
| `priority` | `'normal'` \| `'high'` | `'normal'` | `'normal'` adds the message to the polite region, which waits until the screen reader is idle, unless it is added together with a `'high'` one; `'high'` adds it to the assertive region, which interrupts; keep it for the few messages that cannot wait. Some screen readers read both as polite. |
| `timeout` | number | `7000` | Time (ms) the message stays in the region once added; `0` keeps it until it is removed. |

`announce()` returns a function that removes the message, or cancels it before it is added, for a status that a newer one replaces. It is the function `@coreui/coreui-pro` exports, so Vue components and vanilla plugins on one page add to the same regions, each copy with its own queue, and a dialog holds only the queue of the copy it comes with.

# Color contrast

> Contrast requirements for text, controls and focus indicators, and how to keep the CoreUI for Vue palette and themes within them.

WCAG asks for a [contrast ratio of 4.5:1 for text](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/contrast-minimum.html) (3:1 for large text), and 3:1 for the parts of a control and the graphics a user needs to see, such as a field's border, a checkbox or a focus indicator ([non-text contrast](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/non-text-contrast.html)).

## Default palette

Some combinations of colors that currently make up CoreUI's default palette—used throughout the framework for things such as button variations, alert variations, form validation indicators—may lead to *insufficient* color contrast (below the recommended [WCAG 2.2 text color contrast ratio of 4.5:1](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#contrast-minimum) and the [WCAG 2.2 non-text color contrast ratio of 3:1](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#non-text-contrast)), particularly when used against a light background. Authors are encouraged to test their specific uses of color and, where necessary, manually modify/extend these default colors to ensure adequate color contrast ratios.

The [color](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/customize/color/#all-colors) page shows the contrast ratio of each palette color against white and black.

## Theme colors

Each theme color comes as a family of slots, and every foreground slot is tuned against one background slot: `contrast` on `bg`, `fg` on `bg-subtle`, `fg-emphasis` on `bg-muted`. Components pair them that way. When you build your own surfaces, use the same [pairings](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/customize/theme/#pairings); a foreground read against another background is where contrast falls apart. When you add a theme color or change one, check every pairing again, in both [color modes](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/customize/color-modes/).

Fading a color lowers its contrast as well: the [link opacity](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/utilities/link/#link-opacity) and [opacity](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/utilities/opacity/) utilities can take a link or a text below 4.5:1.

## Focus indicators

Focusable components draw a focus ring from the `--cui-focus-ring-*` tokens, in the color of their theme. Controls you click to act, such as buttons, checkboxes and pagination links, show it on keyboard focus; fields you type into show it on any focus. If you change the ring's color, width or offset, keep it at 3:1 against the colors around it. The [focus ring](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/helpers/focus-ring/) helper gives your own elements the same ring.

## Color alone

Color must not be the only way a meaning is conveyed ([use of color](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/use-of-color.html)). A red border on an invalid field needs a message that says what is wrong, a danger alert needs words that say it is one, and a link inside a paragraph needs an underline or another cue besides its color. Where the text cannot carry it, add it with [visually hidden content](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/accessibility/overview/#visually-hidden-content).


---

# Reduced motion

> How CoreUI for Vue honours the prefers-reduced-motion setting in its transitions, animations and scrolling.

CoreUI for Vue includes support for the [`prefers-reduced-motion` media feature](https://www.w3.org/TR/mediaqueries-5/#prefers-reduced-motion). In browsers/environments that allow the user to specify their preference for reduced motion, most CSS transition effects in CoreUI for Vue (for instance, when a modal dialog is opened or closed, or the sliding animation in carousels) will be disabled, and meaningful animations (such as spinners) will be slowed down.

On browsers that support `prefers-reduced-motion`, and where the user has *not* explicitly signaled that they'd prefer reduced motion (i.e. where `prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference`), CoreUI for Vue enables smooth scrolling using the `scroll-behavior` property.

## Options

| Variable | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `$enable-reduced-motion` | `true` | Wraps every component transition in `prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference`, so the transition runs only for users who have not asked for less motion. |
| `$enable-smooth-scroll` | `true` | Applies `scroll-behavior: smooth`, except for users asking for reduced motion. |

See [options](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/customize/options/) for the other global switches, and [transitions](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/customize/transitions/) for how components run their transitions.

## Your own animations

Wrap the animations and transitions you add in the same query, so they run only for users who have not asked for less motion:

```css
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) {
  .banner {
    animation: slide-in .3s ease-out;
  }
}
```

An animation that starts by itself and lasts longer than five seconds also needs a way to pause or stop it ([pause, stop, hide](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/pause-stop-hide.html)), whatever the user's setting. The [carousel](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/components/carousel/) has one.

# LLMs.txt

> LLM-optimized documentation endpoints for CoreUI for Vue — llms.txt, llms-full.txt, and a Markdown version of every page.

## Introduction

[llms.txt](https://llmstxt.org) is an emerging standard that helps AI models understand and navigate documentation. The CoreUI for Vue docs expose three LLM-friendly endpoints so assistants can retrieve accurate, up-to-date content straight from the source.

For a richer, tool-based integration, see [MCP Server](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/ai-tools/mcp/).

## /llms.txt

A structured index of the documentation — every page as a titled, described link, grouped by section. It gives an LLM a compact map of what exists and where.

[Open llms.txt](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/llms.txt)

## /llms-full.txt

The entire documentation concatenated into a single Markdown file, so a model can ingest the whole set in one request.

[Open llms-full.txt](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/llms-full.txt)

## Markdown version of any page

Append `.md` to any documentation page URL to get its clean Markdown version, without the site chrome.

For example: [/vue/docs/components/accordion.md](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/components/accordion.md)

# MCP Server

> Bring the CoreUI for Vue documentation into your AI coding assistant with the @coreui/docs-mcp Model Context Protocol server.

## Introduction

[Model Context Protocol (MCP)](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) is an open standard that lets AI assistants connect to external tools and data sources. The **`@coreui/docs-mcp`** server gives your assistant direct access to the official CoreUI documentation, so it answers from the current docs instead of relying on stale training data.

It provides:

- **Component documentation** — pages, props, events, and slots.
- **Live content** — read on demand from `coreui.io`, always matching the latest release.
- **Cross-framework links** — where each component is documented for Angular, Bootstrap, React, and Vue.
- **Coverage of Angular, Bootstrap, React, and Vue** from a single server.

The server runs locally over stdio via `npx` — no global install required.

## Installation

### Claude Code

Add the server with the CLI, then start a new session and run `/mcp` to verify the connection:

```bash
claude mcp add coreui-docs -s user -- npx -y @coreui/docs-mcp --framework vue
```

### Cursor

Create `.cursor/mcp.json` in your project (or `~/.cursor/mcp.json` for global configuration):

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "coreui-docs": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "@coreui/docs-mcp", "--framework", "vue"]
    }
  }
}
```

### VS Code

Create `.vscode/mcp.json` in your project. Note that VS Code uses the `servers` key:

```json
{
  "servers": {
    "coreui-docs": {
      "type": "stdio",
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "@coreui/docs-mcp", "--framework", "vue"]
    }
  }
}
```

### Windsurf

Edit `~/.codeium/windsurf/mcp_config.json`:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "coreui-docs": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "@coreui/docs-mcp", "--framework", "vue"]
    }
  }
}
```

### Claude Desktop

Edit `claude_desktop_config.json` (Settings → Developer → Edit Config):

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "coreui-docs": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "@coreui/docs-mcp", "--framework", "vue"]
    }
  }
}
```

### OpenAI Codex

Add it with the CLI, or edit `~/.codex/config.toml` directly:

```bash
codex mcp add coreui-docs -- npx -y @coreui/docs-mcp --framework vue
```

```toml
[mcp_servers.coreui-docs]
command = "npx"
args = ["-y", "@coreui/docs-mcp", "--framework", "vue"]
```

## Tools

Once connected, your assistant can call the following tools:

| Tool | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `list_components` | List documentation pages, optionally filtered by section or a substring. |
| `search_docs` | Search the documentation and return the best matching pages. |
| `get_doc_page` | Fetch the full Markdown of a page by slug, component name, or URL. |
| `get_component_api` | Get the structured API (props, events, slots) for a component. |
| `get_cross_framework_links` | Get documentation URLs for a component across every CoreUI framework. |

## Configuration

| Flag | Environment variable | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--framework <list>` | `COREUI_DOCS_FRAMEWORKS` | `angular,bootstrap,react,vue` | Enabled editions (comma-separated). The first is the default for tools. |
| `--base-url <url>` | `COREUI_DOCS_BASE_URL` | `https://coreui.io` | Origin of the CoreUI site. The `/<framework>/docs` path is appended automatically — override only for a staging or self-hosted mirror. |
| `--ttl <minutes>` | `COREUI_DOCS_TTL_MINUTES` | `360` | Cache freshness window. |
| — | `COREUI_DOCS_CACHE_DIR` | OS cache directory | On-disk cache location. |

## Example prompts

Once installed, try asking your AI assistant:

- "How do I use the CoreUI Vue Multi Select component?"
- "What props does the CoreUI Vue Date Picker accept?"
- "Show me the CoreUI Vue Modal documentation."
- "Where is the Accordion documented across CoreUI frameworks?"

The package is open source and published as [`@coreui/docs-mcp`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@coreui/docs-mcp).

# Agent Skills

> Step-by-step playbooks that teach AI coding agents to install CoreUI for Vue and migrate to v6, shipped in the @coreui/vue-pro package.

## Introduction

Agent skills are `SKILL.md` files in the [Agent Skills](https://skills.sh) format. Each one is a focused playbook for one task: installing CoreUI for Vue, or migrating a project to v6. The skill's `description` tells your agent when it applies, and its steps keep the agent on the documented path instead of on stale training data.

The skills ship inside the `@coreui/vue-pro` npm package, in its `skills/` folder, so they always match the version you installed. The [MCP Server](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/ai-tools/mcp/) and [LLMs.txt](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/ai-tools/llms-txt/) answer questions about the docs; the skills walk an agent through a whole change. Always review an agent's changes against the matching documentation page.

## Install

Sync the skills from the packages your project already depends on:

```sh
npm install -D skills
npx skills experimental_sync -y
```

The [Skills CLI](https://www.npmjs.com/package/skills) scans your dependencies, finds the `skills/` folder in `@coreui/vue-pro` and links each skill into your agent, so the skills update with the package. The sync command is marked experimental by the CLI.

`@coreui/vue-pro` also points the CLI at the skills of `@coreui/coreui-pro`, which it installs as a dependency. They cover the stylesheet side: `coreui-theme-colors` (theme colors, brand themes, color modes), `coreui-v6-install` (Sass builds), `coreui-v5-v6-migration` and `coreui-v4-v5-migration` (classes, Sass and tokens), `coreui-utility-api`, `coreui-component` and `coreui-from-bootstrap`.

To use one skill without the CLI, point your agent at its file, for example `node_modules/@coreui/vue-pro/skills/coreui-vue-v6-install/SKILL.md`, and describe what you want to do.

## Skills

| Skill | Use it when | Guide |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `coreui-vue-v6-install` | Adding CoreUI for Vue to a project and setting up its styles, the unstyled entry, color modes and the build. | [Install](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/getting-started/install/) |
| `coreui-vue-v5-v6-migration` | Upgrading a project from `@coreui/vue-pro` 5.x to 6.x: dependencies, stylesheets, components, props and events. | [Migration to v6](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/migration/v6/) |
| `coreui-vue-v4-v6-migration` | Upgrading a `@coreui/vue-pro` 4.x project straight to 6.x: the 4.x to 5.x changes first, then the 5.x to 6.x skill, with the props that change twice. | [Migration to v6](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/migration/v6/) |
| `coreui-vue-v4-v5-migration` | Upgrading a project from `@coreui/vue-pro` 4.x to 5.x: dependencies, renamed components and props, events and callbacks. | [Migration to v5](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/migration/v5/) |

# CoreUI + Vue + Nuxt

> Learn how to use CoreUI for Vue.js components in your Nuxt project.

This guide walks you through adding CoreUI for Vue.js to a Nuxt project.

## Create a project

Scaffold a new Nuxt application with the official command and answer the prompts.

```sh
npm create nuxt@latest my-app
cd my-app
```

## Install CoreUI

Install the Vue components together with the CSS library that styles them.

```bash tab={"label":"CoreUI"}
npm install @coreui/vue @coreui/coreui
```

```bash tab={"label":"CoreUI PRO"}
npm install @coreui/vue-pro @coreui/coreui-pro
```

## Import styles

Add the stylesheet to `nuxt.config.ts` so it loads for every route.

```ts tab={"label":"CoreUI"}
export default defineNuxtConfig({
  css: ['@coreui/coreui/dist/css/coreui.min.css'],
})
```

```ts tab={"label":"CoreUI PRO"}
export default defineNuxtConfig({
  css: ['@coreui/coreui-pro/dist/css/coreui.min.css'],
})
```

## Use components

Render your first CoreUI component in `app/app.vue`.

```vue tab={"label":"CoreUI"}
<template>
  <CButton theme="primary">Primary button</CButton>
</template>

<script setup lang="ts">
import { CButton } from '@coreui/vue'
</script>
```

```vue tab={"label":"CoreUI PRO"}
<template>
  <CButton theme="primary">Primary button</CButton>
</template>

<script setup lang="ts">
import { CButton } from '@coreui/vue-pro'
</script>
```

Start the development server and open `http://localhost:3000` to see the button rendered with CoreUI's styles.

```sh
npm run dev
```

> The components render on the server as they are: every read of window or document is guarded, and the ids they generate come from Vue's useId(), which produces the same value on both sides of hydration. Reach for &lt;ClientOnly&gt; when your own code around them needs the DOM, not for the components themselves.

# CoreUI & Tailwind CSS

> How to run CoreUI for Vue components next to Tailwind's utilities: one cascade layer order, no second reset, and Tailwind reading our design tokens.

## Two libraries, one cascade

CoreUI ships its utilities as a separate stylesheet, so a project that prefers Tailwind's utilities can leave ours out entirely and keep the components. What has to be agreed between the two is the cascade: both libraries put their rules in named `@layer`s, and two of the names are the same.

CoreUI declares:

```css
@layer colors, config, root, reboot, layout, content, forms, components, custom, helpers, utilities;
```

Tailwind 4 declares:

```css
@layer theme, base, components, utilities;
```

Layers with the same name are one layer, and the browser fixes the order of every layer at its **first** mention. Import Tailwind first and CoreUI's `root`, `reboot` and `forms` land after Tailwind's `utilities`, so a `.p-4` loses to Reboot. Import CoreUI first and Tailwind's `base` — its reset, Preflight — lands after our `forms` and `utilities`, and undoes them on every element it touches. Neither order works on its own.

The fix is one line, written by you, before either stylesheet: a single `@layer` statement that interleaves the two lists. The shared `components` and `utilities` names merge, which is what you want — Tailwind's `@utility` additions sit in the same layer as ours, and your `@layer components` in the same layer as our components.

```css
/* app.css */
@layer theme, base, colors, config, root, reboot, layout, content, forms, components, custom, helpers, utilities;

@import "tailwindcss/theme.css" layer(theme);
@import "tailwindcss/utilities.css" layer(utilities);

@import "@coreui/coreui-pro/css/base.css";
```

The component stylesheets are not listed: every component [imports its own](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/customize/optimize/#per-component-stylesheets) when it is imported, and each of those files opens with CoreUI's `@layer` declaration. That is why `app.css` has to be the **first** stylesheet the bundler meets — before any component import — so that the interleaved order is the one that sticks:

```ts
// main.ts
import './app.css'
import { CButton } from '@coreui/vue-pro'
```

Two decisions are baked into `app.css`:

- **One reset, not two.** `@import "tailwindcss"` also brings Preflight; the two explicit imports above bring Tailwind's theme and utilities and leave the reset out, because `base.css` already carries [Reboot](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/content/reboot/). Two resets on one page never agree on form controls and headings.
- **CoreUI's utilities stay out.** `coreui-utilities.css` is not imported. Nothing in a component depends on it, so the components render the same. If you do want both sets, import ours too — they share the `utilities` layer, and the later file wins on a name both define. That includes the numbered spacing classes: `p-4` is `.75rem` in CoreUI and `1rem` in Tailwind, and only steps `0`, `1` and `12` give the same value in both.

## Class names both libraries use

Sixty-odd class names exist in both utility sets — `flex`, `border`, `shadow`, `rounded`, `p-1`, `text-center` — which stops mattering the moment our utilities are not loaded. Four names are CoreUI **component or layout** classes that Tailwind also defines as utilities:

| Class | CoreUI | Tailwind |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `.grid` | the [CSS grid](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/layout/css-grid/) container: twelve columns and a gap | `display: grid` |
| `.container` | the [responsive container](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/layout/containers/) with its max-widths | a max-width container of its own |
| `.table` | the [table](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/components/table/) component | `display: table` |
| `.collapse` | the [collapse](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/components/collapse/) component | `border-collapse: collapse` |

`.table` and `.collapse` are harmless — Tailwind's declaration is one the component already carries. `.grid` and `.container` are not: writing Tailwind's `grid` on an element gives it our twelve-column template and gutter. Either leave `layout/grid.css` and `layout/containers.css` out when you use Tailwind's, or give Tailwind a prefix so its classes cannot meet ours (the `layout/grid.css` file is what `CRow`/`CCol` import, so the prefix is the way when you use those):

```css
@import "tailwindcss/theme.css" layer(theme) prefix(tw);
@import "tailwindcss/utilities.css" layer(utilities) prefix(tw);
```

Tailwind's classes are then written `tw:grid`, `tw:p-4`, and no name is shared.

## Tailwind reading CoreUI's tokens

Tailwind's utilities take their values from its `@theme` block, and a theme value can be a `var()`. Point the entries at CoreUI's tokens and `bg-primary`, `p-4` and `rounded-md` follow our palette, spacing scale and radius — including the color mode, because our tokens resolve through `light-dark()`:

```css
@theme {
  --color-primary: var(--cui-primary-base);
  --color-primary-fg: var(--cui-primary-fg);
  --color-success: var(--cui-success-base);
  --color-danger: var(--cui-danger-base);
  --color-body: var(--cui-bg-body);
  --color-fg: var(--cui-fg-body);

  --spacing: var(--cui-spacer-1);

  --radius-sm: var(--cui-radius-2);
  --radius-md: var(--cui-radius-3);
  --radius-lg: var(--cui-radius-5);

  --font-sans: var(--cui-font-sans-serif);
}
```

`--spacing` is Tailwind's multiplier — `p-4` is four times it — and `--cui-spacer-1` is a quarter of `--cui-spacer`, so Tailwind's spacing follows `--cui-spacer`. The step numbers do not line up with ours, so pick one set of spacing classes per page. Override `--cui-primary-base` on `:root` and both libraries repaint. Every token that can be mapped is listed on the [CSS variables](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/customize/css-variables/) page.

The other direction needs nothing: a component reads its color from the [theme slots](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/customize/theme/) on the element, so `<CButton theme="primary">` is themed the same way whether Tailwind is on the page or not, and a `.theme-brand` class of your own works next to Tailwind's `bg-*` classes.

## What CoreUI's components never need

The components do not use utility classes internally, so leaving `coreui-utilities.css` out cannot break one. The classes our JavaScript toggles — `show`, `active`, `collapsing`, `disabled` — are component states that live in the component stylesheets, not utilities, and they are unaffected by Tailwind's content scanning: they are not in your markup, and they do not need to be.

# Customize

> Learn how to theme, customize, and extend CoreUI for Vue with Sass, a boatload of global options, an expansive color system, and more.

## Overview

There are multiple ways to customize CoreUI for Vue. Your best path can depend on your project, the complexity of your build tools, the version of CoreUI for Vue you're using, browser support, and more.

Our two preferred methods are:

1. Using CoreUI for Vue [via package manager](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/getting-started/install/#package-managers) so you can use and extend our source files.
2. Using CoreUI's compiled distribution files so you can add onto or override CoreUI's styles.

While we cannot go into details here on how to use every package manager, we can give some guidance on [using CoreUI for Vue with your own Sass compiler](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/customize/sass/).

For those who want to use the distribution files, review the [getting started page](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/getting-started/introduction/) for how to include those files. From there, consult the docs for the layout, components, and behaviors you'd like to use.

As you familiarize yourself with CoreUI for Vue, continue exploring this section for more details on how to utilize our global options, making use of and changing our color system, how we build our components, how to use our growing list of CSS custom properties, and how to optimize your code when building with CoreUI for Vue.

In v6, **CSS custom properties are the first-class customization layer**: every design decision the library makes is emitted as a token you can override at run time, and Sass is the configuration language that generates them. Where each kind of override belongs — a token on a selector, a map handed to `@use … with ()`, a classic variable — is laid out on [Architecture](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/customize/architecture/).

## CSPs and embedded SVGs

Several CoreUI components include embedded SVGs in our CSS to style components consistently and easily across browsers and devices. **For organizations with more strict <abbr title="Content Security Policy">CSP</abbr> configurations**, we've documented all instances of our embedded SVGs (all of which are applied via `background-image`) so you can more thoroughly review your options.

- [Accordion](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/components/accordion/)
- [Carousel controls](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/components/carousel/#with-controls)
- [Close button](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/components/close-button/) (used in alerts and modals)
- [Form checkboxes](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/forms/checkbox/)
- [Form radio buttons](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/forms/radio/)
- [Form switches](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/forms/switch/)
- [Form validation icons](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/forms/validation/)
- [Navbar toggle buttons](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/components/navbar/#responsive-behaviors)
- [Select menus](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/forms/select/)

Based on [community conversation](https://github.com/twbs/bootstrap/issues/25394), some options for addressing this in your own codebase include replacing the URLs with locally hosted assets, removing the images and using inline images (not possible in all components), and modifying your CSP. Our recommendation is to carefully review your own security policies and decide on the best path forward, if necessary.
