# Architecture

> How the v6 styling system is put together: cascade layers, design tokens computed in the browser, per-component token surfaces, and theme slots.

_Added in 6.0.0._

Four mechanisms carry the whole v6 styling system. Each one has a page of its own for the details; this page shows how they fit together, and where your overrides plug in.

Where each piece lives, from the raw hue up to the component:

| Layer | File | What it defines |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Color scales | `scss/_colors.scss` | `$color-tokens`, emitted on `:root, :host` in the `colors` layer: one base token per color, expanded into the `100`–`900` steps with `color-mix()` against `$tint-color` / `$shade-color`. The mix names the base token, not its value, so overriding `--cui-primary` retints the whole scale in the browser. The grays are hand-picked stops rather than a mix, because a neutral ramp has to stay neutral. |
| Theme colors | `scss/_theme.scss` | `$theme-colors`, one nested map per role (`primary`, `danger`, …), each holding `base`, `fg`, `fg-emphasis`, `bg`, `bg-subtle`, `bg-muted`, `border`, `focus-ring` and `contrast` |
| Global tokens | `scss/_root.scss` | `$root-tokens`, everything else emitted on `:root, :host` — spacing, radii, typography, z-index and the surface ladders |
| Component tokens | the component's own partial | `$alert-tokens`, `$card-tokens` and the rest, emitted on the component's base class |

Each layer reads the one below it, so a change low down travels upward: retint `--cui-primary-500` and every slot of that theme color follows, along with every component reading those slots.

## Cascade layers

Every rule the library ships lives in a [cascade layer](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/@layer). The order is declared once, at the top of the bundle:

```css
@layer colors, config, root, reboot, layout, content, forms, components, custom, helpers, utilities;
```

Later layers beat earlier ones regardless of selector specificity, which settles by declaration the fights v5 settled with `!important` and specificity hacks:

- **Utilities win over components** because `utilities` comes last — no `!important` involved, and no switch to bring it back.
- **Your unlayered CSS wins over everything of ours**, because unlayered styles beat every layer. A plain `.card { … }` in your stylesheet overrides the library no matter how simple the selector.
- **`colors` is where the palette ships**, below everything else, so your own `@layer colors` block sits in the same layer and overrides a token like `--cui-primary-500` by source order alone.
- **Two layers are empty and reserved for you.** `config` sits below `root`, for a configuration sheet the whole library should read but never fight; `custom` slots between `components` and `helpers`, for component overrides that should still lose to utilities. Put your CSS in `@layer custom` when you want `.text-center` on the element to keep working.

One caveat: if your build concatenates our CSS with other stylesheets, make sure the layer declaration emitted at the top of the bundle survives minification — a minifier that predates `@layer` can strip it, and with it the whole ordering.

## Design tokens

Global design decisions — colors, spacing, typography, borders, shadows — are emitted as CSS custom properties on `:root` (the palette in the `colors` layer, everything else in `root`). Components never read Sass variables at run time; they read tokens:

```css
.alert {
  padding: var(--cui-alert-padding-y) var(--cui-alert-padding-x);
}
```

Two consequences follow:

- **Derived values are computed in the browser, not frozen at build time.** A size that depends on another size is written as `calc(var(--cui-…) * …)`, so overriding the source token at run time propagates to everything derived from it. Sass arithmetic would have baked the result into the file.
- **A token resolves where it is declared.** Overriding `--cui-body-font-size` on a descendant does not re-resolve `:root`-computed tokens that were derived from it — that is how `var()` substitution works everywhere, not a library rule. Set global tokens globally; set component tokens on the component.

The full token reference lives on [CSS variables](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/customize/css-variables/).

## Component tokens

Every component declares its complete styling surface as custom properties on its root class, built from a `$<component>-tokens` Sass map:

```scss
@mixin tokens($map) {
  @each $prop, $value in $map {
    #{$prop}: #{$value};
  }
}
```

That gives you three override levels, from no build step to full build:

1. **At run time, with CSS** — set the token on the component or any ancestor scope; no compilation involved:

   ```css
   .my-sidebar .alert { --cui-alert-bg: hotpink; }
   ```

2. **At build time, per surface** — hand the map your overrides through [Sass modules](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/customize/sass/); `null` removes a token entirely:

   ```scss
   @use "@coreui/coreui/scss/coreui" with (
     $alert-tokens: (
       --cui-alert-bg: hotpink,
       --cui-alert-margin-bottom: null,
     )
   );
   ```

3. **At build time, per variable** — the classic `$alert-padding-y: 2rem` overrides keep working, because the map defaults are built from the same Sass variables. Per-component Sass variables are a transitional layer, kept for migration; the tokens are the API that stays.

## Theme slots

Components do not read colors directly — they read them through `--cui-theme-*` slots with a fallback to their own default:

```css
.nav-link {
  color: var(--cui-theme-fg, var(--cui-nav-link-color));
}
```

When no theme class is present, the slot is unset and the fallback applies. A theme class — `.alert-danger`, `.theme-primary` — fills the slots for its subtree, and every component inside follows the theme without owning a single state rule:

```css
.theme-danger {
  --cui-theme-fg: var(--cui-danger-fg);
  --cui-theme-bg-subtle: var(--cui-danger-bg-subtle);
  /* … */
}
```

The slot values come from per-color scales generated with `color-mix()` from each color's base token, and the interactive states are derived at run time with relative color syntax — `oklch(from var(--cui-primary-base) calc(l * .85) c h)` — so overriding `--cui-primary` alone re-colors the subtle backgrounds, borders, emphasis text, hover and active states with it. The color system is documented on [Color](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/customize/color/), the scheme switching on [Color modes](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/customize/color-modes/).


---

# Sass

> Utilize our source Sass files to take advantage of variables, maps, mixins, and functions to help you build faster and customize your project.

Utilize our source Sass files to take advantage of variables, maps, mixins, and more.

## File structure

Whenever possible, avoid modifying CoreUI's core files. For Sass, that means creating your own stylesheet that imports CoreUI so you can modify and extend it. Assuming you're using a package manager like npm, you'll have a file structure that looks like this:

```text
your-project/
├── scss
│   └── custom.scss
└── node_modules/
    └── @coreui/coreui
        ├── js
        └── scss
```

If you've downloaded our source files and aren't using a package manager, you'll want to manually create something similar to that structure, keeping CoreUI's source files separate from your own.

```text
your-project/
├── scss
│   └── custom.scss
└── @coreui/coreui/
    ├── js
    └── scss
```

## Importing

In your `custom.scss`, you'll load CoreUI's source Sass files with `@use`. You have two options: include all of CoreUI, or pick the parts you need. We encourage the latter, though be aware there are some requirements and dependencies across our components. You also will need to include some JavaScript for our plugins.

> v6 is @use only. The *.import.scss files that let @import reach our modules are gone, so an @import of anything in scss/ no longer resolves. @import is deprecated in Dart Sass and is removed in 3.0.0 — read the migration guide if you are still on it.

```scss
// Custom.scss
// Option A: Include all of CoreUI

@use "@coreui/coreui/scss/coreui";

// Then add additional custom code here
```

```scss
// Custom.scss
// Option B: Include parts of CoreUI

// 1. Include root first (configuration, colors, theme tokens, and CSS layers)
@use "@coreui/coreui/scss/root";

// 2. Optionally include any other parts as needed
@use "@coreui/coreui/scss/utilities";
@use "@coreui/coreui/scss/content/reboot";
@use "@coreui/coreui/scss/content/type";
@use "@coreui/coreui/scss/content/images";
@use "@coreui/coreui/scss/layout/containers";
@use "@coreui/coreui/scss/layout/grid";
@use "@coreui/coreui/scss/helpers";

// 3. Optionally include utilities API last to generate classes based on the Sass map in `_utilities.scss`
@use "@coreui/coreui/scss/utilities/api";

// 4. Add additional custom code here
```

With that setup in place, you can begin to modify any of the Sass variables and maps in your `custom.scss`. You can also start to add parts of CoreUI under the `// Optional` section as needed. We suggest using the full stack from our `coreui.scss` file as your starting point.

Partials live in the directory named after the cascade layer they emit into, so `scss/content/`, `scss/layout/`, `scss/forms/` and `scss/buttons/` hold what used to sit at the root.

The library's configuration is split across four modules, each loadable on its own: `scss/config` holds the global settings — options, spacing, breakpoints, borders, shadows, typography, z-index; `scss/colors` the palette and the grays; `scss/theme` the theme colours, the `$theme-colors` map and the runtime colour scale; and each component keeps its own variables at the top of its partial.

## Compiling

In order to use your custom Sass code as CSS in the browser, you need a Sass compiler. In a typical Vue setup your build tool already provides one — Vite, and most other bundlers, compile `.scss` files as soon as the `sass` package is installed. Import your `custom.scss` from your app's entry point instead of the prebuilt CSS, and every `with ()` override on this page applies:

```js
import './scss/custom.scss'
```

## Variable defaults

Every Sass variable in CoreUI includes the `!default` flag allowing you to override the variable's default value in your own Sass without modifying CoreUI's source code. Copy and paste variables as needed, modify their values, and remove the `!default` flag. If a variable has already been assigned, then it won't be re-assigned by the default values in CoreUI.

The global settings live in `@coreui/coreui/scss/_config.scss`, the palette in `_colors.scss`, the theme colours in `_theme.scss`, and each component's variables at the top of its own partial. Some variables are set to `null`, these variables don't output the property unless they are overridden in your configuration.

Variable overrides must come after our functions are imported, but before the rest of the imports.

Here's an example that changes the `background-color` and `color` for the `<body>` when importing and compiling CoreUI via npm:

```scss
@use "@coreui/coreui/scss/coreui" with (
  $theme-bgs: ("body": #000),
  $theme-fgs: ("body": #111)
)
```

Repeat as necessary for any variable in CoreUI, including the global options below.

## Token defaults

Every CSS custom property the library emits is built from a Sass map you can override the same way: `$color-tokens` holds the palette, `$root-tokens` everything else declared on `:root`, and each component keeps its surface in `$<component>-tokens`. Hand the map your overrides through `with ()` — you only include the keys you want to change, and a `null` value removes the token from the output entirely:

```scss
@use "@coreui/coreui/scss/coreui" with (
  $root-tokens: (
    --cui-radius-5: .25rem,
    --cui-spacer: 1.5rem,
  ),
  $alert-tokens: (
    --cui-alert-padding-x: 2rem,
    --cui-alert-margin-bottom: null,
  )
);
```

The two levels coexist: classic variable overrides like `$alert-padding-y: 2rem` keep working, because the token map's defaults are built from those same variables — the map override just wins when both target one token. And because the output is a CSS custom property, the third level needs no compiler at all: set `--cui-alert-padding-x` on any selector at run time. [Architecture](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/customize/architecture/#component-tokens) walks through when each level is the right one.

## Maps and loops

CoreUI includes a handful of Sass maps, key value pairs that make it easier to generate families of related CSS. We use Sass maps for our colors, grid breakpoints, and more. Just like Sass variables, all Sass maps include the `!default` flag and can be overridden and extended.

Some of our Sass maps are merged into empty ones by default. This is done to allow easy expansion of a given Sass map, but comes at the cost of making _removing_ items from a map slightly more difficult.

### Modify map

Each theme color's base value is a standalone variable. To modify an existing color in our `$theme-colors` map, add the following to your custom Sass file:

```scss
$primary: #0074d9;
$danger: #ff4136;
```

The variable feeds the palette, whose `500` stop the entry in CoreUI's `$theme-colors` map points its `base` at, and the rest of the entry — the subtle backgrounds, borders and emphasis text — reads the runtime scale mixed from that stop, so overriding the one variable retints the whole family:

```scss
$theme-colors: (
  "primary": (
    "base": var(--cui-primary-500),
    // …the remaining slots read the primary scale
  ),
  "danger": (
    "base": var(--cui-danger-500),
    // …
  ),
);
```

### Add to map

Add new colors to `$theme-colors`, or any other map, through `with ()`: `defaults()` merges your entries on top of the built-ins, so you pass only what you add. A theme colour entry is a map of slots that read one hue of the palette: add the hue to `$colors`, point `base` and `bg` at its `500` stop, and the remaining slots at the 025–975 scale the library mixes from it at runtime, the same way the built-in colours do.

```scss
@use "@coreui/coreui/scss/coreui" with (
  $theme-colors: (
    "custom-color": (
      "base":        var(--cui-custom-color-500),
      "fg":          light-dark(var(--cui-custom-color-600), var(--cui-custom-color-400)),
      "fg-emphasis": light-dark(var(--cui-custom-color-800), var(--cui-custom-color-200)),
      "bg":          var(--cui-custom-color-500),
      "bg-subtle":   light-dark(var(--cui-custom-color-100), var(--cui-custom-color-900)),
      "bg-muted":    light-dark(var(--cui-custom-color-200), var(--cui-custom-color-800)),
      "border":      light-dark(var(--cui-custom-color-300), var(--cui-custom-color-600)),
      "focus-ring":  color-mix(in oklch, var(--cui-custom-color-500) calc(var(--cui-focus-ring-opacity) * 100%), transparent),
      "contrast":    var(--cui-white),
    ),
  )
);
```

The merge is one level deep: to change one slot of a built-in colour, pass that colour's whole sub-map.

### Remove from map

To remove colors from `$theme-colors`, or any other map, set the key to `null` — `defaults()` drops it from the output, and the derived `$theme-colors-*` families follow, because they are read from the merged map:

```scss
@use "@coreui/coreui/scss/coreui" with (
  $theme-colors: (
    "info": null,
  )
);
```

### Size maps

Components with size modifiers declare them in a `$<component>-sizes` map, written as a plain list — `defaults()` turns it into a map where every key is `true`:

```scss
$pagination-sizes: defaults(
  ("sm", "lg"),
  $pagination-sizes
);
```

A loop then emits one modifier class per key:

```scss
@each $size, $_ in $pagination-sizes {
  .pagination-#{$size} {
    --cui-pagination-min-height: var(--cui-btn-input-#{$size}-min-height);
    --cui-pagination-padding-y: var(--cui-btn-input-#{$size}-padding-y);
    --cui-pagination-padding-x: var(--cui-btn-input-#{$size}-padding-x);
    --cui-pagination-font-size: var(--cui-btn-input-#{$size}-font-size);
    --cui-pagination-border-radius: var(--cui-btn-input-#{$size}-border-radius);
  }
}
```

Removing a size you don't ship is one `null`:

```scss
@use "@coreui/coreui/scss/coreui" with (
  $pagination-sizes: ("sm": null)
);
```

Adding a key generates the class, but the class is only as good as the tokens it reads — here `--cui-btn-input-<size>-*` — so a new size also needs those tokens declared. Removing is the everyday operation; adding is a design-system extension.

### Variant maps

Style variants follow the same pattern in `$<component>-variants`: each entry names a variant and maps CSS properties to [theme slots](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/customize/theme/):

```scss
$alert-variants: defaults(
  (
    "solid": (
      "color": "contrast",
      "bg": "bg",
      "border-color": "bg"
    )
  ),
  $alert-variants
);
```

The loop turns every entry into a `.{component}-{variant}` class that re-points the component's tokens at the slots:

```scss
@each $variant, $properties in $alert-variants {
  .alert-#{$variant} {
    @each $property, $value in $properties {
      @if $value == "transparent" {
        --cui-alert-#{$property}: transparent;
      } @else {
        --cui-alert-#{$property}: var(--cui-theme-#{$value});
      }
    }

    --cui-hr-border-color: var(--cui-theme-border, currentcolor);

    @each $property, $value in $properties {
      @if $property == "bg" {
        background-color: var(--cui-alert-bg);
      } @else {
        #{$property}: var(--cui-alert-#{$property});
      }
    }
  }
}
```

Add your own variant by merging an entry — the value side names a `--cui-theme-*` slot, so the variant follows every theme color automatically:

```scss
@use "@coreui/coreui/scss/coreui" with (
  $alert-variants: (
    "outline": (
      "color": "fg",
      "bg": "transparent",
      "border-color": "border"
    )
  )
);
```

Button variants use a richer, nested shape (`base` / `hover` / `active` states per variant) — see the `btn-variants` block in `scss/buttons/_button.scss` for the reference.

## Required keys

CoreUI assumes the presence of some specific keys within Sass maps as we used and extend these ourselves. As you customize the included maps, you may encounter errors where a specific Sass map's key is being used.

For example, we use the `primary`, `success`, and `danger` keys from `$theme-colors` for links, buttons, and form states. Replacing the values of these keys should present no issues, but removing them may cause Sass compilation issues. In these instances, you'll need to modify the Sass code that makes use of those values.

## Functions

### Defaults

`defaults()` is the merge behind every overridable map on this page — token maps, size maps, variant maps. It layers your overrides on top of the library's defaults, drops every key whose value is `null`, and accepts a plain list as the defaults (each item becomes a key set to `true`, which is how the size maps are written):

```scss
// Merge overrides on top of defaults, stripping null and empty entries.
// Null values let users remove map keys via @use ... with().
// Accepts a list as $defaults (converted to a map with `true` values).
@function defaults($defaults, $overrides) {
  @if meta.type-of($defaults) == "list" {
    $map: ();
    @each $key in $defaults {
      $map: map.merge($map, ($key: true));
    }
    $defaults: $map;
  }
  $merged: map.merge($defaults, $overrides);
  @each $key, $value in $merged {
    @if $value == null or $value == "" {
      $merged: map.remove($merged, $key);
    }
  }
  @return $merged;
}
```

That one function is why `with ()` overrides are always partial — you pass only what changes — and why `null` is the removal syntax everywhere.

### Colors

Next to the [Sass maps](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/customize/color/#color-sass-maps) we have, theme colors can also be used as standalone variables, like `$primary`.

```scss
.custom-element {
  color: $gray-100;
  background-color: $dark;
}
```

You can lighten or darken colors with CoreUI's `tint-color()` and `shade-color()` functions. These functions will mix colors with black or white, unlike Sass' native `lighten()` and `darken()` functions which will change the lightness by a fixed amount, which often doesn't lead to the desired effect.

```scss
// Tint a color: mix a color with white
@function tint-color($color, $weight) {
  @return mix(white, $color, $weight);
}

// Shade a color: mix a color with black
@function shade-color($color, $weight) {
  @return mix(black, $color, $weight);
}

// Shade the color if the weight is positive, else tint it
@function shift-color($color, $weight) {
  @return if($weight > 0, shade-color($color, $weight), tint-color($color, -$weight));
}
```

In practice, you'd call the function and pass in the color and weight parameters.

```scss
@use "@coreui/coreui/scss/functions/color" as *;

.custom-element {
  color: tint-color($primary, 10%);
}

.custom-element-2 {
  color: shade-color($danger, 30%);
}
```

### Color contrast

In order to meet the [Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG)](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG/) contrast requirements, authors **must** provide a minimum [text color contrast of 4.5:1](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG/#contrast-minimum) and a minimum [non-text color contrast of 3:1](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG/#non-text-contrast), with very few exceptions.

An additional function we include in CoreUI is the color contrast function, `color-contrast`. It utilizes the [WCAG 2.0 algorithm](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG20-TECHS/G17.html#G17-tests) for calculating contrast thresholds based on [relative luminance](https://www.w3.org/WAI/GL/wiki/Relative_luminance) in a `sRGB` colorspace to automatically return a light (`#fff`), dark (`#212529`) or black (`#000`) contrast color based on the specified base color. This function is especially useful for mixins or loops where you're generating multiple classes.

For example, to generate color swatches from our `$theme-colors` map:

```scss
@use "@coreui/coreui/scss/functions/color-contrast" as *;

@each $color, $value in $theme-colors {
  .swatch-#{$color} {
    color: color-contrast($value);
  }
}
```

It can also be used for one-off contrast needs:

```scss
@use "@coreui/coreui/scss/functions/color-contrast" as *;

.custom-element {
  color: color-contrast(#000); // returns `color: #fff`
}
```

You can also specify a base color with our color map functions:

```scss
@use "@coreui/coreui/scss/functions/color-contrast" as *;

.custom-element {
  color: color-contrast($dark); // returns `color: #fff`
}
```

### Escape SVG

We use the `escape-svg` function to escape the `<`, `>` and `#` characters for SVG background images. When using the `escape-svg` function, data URIs must be quoted.

### Map helpers

The theme system keeps its definitions nested — one entry per color, holding every slot. `map-get-nested()` flattens that for consumers that want a single family across all colors:

```scss
@function map-get-nested($map, $key) {
  $result: ();
  @each $name, $values in $map {
    @if meta.type-of($values) == "map" and map.has-key($values, $key) {
      $result: map.merge($result, ($name: map.get($values, $key)));
    }
  }
  @return $result;
}
```

```scss
@use "@coreui/coreui/scss/functions/maps" as *;
@use "@coreui/coreui/scss/theme" as *;

$subtle-backgrounds: map-get-nested($theme-colors, "bg-subtle");
// => ("primary": …, "secondary": …, "success": …, …)
```

Entries without the key are skipped, so a color that drops a slot drops out of the family rather than landing in it as `null`.

`scss/functions/maps` also carries `map-get-multiple()` (pick several keys) and `map-merge-multiple()` (merge several maps).

## Mixins

Our `@coreui/coreui/scss/mixins/` directory has a ton of mixins that power parts of CoreUI and can also be used across your own project.

### Color schemes

A shorthand mixin for the `prefers-color-scheme` media query is available with support for `light`, `dark`, and custom color schemes.

```scss
@mixin color-scheme($name) {
  @media (prefers-color-scheme: #{$name}) {
    @content;
  }
}
```

```scss
@use "@coreui/coreui/scss/mixins/color-scheme" as *;

.custom-element {
  @include color-scheme(dark) {
    // Insert dark mode styles here
  }

  @include color-scheme(custom-named-scheme) {
    // Insert custom color scheme styles here
  }
}
```

### Mask icons

An icon carried as a `background-image` paints the colour baked into the SVG, so it cannot follow a theme. `mask-icon()` renders the shape through a CSS mask instead, which paints it with the element's `background-color` — so the icon takes whatever token that property reads.

```scss
@mixin mask-icon($icon: null, $size: contain, $position: center) {
  @if $icon != null {
    mask-image: $icon;
  }
  mask-repeat: no-repeat;
  @if $position != null {
    mask-position: $position;
  }
  @if $size != null {
    mask-size: $size;
  }
}
```

```scss
@use "@coreui/coreui-pro/scss/mixins/mask-icon" as *;

.my-toggle {
  @include mask-icon(url("data:image/svg+xml,…"));
  background-color: var(--cui-theme-fg, var(--cui-fg-2));
}
```

Pass `null` for the icon when the shape is applied conditionally — per state, or per direction — and set `mask-image` in the branch that needs it.

# Options

> Quickly customize CoreUI for Vue with built-in variables to easily toggle global CSS preferences for controlling style and behavior.

Customize CoreUI for Vue with our built-in custom variables file and easily toggle global CSS preferences with new `$enable-*` Sass variables. Override a variable's value and recompile with `npm run test` as needed.

You can find and customize these variables for key global options in CoreUI's `@coreui/coreui/scss/_variables.scss` file.

| Variable                       | Values                             | Description                                                                            |
| ------------------------------ | ---------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `$spacer`                      | `1rem` (default), or any value > 0 | Specifies the default spacer value to programmatically generate our [margin](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/utilities/margin/), [padding](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/utilities/padding/) and [gap](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/utilities/gap/) utilities. |
| `$enable-dark-mode`            | `true` (default) or `false`        | Enables built-in dark mode support across the project and its components. |
| `$enable-rounded`              | `true` (default) or `false`        | Enables predefined `border-radius` styles on various components. |
| `$enable-shadows`              | `true` or `false` (default)        | Enables predefined decorative `box-shadow` styles on various components. Does not affect `box-shadow`s used for focus states. |
| `$enable-gradients`            | `true` or `false` (default)        | Enables predefined gradients via `background-image` styles on various components. |
| `$enable-transitions`          | `true` (default) or `false`        | Enables predefined `transition`s on various components. |
| `$enable-reduced-motion`       | `true` (default) or `false`        | Enables the [`prefers-reduced-motion` media query](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/accessibility/reduced-motion/), which suppresses certain animations/transitions based on the users' browser/operating system preferences. |
| `$enable-grid-classes`         | `true` (default) or `false`        | Enables the generation of CSS classes for the grid system (e.g. `.row`, `.col-md-1`, etc.). |
| `$enable-container-classes`    | `true` (default) or `false`        | Enables the generation of CSS classes for layout containers. (New in v4.2.0) |
| `$enable-caret`                | `true` (default) or `false`        | Enables pseudo element caret on `.dropdown-toggle`. |
| `$enable-button-pointers`      | `true` (default) or `false`        | Add "hand" cursor to non-disabled button elements. |
| `$enable-cssgrid`              | `true` (default) or `false`        | Enables the generation of the [CSS Grid layout](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/layout/css-grid/) classes (e.g. `.grid`, `.g-col-6`). |
| `$enable-deprecation-messages` | `true` (default) or `false`        | Set to `false` to hide warnings when using any of the deprecated mixins and functions that are planned to be removed in `v6`. |
| `$enable-smooth-scroll`        | `true` (default) or `false`        | Applies `scroll-behavior: smooth` globally, except for users asking for reduced motion through [`prefers-reduced-motion` media query](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/accessibility/reduced-motion/) |
| `$enable-ltr`                  | `false` or `false` (default)       | Enables Left-to-Right |
| `$enable-rtl`                  | `true` (default) or `false`        | Enables Right-to-Left |

# Color

> CoreUI for Vue is supported by an extensive color system that themes our styles and components. This enables more comprehensive customization and extension for any project.

## Colors

_Added in 5.0.0._

The palette below covers two different jobs. `secondary` and `tertiary` text and background colors describe **surfaces** — the page, its dividers, its disabled states. The `{color}-bg-subtle`, `{color}-border`, and `{color}-fg-emphasis` sets are **tinted variants of the theme colors**, so that a single theme color can carry a background, a border, and a readable text tone that all shift together between color modes.

All of them are declared globally on `:root` and are available through Sass and CSS variables (but not through our color maps or utility classes).

Each family is generated, not hand-listed: one base token per color, and the `100`–`900` steps mixed from it with `color-mix()`. The mix names the base token rather than its value, so **overriding `--cui-primary` retints its whole scale in the browser** — no rebuild, both color schemes at once. [Notes on Sass](#notes-on-sass) covers the stops and the mixing space, and [Architecture](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/customize/architecture/) shows where this sits relative to the theme and component tokens.

To fade any of these colors, mix it toward `transparent` rather than reaching for a channel triplet — `color-mix(in srgb, var(--cui-bg-4) 50%, transparent)`.

**Heads up!** The surface colors and the theme colors overlap in name without overlapping in purpose: `--cui-secondary-color` is body text at a lighter weight, while `--cui-secondary` is the theme color that `.btn-secondary` and friends are built from. The same split applies to `light` and `dark`.

### Using the colors

These colors are accessible via CSS variables and utility classes—like `--cui-primary-bg-subtle` and `.bg-subtle-primary`—allowing you to compose your own CSS rules with the variables, or to quickly apply styles via classes. The utilities are built with the color's associated CSS variables, and since we customize those CSS variables for dark mode, they are also adaptive to color mode by default.

```html
<div class="p-4 fg-emphasis-primary bg-subtle-primary border border-subtle-primary rounded-3">
  Example element with utilities
</div>
```

## Theme colors

We use a subset of all colors to create a smaller color palette for generating color schemes, also available as Sass variables and a Sass map in CoreUI's `scss/_theme.scss` file.

<div class="row">
  {getData('theme-colors').map((c) => (
    <div class="col-md-4">
      <div class={`p-4 mb-4 text-bg-${c.name} rounded-3`}>{c.title}</div>
    </div>
  ))}
</div>

All these colors are available as a Sass map, `$theme-colors`.

Check out [our Sass maps and loops docs](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/customize/sass/#maps-and-loops) for how to modify these colors.

## From colors to theme

The `--cui-{color}-{stop}` tokens are the palette: one scale per theme color and the neutral ramp. On their own they style nothing — the **theme layer** reads them, where each color picks up semantic slots and every theme-aware component follows. The pipeline, end to end:

1. **`$colors`** (`scss/_colors.scss`) defines the base hues, and each one gets a 100–900 scale of `color-mix()` tokens on `:root` — `--cui-primary-300` and friends, mixed in the browser from the color's own token.
2. **`$theme-colors`** (`scss/_theme.scss`) maps each semantic name to a family of slots (`base`, `bg`, `contrast`, `fg`, `fg-emphasis`, `bg-subtle`, `bg-muted`, `border`, `focus-ring`). `base` and `bg` point at one stop of a hue — `primary` reads `var(--cui-primary-500)` — and the other slots read that hue's scale through `light-dark()`, so every slot adapts to the color mode.
3. The slots are emitted as **`--cui-{name}-{slot}`** tokens — `--cui-primary-bg-subtle` — the ones the table at the top of this page shows.
4. **`.theme-{name}`** classes remap them onto generic **`--cui-theme-{slot}`** tokens that components read — so one class restyles any theme-aware component, and overriding `--cui-primary-500` alone retints the whole family.

The theme layer — the slots, the runtime scale, the classes — is documented in full on [Theme](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/customize/theme/), and the mechanics of the slot indirection on [Architecture](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/customize/architecture/#theme-slots). The rest of this page stays on the base color layer.

## All colors

The palette is the five chromatic theme colors and the neutral ramp, available as Sass variables and a Sass map in `scss/_colors.scss`. Each gets a 025–975 scale of tokens; the [theme layer](#theme-colors) reads them, and the utilities read the theme layer, so there is no separate set of hue classes to keep in step.

Be sure to monitor contrast ratios as you customize colors. As shown below, we've added three contrast ratios to each of the main colors—one for the swatch's current colors, one for against white, and one for against black.

<div class="row font-monospace">
  {getData('colors').map((color) => {
    if (color.name !== 'white' && color.name !== 'gray' && color.name !== 'gray-dark') {
      return (
        <div class="col-md-4 mb-4">
          <div class={`p-4 mb-3 position-relative swatch-${color.name}`}>
            <strong class="d-block">${color.name}</strong>
            {color.hex}
          </div>
          {getSequence(100, 900, 100).map((value) => (
            <div class={`p-4 docs-${color.name}-${value}`}>${color.name}-{value}</div>
          ))}
        </div>
      )
    }
  })}

  <div class="col-md-4 mb-4">
    <div class="p-4 mb-3 position-relative swatch-gray-500">
      <strong class="d-block">$gray-500</strong>
      #aab3c5
    </div>
    {getData('grays').map((gray) => (
      <div class={`p-4 docs-gray-${gray.name}`}>$gray-{gray.name}</div>
    ))}
  </div>

  <div class="col-md-4 mb-4">
    <div class="p-4 mb-3 docs-black fg-white">
      <strong class="d-block">$black</strong>
      #000
    </div>
    <div class="p-4 mb-3 docs-white border">
      <strong class="d-block">$white</strong>
      #fff
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

### Notes on Sass

The tints and shades are not Sass variables any more. Every palette color gets
a 025–975 scale of `color-mix()` custom properties on `:root`, mixed in the
browser from its `500` stop — override `--cui-primary-500` and the whole family
follows, in both color schemes. See
[the theme colors page](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/customize/theme/).

`tint-color()` and `shade-color()` still exist in `scss/functions/_color.scss` for
Sass-side blending. They use `mix()`, which is not the same as `lighten()` and
`darken()`: the former blends the color with white or black, the latter only
adjusts its lightness value.

## Color Sass maps

CoreUI's source Sass files include three maps to help you quickly and easily loop over a list of colors and their values.

- `$colors` lists all our available base (`500`) colors
- `$theme-colors` lists all semantically named theme colors (shown below)
- `$grays` lists all tints and shades of gray

Within `scss/_colors.scss`, you'll find CoreUI's color variables and Sass map. Here's an example of the `$colors` Sass map:

```scss
$colors: () !default;

// stylelint-disable-next-line scss/dollar-variable-default
$colors: defaults(
  (
    "primary":    $primary,
    "success":    $success,
    "info":       $info,
    "warning":    $warning,
    "danger":     $danger,
    "gray":       $gray
  ),
  $colors
);
```

Add, remove, or modify values within the map to update how they're used in many other components. Unfortunately at this time, not _every_ component utilizes this Sass map. Future updates will strive to improve upon this. Until then, plan on making use of the `${color}` variables and this Sass map.

### Example

Here's how you can use these in your Sass:

```scss
@use "@coreui/coreui/scss/colors" as *;

.alpha { color: $purple; }
.beta {
  color: $warning;
  background-color: $gray-900;
}
```

The numbered shades — `$yellow-300`, `$indigo-900` and the rest — are gone in v6.
Each theme color gets its 100–900 scale as `color-mix()` tokens on `:root`
instead, so read `var(--cui-primary-300)` where you used to write
`$blue-300`. See [the theme colors page](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/customize/theme/).

[Color](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/utilities/colors/) and [background](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/utilities/background/) utility classes are also available for setting `color` and `background-color` using the `500` color values.

## Generating utilities

_Added in 4.1.0._

We don't ship `color` and `background-color` utilities for every color in the
palette, but you can generate them with the [utility API](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/utilities/api/).

1. Load the color maps and the utilities module in a partial.
2. Use our `map-merge-multiple()` function to merge several maps into one.
3. Merge that map into the `values` of any utility group.

Here's an example that generates text color utilities for every palette color and
every theme color's emphasis tone (e.g., `.text-purple`, `.fg-success`).

```scss
// _my-colors.scss
@use "sass:map";
@use "@coreui/coreui/scss/functions/maps" as *;
@use "@coreui/coreui/scss/colors" as *;
@use "@coreui/coreui/scss/theme" as *;
@use "@coreui/coreui/scss/utilities" as *;

$all-colors: map-merge-multiple($colors, map-get-nested($theme-colors, "fg-emphasis"));

$utilities: map.merge(
  $utilities,
  (
    "color": map.merge(
      map.get($utilities, "color"),
      (
        values: map.merge(
          map.get(map.get($utilities, "color"), "values"),
          $all-colors,
        ),
      ),
    ),
  )
);
```

Load the partial before the library, so the merged map is in place when the
utilities API runs:

```scss
// my-coreui.scss
@use "my-colors";
@use "@coreui/coreui/scss/coreui";
```

This will generate new `.text-{color}-{level}` utilities for every color and level. You can do the same for any other utility and property as well.


---

# Theme

> The theme is a set of semantically named colors, each carrying a full family of slots, used to style components, utilities, and more. It is configurable via Sass or CSS and responds to color modes.

## How it works

Theme colors are defined in the `$theme-colors` map in `scss/_theme.scss`. Each entry is a **map of slots** — one semantic name carries the solid color, its contrast color, the readable foregrounds, the subtle and muted backgrounds, the border, and the focus ring, for both light and dark mode via `light-dark()`.

From this one map the library generates:

- a `--cui-{color}-{slot}` custom property per slot on `:root`,
- a `-base` token per color that points at the palette stop it reads (`--cui-primary-base` → `--cui-primary-500`), so the palette's 025–975 runtime scale is the color's scale,
- a [`.theme-{color}` class](#theme-classes) per entry,
- the color variants of themeable components and the `.text-*`, `.bg-*`, and `.border-*` utilities.

## Theme colors

| Theme color | Default value | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `primary` | `oklch(52.945% 0.19103 278.34)` | Main brand color for primary actions |
| `secondary` | `var(--cui-gray-200)` | Less prominent actions and states |
| `success` | `oklch(61.237% 0.17298 146.95)` | Positive actions and successful states |
| `info` | `oklch(67.55% 0.17646 252.26)` | Informational messages and neutral states |
| `warning` | `oklch(80.791% 0.16473 78.5)` | Cautionary messages and states |
| `danger` | `oklch(63.864% 0.18175 23.81)` | Destructive actions and error states |
| `inverse` | `var(--cui-gray-900)` | Surfaces that flip against the page, e.g. a dark bar on a light page |

The five chromatic colors are entries of the [palette](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/customize/color/#all-colors) under the same name: `base` and `bg` read `--cui-primary-500`, and the rest of the slots read that scale. Override `$primary`, or the `--cui-primary-500` token at run time, and the whole family retints. `secondary` and `inverse` read gray stops: their `base` is one stop, and their `bg` flips between the schemes.

## Color slots

Every entry defines the same slots, emitted as `--cui-{color}-{slot}` on `:root`:

| Slot | Emitted token | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `base` | `--cui-primary-base` | The color itself, e.g. a solid button background. There is no bare `--cui-primary`: the slot is the token, and every utility and component reads it |
| `fg` | `--cui-primary-fg` | The color readable as text, one step lighter than the emphasis |
| `fg-emphasis` | `--cui-primary-fg-emphasis` | High-contrast foreground text |
| `bg` | `--cui-primary-bg` | The action-background slot: what checked, active and filled states read; the same stop as `base` for the hues, a `light-dark()` pair for `secondary` and `inverse` |
| `bg-subtle` | `--cui-primary-bg-subtle` | Subtle background tint for low-emphasis surfaces |
| `bg-muted` | `--cui-primary-bg-muted` | Muted background, between subtle and solid |
| `border` | `--cui-primary-border` | Border color |
| `focus-ring` | `--cui-primary-focus-ring` | The hue the color's focus ring mixes from |
| `contrast` | `--cui-primary-contrast` | Text and icons sitting on the solid base |

The slot values are `light-dark()` pairs of stops from the runtime scale, so a theme color reads correctly in both color modes without a second set of definitions:

```scss
$theme-colors: () !default;
// stylelint-disable-next-line scss/dollar-variable-default
$theme-colors: defaults(
  (
    "primary": (
      "base":          var(--cui-primary-500),
      "fg":            light-dark(var(--cui-primary-600), var(--cui-primary-400)),
      "fg-emphasis":   light-dark(var(--cui-primary-800), var(--cui-primary-200)),
      "bg":            var(--cui-primary-500),
      "bg-subtle":     light-dark(var(--cui-primary-100), var(--cui-primary-900)),
      "bg-muted":      light-dark(var(--cui-primary-200), var(--cui-primary-800)),
      "border":        light-dark(var(--cui-primary-300), var(--cui-primary-600)),
      "focus-ring":    color-mix(in oklch, var(--cui-primary-base) calc(var(--cui-focus-ring-opacity) * 100%), transparent),
      "contrast":      var(--cui-white),
    ),
    "secondary": (
      "base":          var(--cui-gray-200),
      "fg":            light-dark(var(--cui-gray-600), var(--cui-gray-400)),
      "fg-emphasis":   light-dark(var(--cui-gray-800), var(--cui-gray-200)),
      "bg":            light-dark(var(--cui-gray-100), var(--cui-gray-600)),
      "bg-subtle":     light-dark(var(--cui-gray-025), var(--cui-gray-800)),
      "bg-muted":      light-dark(var(--cui-gray-050), var(--cui-gray-700)),
      "border":        light-dark(var(--cui-gray-300), var(--cui-gray-600)),
      "focus-ring":    color-mix(in oklch, light-dark(var(--cui-gray-500), var(--cui-gray-300)) calc(var(--cui-focus-ring-opacity) * 100%), transparent),
      "contrast":      light-dark(var(--cui-gray-900), var(--cui-white)),
    ),
    "success": (
      "base":          var(--cui-success-500),
      "fg":            light-dark(var(--cui-success-600), var(--cui-success-400)),
      "fg-emphasis":   light-dark(var(--cui-success-800), var(--cui-success-200)),
      "bg":            var(--cui-success-500),
      "bg-subtle":     light-dark(var(--cui-success-100), var(--cui-success-900)),
      "bg-muted":      light-dark(var(--cui-success-200), var(--cui-success-800)),
      "border":        light-dark(var(--cui-success-300), var(--cui-success-600)),
      "focus-ring":    color-mix(in oklch, var(--cui-success-base) calc(var(--cui-focus-ring-opacity) * 100%), transparent),
      "contrast":      var(--cui-white),
    ),
    "info": (
      "base":          var(--cui-info-500),
      "fg":            light-dark(var(--cui-info-700), var(--cui-info-300)),
      "fg-emphasis":   light-dark(var(--cui-info-800), var(--cui-info-200)),
      "bg":            var(--cui-info-500),
      "bg-subtle":     light-dark(var(--cui-info-100), var(--cui-info-900)),
      "bg-muted":      light-dark(var(--cui-info-200), var(--cui-info-800)),
      "border":        light-dark(var(--cui-info-300), var(--cui-info-600)),
      "focus-ring":    color-mix(in oklch, var(--cui-info-base) calc(var(--cui-focus-ring-opacity) * 100%), transparent),
      "contrast":      var(--cui-white),
    ),
    "warning": (
      "base":          var(--cui-warning-500),
      "fg":            light-dark(var(--cui-warning-700), var(--cui-warning-300)),
      "fg-emphasis":   light-dark(var(--cui-warning-800), var(--cui-warning-200)),
      "bg":            var(--cui-warning-500),
      "bg-subtle":     light-dark(var(--cui-warning-100), var(--cui-warning-900)),
      "bg-muted":      light-dark(var(--cui-warning-200), var(--cui-warning-800)),
      "border":        light-dark(var(--cui-warning-300), var(--cui-warning-600)),
      "focus-ring":    color-mix(in oklch, var(--cui-warning-base) calc(var(--cui-focus-ring-opacity) * 100%), transparent),
      "contrast":      var(--cui-black),
    ),
    "danger": (
      "base":          var(--cui-danger-500),
      "fg":            light-dark(var(--cui-danger-600), var(--cui-danger-400)),
      "fg-emphasis":   light-dark(var(--cui-danger-800), var(--cui-danger-200)),
      "bg":            var(--cui-danger-500),
      "bg-subtle":     light-dark(var(--cui-danger-100), var(--cui-danger-900)),
      "bg-muted":      light-dark(var(--cui-danger-200), var(--cui-danger-800)),
      "border":        light-dark(var(--cui-danger-300), var(--cui-danger-600)),
      "focus-ring":    color-mix(in oklch, var(--cui-danger-base) calc(var(--cui-focus-ring-opacity) * 100%), transparent),
      "contrast":      var(--cui-white),
    ),
    "inverse": (
      "base":          var(--cui-gray-900),
      "fg":            light-dark(var(--cui-gray-900), var(--cui-gray-200)),
      "fg-emphasis":   light-dark(var(--cui-black), var(--cui-white)),
      "bg":            light-dark(var(--cui-gray-900), var(--cui-gray-100)),
      "bg-subtle":     light-dark(var(--cui-gray-100), var(--cui-gray-900)),
      "bg-muted":      light-dark(var(--cui-gray-200), var(--cui-gray-700)),
      "border":        light-dark(var(--cui-gray-400), var(--cui-gray-600)),
      "focus-ring":    color-mix(in oklch, light-dark(var(--cui-gray-900), var(--cui-gray-100)) calc(var(--cui-focus-ring-opacity) * 100%), transparent),
      "contrast":      light-dark(var(--cui-white), var(--cui-gray-900)),
    ),
  ),
  $theme-colors
);
```

### Pairings

The slots are not interchangeable — each foreground is tuned against a particular background, so a legible combination is one of these:

- `contrast` on `bg` — text and icons on the solid color
- `fg` on `bg-subtle` — the everyday tinted panel
- `fg-emphasis` on `bg-muted` — the heavier panel, where the foreground has to work harder
- `border` with either `bg-subtle` or `bg-muted`

```html
<div class="theme-primary vstack gap-4">
  <div class="p-4 rounded-3" style="color: var(--cui-theme-contrast); background: var(--cui-theme-bg);">
    contrast on bg
  </div>
  <div class="p-4 rounded-3" style="color: var(--cui-theme-fg); background: var(--cui-theme-bg-subtle); border: 1px solid var(--cui-theme-border);">
    fg on bg-subtle
  </div>
  <div class="p-4 rounded-3" style="color: var(--cui-theme-fg-emphasis); background: var(--cui-theme-bg-muted); border: 1px solid var(--cui-theme-border);">
    fg-emphasis on bg-muted
  </div>
</div>
```

Reading a foreground against a background it was not paired with is where contrast falls apart: `fg` sits close to `bg-muted`, and `contrast` is built for the solid `bg` alone — on any tinted surface it disappears.

## The runtime scale

Every palette color gets a 025–975 scale of `color-mix()` tokens, mixed at runtime from its `500` stop. Override `--cui-primary-500` (or `$primary`) and the whole family — subtle backgrounds, borders, emphasis text — follows, in both color schemes:

```scss
$color-mix-space: oklch !default;
$tint-color:      var(--cui-white) !default;
$shade-color:     var(--cui-black) !default;
```

```scss
$color-tints: () !default;

// stylelint-disable-next-line scss/dollar-variable-default
$color-tints: defaults(
  (
    "025": 94%,
    "050": 90%,
    "100": 80%,
    "200": 60%,
    "300": 40%,
    "400": 20%
  ),
  $color-tints
);

$color-shades: () !default;

// stylelint-disable-next-line scss/dollar-variable-default
$color-shades: defaults(
  (
    "600": 16%,
    "700": 32%,
    "800": 48%,
    "900": 64%,
    "950": 70%,
    "975": 76%
  ),
  $color-shades
);
```

```css
:root {
  --cui-primary-500: #6f42c1; /* the scale, the slots and every component follow */
}
```

## Theme classes

A `.theme-{color}` class is generated for every key of `$theme-colors`. It sets the generic `--cui-theme-*` tokens that themeable components read — see [the theme variants section](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/customize/components/#theme-variants) for the token table and how components consume them. Every themeable Vue component renders the class through its `theme` prop, e.g. `<CBadge theme="danger">`.

```scss
@mixin generate-theme-classes() {
  @each $state in map.keys($theme-colors) {
    .theme-#{$state} {
      @include theme-tokens($state);
    }
  }

  @include generate-theme-reset();
}
```

Because the tokens are ordinary custom properties, they inherit: put a `.theme-*` class on a container and every themeable component inside follows it. Components read the slots on the property and fall back to their own tokens, so under a theme class the theme wins over a component token set on the element; a variant class such as `.btn-solid` or `.alert-solid` maps its tokens to the slots, so there the component token is still the override point. To recolor one themed element, set the slot itself (`--cui-theme-bg-subtle`, `--cui-theme-bg`, …).

```html
<div class="theme-primary d-flex gap-3 align-items-center">
  <CBadge>Regional</CBadge>
  <CBadge theme="danger">Local override</CBadge>
</div>
```

## Adding a theme color

A new theme color is a hue in `$colors` and one entry in the map. The hue gets its runtime scale, and the entry points the slots at it; the library generates the tokens and the `.theme-*` class:

```scss
@use "@coreui/coreui/scss/coreui" with (
  $theme-colors: (
    "brand": (
      "base":        var(--cui-brand-500),
      "fg":          light-dark(var(--cui-brand-600), var(--cui-brand-400)),
      "fg-emphasis": light-dark(var(--cui-brand-800), var(--cui-brand-200)),
      "bg":          var(--cui-brand-500),
      "bg-subtle":   light-dark(var(--cui-brand-100), var(--cui-brand-900)),
      "bg-muted":    light-dark(var(--cui-brand-200), var(--cui-brand-800)),
      "border":      light-dark(var(--cui-brand-300), var(--cui-brand-600)),
      "focus-ring":  color-mix(in oklch, var(--cui-brand-500) calc(var(--cui-focus-ring-opacity) * 100%), transparent),
      "contrast":    var(--cui-white),
    ),
  )
);
```

Each theme color is a nested map and the merge is one level deep: pass the whole sub-map to change a built-in color, and set a color to `null` to remove it.

For a runtime-only brand — no Sass compilation — set the generic tokens on a container instead, as shown in [the theme variants section](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/customize/components/#theme-variants).

## Theme utilities

Four style utilities pair a themed surface with its matching text color — compose them with any `.theme-{color}` class to color arbitrary markup the same way the components do. The full reference, with every pairing per color, lives on [the theme utilities page](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/utilities/theme/):

```scss
// Theme style utilities — pair with .theme-{color} to apply coordinated
// background and text colors
"theme-contrast": (
  property: (
    "background-color": var(--cui-theme-bg),
    "color": var(--cui-theme-contrast)
  ),
  class: theme-contrast,
  values: (null: null)
),
"theme-subtle": (
  property: (
    "background-color": var(--cui-theme-bg-subtle),
    "color": var(--cui-theme-fg)
  ),
  class: theme-subtle,
  values: (null: null)
),
"theme-muted": (
  property: (
    "background-color": var(--cui-theme-bg-muted),
    "color": var(--cui-theme-fg-emphasis)
  ),
  class: theme-muted,
  values: (null: null)
),
"theme-border": (
  property: border,
  class: theme-border,
  values: (null: var(--cui-border-width) solid var(--cui-theme-border))
),
```

```html
<div class="theme-success d-flex flex-column gap-3">
  <div class="theme-contrast p-3 rounded">Solid surface with contrast text</div>
  <div class="theme-subtle p-3 rounded">Subtle surface with readable text</div>
  <div class="theme-muted p-3 rounded">Muted surface with emphasis text</div>
  <div class="theme-border p-3 rounded">Themed border</div>
</div>
```

## Customizing

### CSS variables

Each theme class carries its own interaction shades, computed from the color in the browser, so a component asking for "this color, one step darker" reads a token instead of recomputing it. How far a shade travels is set on `:root`, which makes the strength of every hover and active state one override, on the page or on a subtree.

```scss
--cui-theme-hover-lightness: .85,
--cui-theme-hover-chroma: 1.1,
--cui-theme-active-lightness: .8,
--cui-theme-active-chroma: 1.15,
```

### Sass maps

The slots of a theme color are the contract between its `.theme-*` class and the components reading it: every slot of the entry becomes a `--cui-theme-{slot}` token on the class, and `.theme-reset` clears the union of them. Add a slot to an entry and its class gains that token.

A color that is already dark brightens instead of darkening, which no single multiplier handles. `$theme-state-colors` is the escape hatch: name a theme color and give its `hover` and `active` values outright, and the multipliers above are skipped for it.

```scss
$theme-state-colors: () !default;
// stylelint-disable-next-line scss/dollar-variable-default
$theme-state-colors: defaults(
  (
    "secondary": (
      "hover":  light-dark(var(--cui-gray-200), var(--cui-gray-700)),
      "active": light-dark(var(--cui-gray-300), var(--cui-gray-800))
    ),
    "inverse": (
      "hover":  light-dark(var(--cui-gray-800), var(--cui-gray-200)),
      "active": light-dark(var(--cui-gray-700), var(--cui-gray-300))
    )
  ),
  $theme-state-colors
);
```


---

# Color modes

> CoreUI for Vue supports color modes, or themes. Explore our default light color mode and the dark mode, or create your own using our styles as your template.

## Dark mode

**CoreUI for Vue supports color modes, starting with dark mode!** You can implement your own color mode toggler (see below for an example using the `useColorModes` composable) and apply the different color modes as you see fit. We support a light mode (default) and dark mode. Color modes can be toggled globally on the `<html>` element, or on specific components and elements, thanks to the `data-coreui-theme` attribute.

Alternatively, you can also switch to a media query implementation thanks to our color mode mixin—see [the usage section for details](#building-with-sass). Heads up though—this eliminates your ability to change themes on a per-component basis as shown below.

## Example

For example, to change the color mode of a dropdown menu, add `data-coreui-theme="light"` or `data-coreui-theme="dark"` to the parent `.dropdown`. Now, no matter the global color mode, these dropdowns will display with the specified theme value.

```html
<div class="dropdown" data-coreui-theme="light">
  <button class="btn btn-solid theme-secondary dropdown-toggle" type="button" aria-expanded="false">
    Default dropdown
  </button>
  <ul class="dropdown-menu d-block position-static">
    <li><a class="dropdown-item active" href="#">Action</a></li>
    <li><a class="dropdown-item" href="#">Action</a></li>
    <li><a class="dropdown-item" href="#">Another action</a></li>
    <li><a class="dropdown-item" href="#">Something else here</a></li>
    <li><hr class="dropdown-divider"></li>
    <li><a class="dropdown-item" href="#">Separated link</a></li>
  </ul>
</div>

<div class="dropdown" data-coreui-theme="dark">
  <button class="btn btn-solid theme-secondary dropdown-toggle" type="button" aria-expanded="false">
    Dark dropdown
  </button>
  <ul class="dropdown-menu d-block position-static">
    <li><a class="dropdown-item active" href="#">Action</a></li>
    <li><a class="dropdown-item" href="#">Action</a></li>
    <li><a class="dropdown-item" href="#">Another action</a></li>
    <li><a class="dropdown-item" href="#">Something else here</a></li>
    <li><hr class="dropdown-divider"></li>
    <li><a class="dropdown-item" href="#">Separated link</a></li>
  </ul>
</div>
```

## How it works

- As shown above, color mode styles are controlled by the `data-coreui-theme` attribute. This attribute can be applied to the `<html>` element, or to any other element or CoreUI for Vue component. If applied to the `<html>` element, it will apply to everything. If applied to a component or element, it will be scoped to that specific component or element.

- For each color mode you wish to support, you'll need to add new overrides for the shared global CSS variables. We do this already in our `_root.scss` stylesheet for dark mode, with light mode being the default values. In writing color mode specific styles, use the mixin:

  ```scss
  // Color mode variables in _root.scss
  @include color-mode(dark) {
    // CSS variable overrides here...
  }
  ```

- Almost every global color is declared once, as a native [`light-dark()`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/color_value/light-dark) pair, so there is no second set of dark declarations to keep in sync. The `data-coreui-theme="dark"` selector only has to declare `color-scheme: dark` and every pair — plus the native form widgets — follows. The exceptions are values `light-dark()` cannot hold: the colors baked into embedded SVGs (the select chevron, the switch knob) and filters keep their own dark rule.

  Note that `light-dark()` is the *mechanism*, not the switch. `:root` declares `color-scheme: light` outright rather than `light dark`, so a pair resolves to its light value until something sets `color-scheme: dark` — which, in practice, means the `data-coreui-theme` attribute. The operating system preference does not reach the pairs on its own; see [Building with Sass](#building-with-sass) for the media-query build if that is what you want.

## Usage

### Enable dark mode

Enable the built in dark color mode across your entire project by adding the `data-coreui-theme="dark"` attribute to the `<html>` element. This will apply the dark color mode to all components and elements, other than those with a specific `data-coreui-theme` attribute applied. In a typical Vue app that attribute lives in your `index.html`:

```html
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en" data-coreui-theme="dark">
  <head>
    <meta charset="utf-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
    <title>CoreUI for Vue demo</title>
  </head>
  <body>
    <div id="app"></div>
    <script type="module" src="/src/main.ts"></script>
  </body>
</html>
```

To let visitors switch modes at run time, use the [`useColorModes` composable](#javascript) instead of hard-coding the attribute.

### Building with Sass

Our dark mode option is available to use for all users of CoreUI for Vue, but it's controlled via data attributes instead of media queries and does not automatically toggle your project's color mode. You can disable our dark mode entirely via Sass by changing `$enable-dark-mode` to `false`.

We use a custom Sass mixin, `color-mode()`, to help you control _how_ color modes are applied. By default, we use a `data` attribute approach, allowing you to create more user-friendly experiences where your visitors can choose to have an automatic dark mode or control their preference. This is also an easy and scalable way to add different themes and more custom color modes beyond light and dark.

In case you want to use media queries and only make color modes automatic, you can change the mixin's default type via Sass variable. Consider the following snippet and its compiled CSS output.

```scss
$color-mode-type: data;

@include color-mode(dark) {
  .element {
    color: var(--cui-primary-fg-emphasis);
    background-color: var(--cui-primary-bg-subtle);
  }
}
```

Outputs to:

```css
[data-coreui-theme=dark] .element {
  color: var(--cui-primary-fg-emphasis);
  background-color: var(--cui-primary-bg-subtle);
}
```

And when setting to `media-query`:

```scss
$color-mode-type: media-query;

@include color-mode(dark) {
  .element {
    color: var(--cui-primary-fg-emphasis);
    background-color: var(--cui-primary-bg-subtle);
  }
}
```

Outputs to:

```css
@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) {
  .element {
    color: var(--cui-primary-fg-emphasis);
    background-color: var(--cui-primary-bg-subtle);
  }
}
```

## Custom color modes

While the primary use case for color modes is light and dark mode, custom color modes are also possible. Create your own `data-coreui-theme` selector with a custom value as the name of your color mode, then modify our Sass and CSS variables as needed. Set `color-scheme` on your selector as well, so the `light-dark()` pairs and the native widgets pick the right side.

For example, you can create a "blue theme" with the selector `data-coreui-theme="blue"`. In your custom Sass or CSS file, add the new selector and override any global or component CSS variables as needed. If you're using Sass, you can also use Sass's functions within your CSS variable overrides.

```scss
[data-coreui-theme="blue"] {
  --cui-body-color: var(--cui-white);
  --cui-body-color-rgb: #{to-rgb(#fff)};
  --cui-body-bg: #{$cd-blue-500};
  --cui-body-bg-rgb: #{to-rgb($cd-blue-500)};
  --cui-tertiary-bg: #{$cd-blue-600};

  .dropdown-menu {
    --cui-dropdown-bg: #{color.mix($cd-blue-500, $cd-blue-600, 50%, rgb)};
    --cui-dropdown-link-active-bg: #{$cd-blue-700};
  }

  .btn-secondary {
    --cui-btn-bg: #{$cd-btn-secondary-bg};
    --cui-btn-border-color: #{rgba(#fff, .25)};
    --cui-btn-hover-bg: #{color.scale($cd-btn-secondary-bg, $lightness: -8%)}; // stylelint-disable-line scss/at-function-named-arguments
    --cui-btn-hover-border-color: #{rgba(#fff, .25)};
    --cui-btn-active-bg: #{color.scale($cd-btn-secondary-bg, $lightness: -16%)}; // stylelint-disable-line scss/at-function-named-arguments
    --cui-btn-active-border-color: #{rgba(#fff, .5)};
    --cui-btn-focus-border-color: #{rgba(#fff, .5)};
    --cui-btn-focus-box-shadow: 0 0 0 .25rem rgba(255, 255, 255, .2);
  }
}
```

```html
<div data-coreui-theme="blue">
  ...
</div>
```

## JavaScript

To allow visitors or users to toggle color modes, you'll need a control that sets the `data-coreui-theme` attribute on the root element, `<html>`. In CoreUI for Vue that job is done by the `useColorModes` composable: it initially defers to the user's current system color mode, persists an explicit choice in `localStorage`, and applies the attribute for you.

The composable takes the `localStorage` key as its only argument and returns three things: `colorMode`, a ref holding the current value; `setColorMode`, which stores the choice and sets the attribute (pass `'light'`, `'dark'`, or `'auto'` to follow the system preference); and `isColorModeSet`, which tells you whether the visitor has made an explicit choice yet. Call `setColorMode` as early as possible — before your first paint — to reduce potential screen flickering while your app loads.

```vue
<script setup>
import { CButton, CButtonGroup, useColorModes } from '@coreui/vue-pro'

const { colorMode, setColorMode } = useColorModes('coreui-vue-color-scheme')
</script>

<template>
  <CButtonGroup aria-label="Toggle theme">
    <CButton :active="colorMode === 'light'" @click="setColorMode('light')">
      Light
    </CButton>
    <CButton :active="colorMode === 'dark'" @click="setColorMode('dark')">
      Dark
    </CButton>
    <CButton :active="colorMode === 'auto'" @click="setColorMode('auto')">
      Auto
    </CButton>
  </CButtonGroup>
</template>
```

While no stored choice exists, the composable resolves to the system preference and keeps following it when it changes. Note that if you decide to use media queries for your color modes, the composable is unnecessary — the browser applies the preference on its own.

## Adding theme colors

A theme color is a hue in `$colors` and one entry in the `$theme-colors` map — a map of slots covering both color modes, described on [the Theme page](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/customize/theme/). Merge both and the library generates everything else: the 025–975 runtime scale of the hue, the `--cui-custom-color-*` slot tokens that read it, and the `.theme-custom-color` class.

> Heads up! Reach our Sass with @use. The *.import.scss files that let @import resolve our modules are gone, so the snippet below will not compile behind an @import.

```scss
@use "@coreui/coreui/scss/coreui" with (
  $theme-colors: (
    "custom-color": (
      "base":        var(--cui-custom-color-500),
      "fg":          light-dark(var(--cui-custom-color-600), var(--cui-custom-color-400)),
      "fg-emphasis": light-dark(var(--cui-custom-color-800), var(--cui-custom-color-200)),
      "bg":          var(--cui-custom-color-500),
      "bg-subtle":   light-dark(var(--cui-custom-color-100), var(--cui-custom-color-900)),
      "bg-muted":    light-dark(var(--cui-custom-color-200), var(--cui-custom-color-800)),
      "border":      light-dark(var(--cui-custom-color-300), var(--cui-custom-color-600)),
      "focus-ring":  color-mix(in oklch, var(--cui-custom-color-500) calc(var(--cui-focus-ring-opacity) * 100%), transparent),
      "contrast":    var(--cui-white),
    ),
  )
);
```

The slots are `light-dark()` pairs of the runtime scale, so both color modes are covered by the one entry — there is no second, dark set of maps to fill in.

## Customizing

### CSS variables

Global colors are declared once as `light-dark()` pairs, so the color mode selector — which defaults to `data-coreui-theme` but [can be configured](#building-with-sass) to use a `prefers-color-scheme` media query — only declares the scheme:

```scss
--cui-shadow-strength: 2.4;
--cui-backdrop-opacity: 65%;
```

Do the same in your own color modes: declare `color-scheme` and override only the tokens whose value is genuinely mode-specific.

### Sass variables

_Deprecated in 6.0.0._

Sass variables set these defaults at build time and are removed in v7. The CSS variables above reach the same values without recompiling, and can be set on a single element.

Each theme color gets a 100–900 scale of `color-mix()` tokens in `:root`, mixed at runtime from the color's own token. The subtle backgrounds, borders and emphasis text are `light-dark()` pairs of those stops, so overriding `$primary` (or the `--cui-primary-500` token at runtime) retints the whole family in both color modes. These set what the scale mixes towards, and in which color space:

```scss
$color-mix-space: oklch !default;
$tint-color:      var(--cui-white) !default;
$shade-color:     var(--cui-black) !default;
```

The one value that cannot be a `light-dark()` pair is a color baked into an SVG, because a data URI cannot read a custom property. The select chevron is the only one left: it carries `--cui-control-select-bg-img` and `--cui-control-select-bg-img-dark` side by side on the control, and dark mode switches which one the `background-image` reads. Both are translucent black and white, so the chevron tints itself against whatever the field sits on.

### Sass maps

The two maps are the stops of that scale: each entry is one step number and how far it mixes towards the tint or the shade color. Add an entry and every theme color gains that stop; set one to `null` to drop it everywhere at once.

```scss
$color-tints: () !default;

// stylelint-disable-next-line scss/dollar-variable-default
$color-tints: defaults(
  (
    "025": 94%,
    "050": 90%,
    "100": 80%,
    "200": 60%,
    "300": 40%,
    "400": 20%
  ),
  $color-tints
);

$color-shades: () !default;

// stylelint-disable-next-line scss/dollar-variable-default
$color-shades: defaults(
  (
    "600": 16%,
    "700": 32%,
    "800": 48%,
    "900": 64%,
    "950": 70%,
    "975": 76%
  ),
  $color-shades
);
```

### Sass mixins

Styles for dark mode, and any custom color modes you create, can be scoped appropriately to the `data-coreui-theme` attribute selector or media query with the customizable `color-mode()` mixin. See the [Sass usage section](#building-with-sass) for more details.

```scss
@mixin color-mode($mode: light, $root: false) {
  @if $color-mode-type == "media-query" {
    @if $root == true {
      @media (prefers-color-scheme: $mode) {
        :root,
        :host {
          @content;
        }
      }
    } @else {
      @media (prefers-color-scheme: $mode) {
        @content;
      }
    }
  } @else {
    [data#{$data-infix}theme="#{$mode}"] {
      @content;
    }
  }
}
```
