# Vue Button Component

> Vue button component for actions in tables, forms, cards, and more. CoreUI for Vue.js provides various styles, states, and size. Ready to use and easy to customize.

## Base class

A `<CButton>` without a `color` sets up the shape of a button — size, spacing, radius, the focus ring — and paints it in the neutral surface colour, so it is a usable button on its own.

```html
<template>
  <CButton>Base class</CButton>
</template>

<script setup>
import { CButton } from '@coreui/vue'
</script>
```

## Variants

CoreUI includes a bunch of predefined buttons components, each serving its own semantic purpose. Buttons show what action will happen when the user clicks or touches it. CoreUI buttons are used to initialize operations, both in the background or foreground of an experience.

```html
<template>
  <CButton theme="primary">Primary</CButton>
  <CButton theme="secondary">Secondary</CButton>
  <CButton theme="success">Success</CButton>
  <CButton theme="danger">Danger</CButton>
  <CButton theme="warning">Warning</CButton>
  <CButton theme="info">Info</CButton>
  <CButton theme="secondary">Light</CButton>
  <CButton theme="inverse">Dark</CButton>
  <CButton link>Link</CButton>
</template>

<script setup>
import { CButton } from '@coreui/vue'
</script>
```

> Using color to add meaning only provides a visual indication, which will not be conveyed to users of assistive technologies – such as screen readers. Ensure that information denoted by the color is either obvious from the content itself (e.g. the visible text), or is included through alternative means, such as additional text hidden with the .visually-hidden class.

## Theme variants

_Added in 6.0.0._

A button is a shape plus a colour: `variant` picks the shape — how much ink the button uses — and `theme` picks the colour. A button given a `theme` and no `variant` is solid.

```html
<template>
  <CButton theme="primary">Solid</CButton>
  <CButton theme="primary" variant="outline">Outline</CButton>
  <CButton theme="primary" variant="subtle">Subtle</CButton>
  <CButton theme="primary" variant="ghost">Ghost</CButton>
</template>

<script setup>
import { CButton } from '@coreui/vue'
</script>
```

The theme is a class, so it may sit on any ancestor instead of on each button — theme a toolbar and every button inside follows it.

```html
<template>
  <CButtonGroup class="theme-danger" role="group" aria-label="Themed toolbar">
    <CButton variant="solid">Left</CButton>
    <CButton variant="solid">Middle</CButton>
    <CButton variant="solid">Right</CButton>
  </CButtonGroup>
</template>

<script setup>
import { CButton, CButtonGroup } from '@coreui/vue'
</script>
```

The deprecated `color` property renders the same classes as `theme`; `theme` wins when both are set.

`.btn-link` is the exception. Set the `link` property for a link that behaves like a button — it takes its colour from the link colour, so `theme` and `variant` do not apply to it.

## Icon only

_Added in 6.0.0._

Add `iconOnly` for a button that holds nothing but an icon. It drops the padding and takes its width from its height, so the result is square at every size.

```html
<template>
  <CButton theme="primary" icon-only size="sm" aria-label="Add">
    <svg
      width="1em"
      height="1em"
      viewBox="0 0 16 16"
      fill="none"
      stroke="currentcolor"
      stroke-width="2"
      stroke-linecap="round"
      aria-hidden="true"
    >
      <path d="M8 3v10M3 8h10" />
    </svg>
  </CButton>
  <CButton theme="primary" icon-only aria-label="Add">
    <svg
      width="1em"
      height="1em"
      viewBox="0 0 16 16"
      fill="none"
      stroke="currentcolor"
      stroke-width="2"
      stroke-linecap="round"
      aria-hidden="true"
    >
      <path d="M8 3v10M3 8h10" />
    </svg>
  </CButton>
  <CButton theme="primary" icon-only size="lg" aria-label="Add">
    <svg
      width="1em"
      height="1em"
      viewBox="0 0 16 16"
      fill="none"
      stroke="currentcolor"
      stroke-width="2"
      stroke-linecap="round"
      aria-hidden="true"
    >
      <path d="M8 3v10M3 8h10" />
    </svg>
  </CButton>
</template>

<script setup>
import { CButton } from '@coreui/vue'
</script>
```

## Disable text wrapping

If you don't want the button text to wrap, you can add the `.text-nowrap` class to the `<CButton>`. In Sass, you can set `$btn-white-space: nowrap` to disable text wrapping for each button.

## Button components

The `<CButton>` component are designed for `<button>` ,  `<a>`  or  `<input>` elements (though some browsers may apply a slightly different rendering).

If you're using `<CButton>` component as `<a>` elements that are used to trigger functionality ex. collapsing content, these links should be given a `role="button"` to adequately communicate their meaning to assistive technologies such as screen readers.

```html
<template>
  <CButton as="a" theme="primary" href="#" role="button">Link</CButton>
  <CButton type="submit" theme="primary">Button</CButton>
  <CButton as="input" type="button" theme="primary" value="Input" />
  <CButton as="input" type="submit" theme="primary" value="Submit" />
  <CButton as="input" type="reset" theme="primary" value="Reset" />
</template>

<script setup>
import { CButton } from '@coreui/vue'
</script>
```

## Outline buttons

### Base outline style

The `variant="outline` property provides a neutral outline button style without any color modifiers. It’s useful as a foundation for minimal buttons without background color or strong visual emphasis.

```html
<template>
  <CButton variant="outline">Base outline button</CButton>
  <CButton variant="outline" active>Active state</CButton>
  <CButton variant="outline" disabled>Disabled state</CButton>
</template>

<script setup>
import { CButton } from '@coreui/vue'
</script>
```

These Vue buttons use a transparent background, subtle border, and inherit text color from the parent context. They’re best suited for minimalist UI elements like modals, toolbars, or secondary actions.

### Themed outline variants

If you need a button, but without the strong background colors, set `color` and `variant=" outline"` props to remove all background colors.

```html
<template>
  <CButton theme="primary" variant="outline">Primary</CButton>
  <CButton theme="secondary" variant="outline">Secondary</CButton>
  <CButton theme="success" variant="outline">Success</CButton>
  <CButton theme="danger" variant="outline">Danger</CButton>
  <CButton theme="warning" variant="outline">Warning</CButton>
  <CButton theme="info" variant="outline">Info</CButton>
  <CButton theme="secondary" variant="outline">Light</CButton>
  <CButton theme="inverse" variant="outline">Dark</CButton>
</template>

<script setup>
import { CButton } from '@coreui/vue'
</script>
```

These outline variants of our Vue.js buttons retain transparent backgrounds by default, but display a background tint on hover or focus to indicate interactivity. They’re ideal for secondary actions when you want to differentiate from the standard buttons visually.

## Ghost buttons

### Base ghost style

Use the `variant="ghost"` property to create ultra-minimalist buttons with no borders and a fully transparent background. These Vue buttons rely solely on text color for visibility and apply a background highlight when hovered over or in an active state.

They’re perfect for interfaces where you want buttons to be present but visually unobtrusive—such as action buttons in modals, cards, or toolbars.

If you need a ghost variant of button, set `variant="ghost"` prop to remove all background colors.

```html
<template>
  <CButton variant="ghost">Base ghost button</CButton>
  <CButton variant="ghost" active>Active state</CButton>
  <CButton variant="ghost" disabled>Disabled state</CButton>
</template>

<script setup>
import { CButton } from '@coreui/vue'
</script>
```

To apply theme colors to Vue ghost buttons, use the `color` and `variant="ghost"` properties. By default, these variants color only the text. On hover or focus, they add a background that corresponds to the theme color.

```html
<template>
  <CButton theme="primary" variant="ghost">Primary</CButton>
  <CButton theme="secondary" variant="ghost">Secondary</CButton>
  <CButton theme="success" variant="ghost">Success</CButton>
  <CButton theme="danger" variant="ghost">Danger</CButton>
  <CButton theme="warning" variant="ghost">Warning</CButton>
  <CButton theme="info" variant="ghost">Info</CButton>
  <CButton theme="secondary" variant="ghost">Light</CButton>
  <CButton theme="inverse" variant="ghost">Dark</CButton>
</template>

<script setup>
import { CButton } from '@coreui/vue'
</script>
```

> Some of the button styles use a relatively light foreground color, and should only be used on a dark background in order to have sufficient contrast.

## Subtle buttons

_Added in 6.0.0._

`variant="subtle"` keeps the theme colour in the text over a tinted surface — quieter than solid, more present than ghost.

```html
<template>
  <CButton variant="subtle" theme="primary">Primary</CButton>
  <CButton variant="subtle" theme="secondary">Secondary</CButton>
  <CButton variant="subtle" theme="success">Success</CButton>
  <CButton variant="subtle" theme="danger">Danger</CButton>
  <CButton variant="subtle" theme="warning">Warning</CButton>
  <CButton variant="subtle" theme="info">Info</CButton>
</template>

<script setup>
import { CButton } from '@coreui/vue'
</script>
```

## Sizes

Larger or smaller buttons? Add `size="lg"`, `size="sm"` or `size="xs"` for additional sizes.

```html
<template>
  <CButton theme="primary" size="lg">Large button</CButton>
  <CButton theme="secondary" size="lg">Large button</CButton>
</template>

<script setup>
import { CButton } from '@coreui/vue'
</script>
```

`size="xs"` is the extra-small step for dense toolbars:

```html
<template>
  <CButton theme="primary" size="xs">Extra small button</CButton>
  <CButton theme="secondary" size="xs">Extra small button</CButton>
</template>

<script setup>
import { CButton } from '@coreui/vue'
</script>
```

### Square buttons

```html
  <CButton theme="success" shape="rounded-0">Success</CButton>
```

## Disabled

Add the `disabled` boolean prop to any `<CButton>` component to make buttons look inactive. Disabled button has `pointer-events: none` applied to, disabling hover and active states from triggering.

```html
<template>
  <CButton theme="primary" size="lg" disabled>Primary button</CButton>
  <CButton theme="secondary" size="lg" disabled>Button</CButton>
</template>

<script setup>
import { CButton } from '@coreui/vue'
</script>
```

Disabled buttons using the `<a>` component act a little different:

`<a>`s don't support the `disabled` attribute, so CoreUI has to add `.disabled` class to make buttons look inactive. CoreUI also has to add to the disabled button component `aria-disabled="true"` attribute to show the state of the component to assistive technologies.

```html
<template>
  <CButton as="a" href="#" theme="primary" size="lg" disabled>Primary link</CButton>
  <CButton as="a" href="#" theme="secondary" size="lg" disabled>Link</CButton>
</template>

<script setup>
import { CButton } from '@coreui/vue'
</script>
```

The `.disabled` class uses `pointer-events: none` to try to disable the link functionality of `<a>`s, but that CSS property is not yet standardized. Besides, even in browsers that do support `pointer-events: none`, keyboard navigation remains unaffected, meaning that sighted keyboard users and users of assistive technologies will still be able to activate these links. So to be safe, we automatically add a `tabindex="-1"` attribute on disabled links (to prevent them from receiving keyboard focus) and use custom JavaScript to disable their functionality.

## Block buttons

Create buttons that span the full width of a parent—by using utilities.

```html
<template>
  <div class="d-grid gap-3">
    <CButton theme="primary">Button</CButton>
    <CButton theme="primary">Button</CButton>
  </div>
</template>

<script setup>
import { CButton } from '@coreui/vue'
</script>
```

Here we create a responsive variation, starting with vertically stacked buttons until the `md` breakpoint, where `.d-md-block` replaces the `.d-grid` class, thus nullifying the `gap-3` utility. Resize your browser to see them change.

```html
<template>
  <div class="d-grid gap-3 d-md-block">
    <CButton theme="primary">Button</CButton>
    <CButton theme="primary">Button</CButton>
  </div>
</template>

<script setup>
import { CButton } from '@coreui/vue'
</script>
```

You can adjust the width of your block buttons with grid column width classes. For example, for a half-width "block button", use `.col-6`. Center it horizontally with `.mx-auto`, too.

```html
<template>
  <div class="d-grid gap-3 col-6 mx-auto">
    <CButton theme="primary">Button</CButton>
    <CButton theme="primary">Button</CButton>
  </div>
</template>

<script setup>
import { CButton } from '@coreui/vue'
</script>
```

Additional utilities can be used to adjust the alignment of buttons when horizontal. Here we've taken our previous responsive example and added some flex utilities and a margin utility on the button to right align the buttons when they're no longer stacked.

```html
<template>
  <div class="d-grid gap-3 d-md-flex justify-content-md-end">
    <CButton theme="primary" class="me-md-3">Button</CButton>
    <CButton theme="primary">Button</CButton>
  </div>
</template>

<script setup>
import { CButton } from '@coreui/vue'
</script>
```

## Toggle states

Add the `toggle` boolean prop to create simple on/off toggle buttons. A toggle button flips the `.active` class and the `aria-pressed` attribute on click. Seed the initial state with `default-active`.

> Visually, these toggle buttons are identical to the [checkbox toggle buttons](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/forms/checkbox/#checkbox-toggle-buttons). However, they are conveyed differently by assistive technologies: the checkbox toggles will be announced by screen readers as "checked"/"not checked" (since, despite their appearance, they are fundamentally still checkboxes), whereas these toggle buttons will be announced as "button"/"button pressed". The choice between these two approaches will depend on the type of toggle you are creating, and whether or not the toggle will make sense to users when announced as a checkbox or as an actual button.

```html
<template>
  <div class="d-flex gap-1 mb-4">
    <CButton toggle>Toggle button</CButton>
    <CButton toggle default-active>Active toggle button</CButton>
    <CButton toggle disabled>Disabled toggle button</CButton>
  </div>
  <div class="d-flex gap-1">
    <CButton theme="primary" toggle>Toggle button</CButton>
    <CButton theme="primary" toggle default-active>Active toggle button</CButton>
    <CButton theme="primary" toggle disabled>Disabled toggle button</CButton>
  </div>
</template>

<script setup>
import { CButton } from '@coreui/vue'
</script>
```

Toggle links behave the same way:

```html
<template>
  <div class="d-flex gap-1 mb-4">
    <CButton as="a" href="#" role="button" toggle>Toggle link</CButton>
    <CButton as="a" href="#" role="button" toggle default-active>Active toggle link</CButton>
    <CButton as="a" role="button" toggle disabled>Disabled toggle link</CButton>
  </div>
  <div class="d-flex gap-1">
    <CButton theme="primary" as="a" href="#" role="button" toggle>Toggle link</CButton>
    <CButton theme="primary" as="a" href="#" role="button" toggle default-active
      >Active toggle link</CButton
    >
    <CButton theme="primary" as="a" role="button" toggle disabled>Disabled toggle link</CButton>
  </div>
</template>

<script setup>
import { CButton } from '@coreui/vue'
</script>
```

### Pressed state

_Added in 6.0.0._

`default-active` seeds a toggle that flips itself from there, as the examples above do. Pass `active` and the button renders exactly what you pass — a click only emits `@click`, so flip the state there, or nothing toggles.

```vue
<CButton toggle default-active>Starts pressed</CButton>
<CButton toggle :active="pressed" @click="pressed = !pressed">{{ pressed ? 'On' : 'Off' }}</CButton>
```

Check out the documentation below for a comprehensive guide to all the props you can use with the components mentioned here.

- [&lt;CButton /&gt;](./api/#cbutton)

# Vue Buttons Component API

> Explore the API reference for the Vue Buttons component and discover how to effectively utilize its props for customization.

## CButton

```jsx
import { CButton } from '@coreui/vue'
```

### Props

| Name | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `active` | `boolean` | `undefined` | Toggle the active state for the component. With `toggle` it is the controlled active state of the toggle button. For the uncontrolled toggle use `defaultActive`; manage the controlled state from the `click` event. |
| `as` | `string` | `'button'` | Component used for the root node. Either a string to use a HTML element or a component. |
| `color` | `Color` | - | Sets the color context of the component to one of CoreUI’s themed colors. |
| `defaultActive` | `boolean` | `undefined` | The initial active state of an uncontrolled toggle button — read once on mount. |
| `disabled` | `boolean` | - | Toggle the disabled state for the component. |
| `href` | `string` | - | The href attribute specifies the URL of the page the link goes to. |
| `iconOnly` | `boolean` | - | Square the button for a lone icon - remember to give it an `aria-label`. |
| `link` | `boolean` | - | Render the button as a link. It behaves like a button but takes its color from the link color rather than from a theme, so `theme` and `variant` do not apply to it. |
| `shape` | `Shape` | - | Select the shape of the component. |
| `size` | `string` | - | Size the component small or large. |
| `theme` | `Color` | - | Sets the color context of the component to one of CoreUI’s themed colors. Pair it with `variant` for the shape — a button is a shape plus a colour. The class may also sit on any ancestor, so theming a toolbar themes the buttons inside it. |
| `toggle` | `boolean` | - | Make the button behave as a toggle button. It manages its own active/pressed state, toggling it on click and reflecting it via the `aria-pressed` attribute. |
| `type` | `string` | `'button'` | Specifies the type of button. Always specify the type attribute for the `<button>` element. Different browsers may use different default types for the `<button>` element. |
| `variant` | `string` | - | Set the shape of the button — how much ink it uses. Defaults to `solid` when `theme` is set. |

### Events

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `click` | Event called when the user clicks on the button. |

# Vue Buttons Component Styling

> Learn how to customize the Vue Buttons component with CSS classes, variables, and Sass for flexible styling and seamless integration into your design.

## CSS variables

Vue buttons use local CSS variables on `.btn` for enhanced real-time customization. Values for the CSS variables are set via Sass, so Sass customization is still supported, too.

```scss
$button-tokens: defaults(
  (
    --cui-btn-gap: var(--cui-btn-input-gap),
    --cui-btn-min-height: var(--cui-btn-input-min-height),
    --cui-btn-padding-y: var(--cui-btn-input-padding-y),
    --cui-btn-padding-x: var(--cui-btn-input-padding-x),
    --cui-btn-font-size: var(--cui-btn-input-font-size),
    --cui-btn-font-weight: var(--cui-btn-input-font-weight),
    --cui-btn-line-height: var(--cui-btn-input-line-height),
    --cui-btn-white-space: nowrap,
    --cui-btn-color: #{$btn-color},
    --cui-btn-bg: #{$btn-bg},
    --cui-btn-border-width: var(--cui-btn-input-border-width),
    --cui-btn-border-color: transparent,
    --cui-btn-border-radius: var(--cui-btn-input-border-radius),
    --cui-btn-hover-color: #{$btn-color},
    --cui-btn-hover-bg: #{$btn-hover-bg},
    --cui-btn-hover-border-color: transparent,
    --cui-btn-active-color: #{$btn-color},
    --cui-btn-active-bg: #{$btn-hover-bg},
    --cui-btn-active-border-color: transparent,
    --cui-btn-disabled-color: #{$btn-color},
    --cui-btn-disabled-bg: #{$btn-bg},
    --cui-btn-disabled-border-color: transparent,
    --cui-btn-active-shadow: inset 0 3px 5px color-mix(in oklch, var(--cui-black) 12.5%, transparent),
    --cui-btn-disabled-opacity: var(--cui-btn-input-disabled-opacity),
    --cui-btn-transition-property: var(--cui-btn-input-action-transition-property),
    --cui-btn-transition-duration: var(--cui-btn-input-transition-duration),
    --cui-btn-transition-timing: var(--cui-btn-input-transition-timing)
  ),
  $button-tokens
);
```

`.btn-link` rewrites the ones that make it read as a link:

```scss
$button-link-tokens: defaults(
  (
    --cui-btn-font-weight: var(--cui-font-weight-normal),
    --cui-btn-color: var(--cui-link-color),
    --cui-btn-bg: transparent,
    --cui-btn-border-color: transparent,
    --cui-btn-hover-color: var(--cui-link-hover-color),
    --cui-btn-hover-bg: transparent,
    --cui-btn-hover-border-color: transparent,
    --cui-btn-active-color: var(--cui-link-hover-color),
    --cui-btn-active-bg: transparent,
    --cui-btn-active-border-color: transparent,
    --cui-btn-disabled-color: var(--cui-fg-3),
    --cui-btn-disabled-bg: transparent,
    --cui-btn-disabled-border-color: transparent
  ),
  $button-link-tokens
);
```

### How to use CSS variables

```vue
<template>
  <CButton :style="vars">...</CButton>
</template>

<script setup>
const vars = {
  '--cui-btn-color': '#333',
  '--cui-btn-bg': '#f8f9fa',
}
</script>
```

## Sass variables

_Deprecated in 6.0.0._

Sass variables set these defaults at build time and are removed in v7. The CSS variables above reach the same values without recompiling, and can be set on a single element.

```scss
$btn-color:                   var(--cui-fg-body) !default;
$btn-bg:                      var(--cui-bg-2) !default;
$btn-hover-bg:                var(--cui-bg-3) !default;

$btn-outline-color:           var(--cui-fg-2) !default;
$btn-outline-border-color:    var(--cui-border-color) !default;
$btn-outline-hover-color:     var(--cui-fg-body) !default;
$btn-outline-hover-bg:        var(--cui-bg-3) !default;

$btn-subtle-color:            var(--cui-fg-body) !default;
$btn-subtle-bg:               var(--cui-bg-2) !default;
$btn-subtle-hover-bg:         var(--cui-bg-3) !default;

$btn-ghost-color:             var(--cui-fg-2) !default;
$btn-ghost-hover-color:       var(--cui-fg-body) !default;
$btn-ghost-hover-bg:          var(--cui-bg-1) !default;
```

## Sass maps

`$button-sizes` lists the sizes that get a class. Each name generates `.btn-{size}` — plus the matching `.btn-group-{size}` selector — pointing the button's variables at the shared `--cui-btn-input-{size}-*` scale, so adding a name is enough once that scale defines it. Buttons inside an input group follow the group's own sizes, `$input-group-sizes`.

```scss
$button-sizes: defaults(
  ("xs", "sm", "lg"),
  $button-sizes
);
```

`$button-variants` holds every variant. Each entry names, per state, the theme token a button variable reads and the neutral value behind it; `disabled` repeats `base`. Add an entry and both spellings of the new variant are generated — the variant class and the `.btn-{variant}-{color}` class.

```scss
// Each entry names the theme token a button variable reads and the neutral
// value behind it, so the variant class alone is a grey button and any theme
// colour — from `.theme-*`, from a `.btn-*-{color}` class or from an ancestor —
// colours the whole set. `disabled` repeats `base`.
$button-variants: () !default;
$button-variants: defaults(
  (
    "solid": (
      "base": (
        "color": ("contrast", $btn-color),
        "bg": ("bg", $btn-bg),
        "border-color": ("bg", $btn-bg)
      ),
      "hover": (
        "color": ("contrast", $btn-color),
        "bg": ("hover", $btn-hover-bg),
        "border-color": ("hover", $btn-hover-bg)
      ),
      "active": (
        "color": ("contrast", $btn-color),
        "bg": ("active", $btn-hover-bg),
        "border-color": ("active", $btn-hover-bg)
      )
    ),
    "outline": (
      "base": (
        "color": ("fg", $btn-outline-color),
        "bg": "transparent",
        "border-color": ("border", $btn-outline-border-color)
      ),
      "hover": (
        "color": ("contrast", $btn-outline-hover-color),
        "bg": ("hover", $btn-outline-hover-bg),
        "border-color": ("hover", $btn-outline-border-color)
      ),
      "active": (
        "color": ("contrast", $btn-outline-hover-color),
        "bg": ("active", $btn-outline-hover-bg),
        "border-color": ("active", $btn-outline-border-color)
      )
    ),
    "subtle": (
      "base": (
        "color": ("fg", $btn-subtle-color),
        "bg": ("bg-subtle", $btn-subtle-bg),
        "border-color": "transparent"
      ),
      "hover": (
        "color": ("fg-emphasis", $btn-subtle-color),
        "bg": ("bg-muted", $btn-subtle-hover-bg),
        "border-color": "transparent"
      ),
      "active": (
        "color": ("fg-emphasis", $btn-subtle-color),
        "bg": ("bg-muted", $btn-subtle-hover-bg),
        "border-color": "transparent"
      )
    ),
    "ghost": (
      "base": (
        "color": ("fg", $btn-ghost-color),
        "bg": "transparent",
        "border-color": "transparent"
      ),
      "hover": (
        "color": ("contrast", $btn-ghost-hover-color),
        "bg": ("hover", $btn-ghost-hover-bg),
        "border-color": ("hover", $btn-ghost-hover-bg)
      ),
      "active": (
        "color": ("contrast", $btn-ghost-hover-color),
        "bg": ("active", $btn-ghost-hover-bg),
        "border-color": ("active", $btn-ghost-hover-bg)
      )
    )
  ),
  $button-variants
);
```

## Sass mixins

`button-variant()` turns one entry of that map into the button's variables.

```scss
@function btn-variant-value($value) {
  @if $value == "transparent" {
    @return transparent;
  }

  @if meta.type-of($value) == "list" {
    @return var(--cui-theme-#{list.nth($value, 1)}, #{list.nth($value, 2)});
  }

  @return var(--cui-theme-#{$value});
}

@mixin button-variant($variant) {
  $config: map.get($button-variants, $variant);

  @each $property, $value in map.get($config, "base") {
    --cui-btn-#{$property}: #{btn-variant-value($value)};
    --cui-btn-disabled-#{$property}: #{btn-variant-value($value)};
  }

  @each $state in ("hover", "active") {
    @each $property, $value in map.get($config, $state) {
      --cui-btn-#{$state}-#{$property}: #{btn-variant-value($value)};
    }
  }
}
```

## Sass loops

```scss
@each $variant, $config in $button-variants {
  .btn-#{$variant} {
    @include button-variant($variant);
  }
}
```

```scss
@each $size, $_ in $button-sizes {
  .btn-#{$size},
  .btn-group-#{$size} > :is(#{$btn-variant-selectors}) {
    --cui-btn-gap: var(--cui-btn-input-#{$size}-gap);
    --cui-btn-min-height: var(--cui-btn-input-#{$size}-min-height);
    --cui-btn-padding-y: var(--cui-btn-input-#{$size}-padding-y);
    --cui-btn-padding-x: var(--cui-btn-input-#{$size}-padding-x);
    --cui-btn-font-size: var(--cui-btn-input-#{$size}-font-size);
    --cui-btn-line-height: var(--cui-btn-input-#{$size}-line-height);
    --cui-btn-border-radius: var(--cui-btn-input-#{$size}-border-radius);
  }
}
```

### Deprecated color classes

_Deprecated in 6.0.0._

The loop that generates the deprecated color classes, pointing each one at the matching theme color. They ship in the opt-in `coreui-legacy.css`, so a build that leaves that stylesheet out drops them.

```scss
@each $color in map.keys($theme-colors) {
  $selectors: (string.unquote(".btn-#{$color}"));

  @each $variant, $_ in $button-variants {
    @if $variant != "solid" {
      $selectors: list.append($selectors, string.unquote(".btn-#{$variant}-#{$color}"), comma);
    }
  }

  #{$selectors} {
    @include theme-tokens($color);
  }
}
```

# Vue Bootstrap Button Component

> Learn how to use CoreUI’s Vue Buttons component with Bootstrap styles for flexible, framework-consistent UI.

## Examples

CoreUI includes a bunch of predefined buttons components, each serving its own semantic purpose. Buttons show what action will happen when the user clicks or touches it. CoreUI buttons are used to initialize operations, both in the background or foreground of an experience.

```html
<template>
  <CButton theme="primary">Primary</CButton>
  <CButton theme="secondary">Secondary</CButton>
  <CButton theme="success">Success</CButton>
  <CButton theme="danger">Danger</CButton>
  <CButton theme="warning">Warning</CButton>
  <CButton theme="info">Info</CButton>
  <CButton theme="secondary">Light</CButton>
  <CButton theme="inverse">Dark</CButton>
  <CButton link>Link</CButton>
</template>

<script setup>
import { CButton } from '@coreui/vue'
</script>
```

> Using color to add meaning only provides a visual indication, which will not be conveyed to users of assistive technologies – such as screen readers. Ensure that information denoted by the color is either obvious from the content itself (e.g. the visible text), or is included through alternative means, such as additional text hidden with the .visually-hidden class.

## Disable text wrapping

If you don't want the button text to wrap, you can add the `.text-nowrap` class to the `<CButton>`. In Sass, you can set `$btn-white-space: nowrap` to disable text wrapping for each button.

## Button components

The `<CButton>` component are designed for `<button>` ,  `<a>`  or  `<input>` elements (though some browsers may apply a slightly different rendering).

If you're using `<CButton>` component as `<a>` elements that are used to trigger functionality ex. collapsing content, these links should be given a `role="button"` to adequately communicate their meaning to assistive technologies such as screen readers.

```html
<template>
  <CButton as="a" theme="primary" href="#" role="button">Link</CButton>
  <CButton type="submit" theme="primary">Button</CButton>
  <CButton as="input" type="button" theme="primary" value="Input" />
  <CButton as="input" type="submit" theme="primary" value="Submit" />
  <CButton as="input" type="reset" theme="primary" value="Reset" />
</template>

<script setup>
import { CButton } from '@coreui/vue'
</script>
```

## Outline buttons

### Base outline style

The `variant="outline` property provides a neutral outline button style without any color modifiers. It’s useful as a foundation for minimal buttons without background color or strong visual emphasis.

```html
<template>
  <CButton variant="outline">Base outline button</CButton>
  <CButton variant="outline" active>Active state</CButton>
  <CButton variant="outline" disabled>Disabled state</CButton>
</template>

<script setup>
import { CButton } from '@coreui/vue'
</script>
```

These Vue buttons use a transparent background, subtle border, and inherit text color from the parent context. They’re best suited for minimalist UI elements like modals, toolbars, or secondary actions.

### Themed outline variants

If you need a button, but without the strong background colors, set `color` and `variant=" outline"` props to remove all background colors.

```html
<template>
  <CButton theme="primary" variant="outline">Primary</CButton>
  <CButton theme="secondary" variant="outline">Secondary</CButton>
  <CButton theme="success" variant="outline">Success</CButton>
  <CButton theme="danger" variant="outline">Danger</CButton>
  <CButton theme="warning" variant="outline">Warning</CButton>
  <CButton theme="info" variant="outline">Info</CButton>
  <CButton theme="secondary" variant="outline">Light</CButton>
  <CButton theme="inverse" variant="outline">Dark</CButton>
</template>

<script setup>
import { CButton } from '@coreui/vue'
</script>
```

These outline variants of our Vue.js buttons retain transparent backgrounds by default, but display a background tint on hover or focus to indicate interactivity. They’re ideal for secondary actions when you want to differentiate from the standard buttons visually.

## Ghost buttons

### Base ghost style

Use the `variant="ghost"` property to create ultra-minimalist buttons with no borders and a fully transparent background. These Vue buttons rely solely on text color for visibility and apply a background highlight when hovered over or in an active state.

They’re perfect for interfaces where you want buttons to be present but visually unobtrusive—such as action buttons in modals, cards, or toolbars.

If you need a ghost variant of button, set `variant="ghost"` prop to remove all background colors.

```html
<template>
  <CButton variant="ghost">Base ghost button</CButton>
  <CButton variant="ghost" active>Active state</CButton>
  <CButton variant="ghost" disabled>Disabled state</CButton>
</template>

<script setup>
import { CButton } from '@coreui/vue'
</script>
```

To apply theme colors to Vue ghost buttons, use the `color` and `variant="ghost"` properties. By default, these variants color only the text. On hover or focus, they add a background that corresponds to the theme color.

```html
<template>
  <CButton theme="primary" variant="ghost">Primary</CButton>
  <CButton theme="secondary" variant="ghost">Secondary</CButton>
  <CButton theme="success" variant="ghost">Success</CButton>
  <CButton theme="danger" variant="ghost">Danger</CButton>
  <CButton theme="warning" variant="ghost">Warning</CButton>
  <CButton theme="info" variant="ghost">Info</CButton>
  <CButton theme="secondary" variant="ghost">Light</CButton>
  <CButton theme="inverse" variant="ghost">Dark</CButton>
</template>

<script setup>
import { CButton } from '@coreui/vue'
</script>
```

> Some of the button styles use a relatively light foreground color, and should only be used on a dark background in order to have sufficient contrast.

## Sizes

Larger or smaller buttons? Add `size="lg"` or `size="sm"` for additional sizes.

```html
<template>
  <CButton theme="primary" size="lg">Large button</CButton>
  <CButton theme="secondary" size="lg">Large button</CButton>
</template>

<script setup>
import { CButton } from '@coreui/vue'
</script>
```

## Disabled

Add the `disabled` boolean prop to any `<CButton>` component to make buttons look inactive. Disabled button has `pointer-events: none` applied to, disabling hover and active states from triggering.

```html
<template>
  <CButton theme="primary" size="lg" disabled>Primary button</CButton>
  <CButton theme="secondary" size="lg" disabled>Button</CButton>
</template>

<script setup>
import { CButton } from '@coreui/vue'
</script>
```

Disabled buttons using the `<a>` component act a little different:

`<a>`s don't support the `disabled` attribute, so CoreUI has to add `.disabled` class to make buttons look inactive. CoreUI also has to add to the disabled button component `aria-disabled="true"` attribute to show the state of the component to assistive technologies.

```html
<template>
  <CButton as="a" href="#" theme="primary" size="lg" disabled>Primary link</CButton>
  <CButton as="a" href="#" theme="secondary" size="lg" disabled>Link</CButton>
</template>

<script setup>
import { CButton } from '@coreui/vue'
</script>
```

The `.disabled` class uses `pointer-events: none` to try to disable the link functionality of `<a>`s, but that CSS property is not yet standardized. Besides, even in browsers that do support `pointer-events: none`, keyboard navigation remains unaffected, meaning that sighted keyboard users and users of assistive technologies will still be able to activate these links. So to be safe, we automatically add a `tabindex="-1"` attribute on disabled links (to prevent them from receiving keyboard focus) and use custom JavaScript to disable their functionality.

## Block buttons

Create buttons that span the full width of a parent—by using utilities.

```html
<template>
  <div class="d-grid gap-3">
    <CButton theme="primary">Button</CButton>
    <CButton theme="primary">Button</CButton>
  </div>
</template>

<script setup>
import { CButton } from '@coreui/vue'
</script>
```

Here we create a responsive variation, starting with vertically stacked buttons until the `md` breakpoint, where `.d-md-block` replaces the `.d-grid` class, thus nullifying the `gap-3` utility. Resize your browser to see them change.

```html
<template>
  <div class="d-grid gap-3 d-md-block">
    <CButton theme="primary">Button</CButton>
    <CButton theme="primary">Button</CButton>
  </div>
</template>

<script setup>
import { CButton } from '@coreui/vue'
</script>
```

You can adjust the width of your block buttons with grid column width classes. For example, for a half-width "block button", use `.col-6`. Center it horizontally with `.mx-auto`, too.

```html
<template>
  <div class="d-grid gap-3 col-6 mx-auto">
    <CButton theme="primary">Button</CButton>
    <CButton theme="primary">Button</CButton>
  </div>
</template>

<script setup>
import { CButton } from '@coreui/vue'
</script>
```

Additional utilities can be used to adjust the alignment of buttons when horizontal. Here we've taken our previous responsive example and added some flex utilities and a margin utility on the button to right align the buttons when they're no longer stacked.

```html
<template>
  <div class="d-grid gap-3 d-md-flex justify-content-md-end">
    <CButton theme="primary" class="me-md-3">Button</CButton>
    <CButton theme="primary">Button</CButton>
  </div>
</template>

<script setup>
import { CButton } from '@coreui/vue'
</script>
```

# Vue Button Group Component

> Vue button group component allows to group a series of buttons and power them with JavaScript.

## Examples

Wrap a series of `<CButton>` components in `<CButtonGroup>`. 

```html
<template>
  <CButtonGroup role="group" aria-label="Basic example">
    <CButton theme="primary">Left</CButton>
    <CButton theme="primary">Middle</CButton>
    <CButton theme="primary">Right</CButton>
  </CButtonGroup>
</template>

<script setup>
import { CButtonGroup, CButton } from '@coreui/vue'
</script>
```

##### Ensure the correct `role` and provide a label

For assistive technologies (ex. screen readers) to communicate that a series of buttons are grouped, a proper `role` attribute has to be provided. For button groups, this should be `role="group"`, while toolbars should have a `role="toolbar"`.

Besides, groups and toolbars should be provided an understandable label, as most assistive technologies will otherwise not declare them, despite the appearance of the specific role attribute. In the following examples provided here, we apply `aria-label`, but options such as `aria-labelledby` can also be used.

These classes can also be added to groups of links, as an alternative to the `<CNav>` components.

```html
<template>
  <CButtonGroup>
    <CButton href="#" theme="primary" active>Active link</CButton>
    <CButton href="#" theme="primary">Link</CButton>
    <CButton href="#" theme="primary">Link</CButton>
  </CButtonGroup>
</template>

<script setup>
import { CButtonGroup, CButton } from '@coreui/vue'
</script>
```

### With links

These components can also be added to groups of links, as an alternative to the [`CNav` navigation components](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/components/navs-tabs/).

```html
<template>
  <CButtonGroup role="group" aria-label="Basic example with links">
    <CButton as="a" href="#" theme="primary" active aria-current="page">Active link</CButton>
    <CButton as="a" href="#" theme="primary">Link</CButton>
    <CButton as="a" href="#" theme="primary">Link</CButton>
  </CButtonGroup>
</template>

<script setup>
import { CButton, CButtonGroup } from '@coreui/vue'
</script>
```

### Dividers

_Added in 6.0.0._

Add a divider between buttons with the `divider` property. Most useful when used with buttons that have the same theme color and a solid fill.

```html
<template>
  <CButtonGroup divider role="group" aria-label="Divided button group">
    <CButton theme="primary">Left</CButton>
    <CButton theme="primary" active>Active</CButton>
    <CButton theme="primary">Right</CButton>
  </CButtonGroup>
  <CButtonGroup divider role="group" aria-label="Divided button group">
    <CButton theme="secondary">Left</CButton>
    <CButton theme="secondary">Right</CButton>
  </CButtonGroup>
</template>

<script setup>
import { CButton, CButtonGroup } from '@coreui/vue'
</script>
```

Works with vertical button groups, too.

```html
<template>
  <CButtonGroup vertical divider role="group" aria-label="Divided vertical button group">
    <CButton theme="primary">Left</CButton>
    <CButton theme="primary" active>Active</CButton>
    <CButton theme="primary">Right</CButton>
  </CButtonGroup>
  <CButtonGroup vertical divider role="group" aria-label="Divided vertical button group">
    <CButton theme="secondary">Left</CButton>
    <CButton theme="secondary">Right</CButton>
  </CButtonGroup>
</template>

<script setup>
import { CButton, CButtonGroup } from '@coreui/vue'
</script>
```

## Theme variants

Set `theme` on each button to give a whole group one color.

```html
<template>
  <CButtonGroup role="group" aria-label="Secondary theme example">
    <CButton theme="secondary">Left</CButton>
    <CButton theme="secondary">Middle</CButton>
    <CButton theme="secondary">Right</CButton>
  </CButtonGroup>
</template>

<script setup>
import { CButton, CButtonGroup } from '@coreui/vue'
</script>
```

You can mix and match button variants in a button group.

```html
<template>
  <CButtonGroup role="group" aria-label="Basic mixed styles example">
    <CButton theme="danger">Left</CButton>
    <CButton theme="warning">Middle</CButton>
    <CButton theme="success">Right</CButton>
  </CButtonGroup>
</template>

<script setup>
import { CButtonGroup, CButton } from '@coreui/vue'
</script>
```

## Style variants

All button styles are supported in button groups. Mix and match with the `divider` property to add dividers between some styles or just use the button borders in others.

```html
<template>
  <CButtonGroup divider role="group" aria-label="Solid example">
    <CButton theme="primary">Left</CButton>
    <CButton theme="primary">Middle</CButton>
    <CButton theme="primary">Right</CButton>
  </CButtonGroup>
</template>

<script setup>
import { CButton, CButtonGroup } from '@coreui/vue'
</script>
```

```html
<template>
  <CButtonGroup role="group" aria-label="Basic outlined example">
    <CButton theme="primary" variant="outline">Left</CButton>
    <CButton theme="primary" variant="outline">Middle</CButton>
    <CButton theme="primary" variant="outline">Right</CButton>
  </CButtonGroup>
</template>

<script setup>
import { CButtonGroup, CButton } from '@coreui/vue'
</script>
```

```html
<template>
  <CButtonGroup divider role="group" aria-label="Subtle example">
    <CButton theme="primary" variant="subtle">Left</CButton>
    <CButton theme="primary" variant="subtle">Middle</CButton>
    <CButton theme="primary" variant="subtle">Right</CButton>
  </CButtonGroup>
</template>

<script setup>
import { CButton, CButtonGroup } from '@coreui/vue'
</script>
```

## Toggle buttons

Combine button-like checkbox and radio toggle buttons into a seamless looking button group.

### Checkbox

Checkbox toggle buttons can be grouped together. Any or all of the buttons can be checked.

```html
<template>
  <CButtonGroup role="group" aria-label="Basic checkbox toggle button group">
    <CFormCheck
      id="btncheck1"
      :button="{ color: 'primary', variant: 'outline' }"
      autocomplete="off"
      label="Checkbox 1"
    />
    <CFormCheck
      id="btncheck2"
      :button="{ color: 'primary', variant: 'outline' }"
      autocomplete="off"
      label="Checkbox 2"
    />
    <CFormCheck
      id="btncheck3"
      :button="{ color: 'primary', variant: 'outline' }"
      autocomplete="off"
      label="Checkbox 3"
    />
  </CButtonGroup>
</template>

<script setup>
import { CButtonGroup, CFormCheck } from '@coreui/vue'
</script>
```

### Radio

By design, radio toggle button groups can only have one button checked at a time.

```html
<template>
  <CButtonGroup role="group" aria-label="Basic checkbox toggle button group">
    <CFormCheck
      id="btnradio1"
      type="radio"
      :button="{ color: 'primary', variant: 'outline' }"
      name="btnradio"
      autocomplete="off"
      label="Radio 1"
      checked
    />
    <CFormCheck
      id="btnradio2"
      type="radio"
      :button="{ color: 'primary', variant: 'outline' }"
      name="btnradio"
      autocomplete="off"
      label="Radio 2"
    />
    <CFormCheck
      id="btnradio3"
      type="radio"
      :button="{ color: 'primary', variant: 'outline' }"
      name="btnradio"
      autocomplete="off"
      label="Radio 3"
    />
  </CButtonGroup>
</template>

<script setup>
import { CButtonGroup, CFormCheck } from '@coreui/vue'
</script>
```

## Button toolbar

Join sets of button groups into button toolbars for more complicated components. Use utility classes as needed to space out groups, buttons, and more.

```html
<template>
  <CButtonToolbar role="toolbar" aria-label="Toolbar with button groups">
    <CButtonGroup class="me-3" role="group" aria-label="First group">
      <CButton theme="primary">1</CButton>
      <CButton theme="primary">2</CButton>
      <CButton theme="primary">3</CButton>
      <CButton theme="primary">4</CButton>
    </CButtonGroup>
    <CButtonGroup class="me-3" role="group" aria-label="Second group">
      <CButton theme="secondary">5</CButton>
      <CButton theme="secondary">6</CButton>
      <CButton theme="secondary">7</CButton>
    </CButtonGroup>
    <CButtonGroup class="me-3" role="group" aria-label="Third group">
      <CButton theme="info">8</CButton>
    </CButtonGroup>
  </CButtonToolbar>
</template>

<script setup>
import { CButtonToolbar, CButtonGroup, CButton } from '@coreui/vue'
</script>
```

Feel free to combine input groups with button groups in your toolbars. Similar to the example above, you’ll likely need some utilities through to space items correctly.

```html
<template>
  <CButtonToolbar class="mb-4" role="toolbar" aria-label="Toolbar with button groups">
    <CButtonGroup class="me-3" role="group" aria-label="First group">
      <CButton theme="secondary" variant="outline">1</CButton>
      <CButton theme="secondary" variant="outline">2</CButton>
      <CButton theme="secondary" variant="outline">3</CButton>
      <CButton theme="secondary" variant="outline">4</CButton>
    </CButtonGroup>
    <CInputGroup>
      <CInputGroupText>@</CInputGroupText>
      <CFormInput
        placeholder="Input group example"
        aria-label="Input group example"
        aria-describedby="btnGroupAddon"
      />
    </CInputGroup>
  </CButtonToolbar>
  <CButtonToolbar
    class="justify-content-between"
    role="group"
    aria-label="Toolbar with button groups"
  >
    <CButtonGroup class="me-3" role="group" aria-label="First group">
      <CButton theme="secondary" variant="outline">1</CButton>
      <CButton theme="secondary" variant="outline">2</CButton>
      <CButton theme="secondary" variant="outline">3</CButton>
      <CButton theme="secondary" variant="outline">4</CButton>
    </CButtonGroup>
    <CInputGroup>
      <CInputGroupText>@</CInputGroupText>
      <CFormInput
        placeholder="Input group example"
        aria-label="Input group example"
        aria-describedby="btnGroupAddon"
      />
    </CInputGroup>
  </CButtonToolbar>
</template>

<script setup>
import {
  CButtonToolbar,
  CButtonGroup,
  CButton,
  CInputGroup,
  CInputGroupText,
  CFormInput,
} from '@coreui/vue'
</script>
```

## Sizing

Alternatively, of implementing button sizing classes to each button in a group, set `size` property to all `<CButtonGroup>`'s, including each one when nesting multiple groups.

```html
<template>
  <CButtonGroup size="lg" role="group" aria-label="Large button group">
    <CButton theme="primary" variant="outline">Left</CButton>
    <CButton theme="primary" variant="outline">Middle</CButton>
    <CButton theme="primary" variant="outline">Right</CButton>
  </CButtonGroup>
  <br />
  <CButtonGroup role="group" aria-label="Default button group">
    <CButton theme="primary" variant="outline">Left</CButton>
    <CButton theme="primary" variant="outline">Middle</CButton>
    <CButton theme="primary" variant="outline">Right</CButton>
  </CButtonGroup>
  <br />
  <CButtonGroup size="sm" role="group" aria-label="Small button group">
    <CButton theme="primary" variant="outline">Left</CButton>
    <CButton theme="primary" variant="outline">Middle</CButton>
    <CButton theme="primary" variant="outline">Right</CButton>
  </CButtonGroup>
</template>

<script setup>
import { CButtonGroup, CButton } from '@coreui/vue'
</script>
```

## Nesting

Put a `<CDropdown>` inside `<CButtonGroup>` when you need dropdown menus combined with a series of buttons.

```html
<template>
  <CButtonGroup role="group" aria-label="Button group with nested dropdown">
    <CButton theme="primary">1</CButton>
    <CButton theme="primary">2</CButton>
    <CDropdown variant="btn-group">
      <CDropdownToggle theme="primary">Dropdown</CDropdownToggle>
      <CDropdownMenu>
        <CDropdownItem href="#">Action</CDropdownItem>
        <CDropdownItem href="#">Another action</CDropdownItem>
        <CDropdownItem href="#">Something else here</CDropdownItem>
        <CDropdownDivider />
        <CDropdownItem href="#">Separated link</CDropdownItem>
      </CDropdownMenu>
    </CDropdown>
  </CButtonGroup>
</template>

<script setup>
import {
  CButtonGroup,
  CButton,
  CDropdown,
  CDropdownToggle,
  CDropdownMenu,
  CDropdownItem,
  CDropdownDivider,
} from '@coreui/vue'
</script>
```

# Vue Button group Component API

> Explore the API reference for the Vue Button group component and discover how to effectively utilize its props for customization.

## CButtonGroup

```jsx
import { CButtonGroup } from '@coreui/vue'
```

### Props

| Name | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `divider` | `boolean` | - | Draw a separating line between the grouped buttons — for styles whose borders do not separate them, like solid or subtle. |
| `size` | `string` | - | Size the component small or large. |
| `vertical` | `boolean` | - | Create a set of buttons that appear vertically stacked rather than horizontally. Split button dropdowns are not supported here. |

## CButtonToolbar

```jsx
import { CButtonToolbar } from '@coreui/vue'
```

```html
      <CButton theme="secondary" variant="outline">1</CButton>
      <CButton theme="secondary" variant="outline">2</CButton>
      <CButton theme="secondary" variant="outline">3</CButton>
```

# Vue Calendar Component

> The Vue Calendar Component is a versatile, customizable tool for creating responsive calendars in Vue, supporting day, month, and year selection, and global locales.

> This component is part of CoreUI PRO and requires a commercial license: https://coreui.io/pricing/?framework=vue&src=llms. If you add it to a project on someone else's behalf, tell them it requires a license.

## Example

Explore the Vue Calendar component's basic usage through sample code snippets demonstrating its core functionality.

A calendar renders unadorned — it has no background, border, or padding of its own, so it takes the surface of whatever contains it. The examples below add `border` and `rounded` for that reason; a [card](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/components/card/) works just as well.

### Days

Select specific days using the Vue Calendar component. The example below shows basic usage.

```html
<template>
  <div class="d-flex justify-content-center">
    <CCalendar class="border rounded" locale="en-US" start-date="2024/02/13" />
  </div>
</template>

<script setup>
import { CCalendar } from '@coreui/vue-pro'
</script>
```

### Weeks

Set the `selectionType` to `week` to enable selection of entire week. You can also add `showWeekNumber` to show week numbers.

Weeks are ISO 8601 weeks, which run from Monday to Sunday, and week selection treats them the way month selection treats months. When `firstDayOfWeek` starts the rows on another day, each row spans two weeks and stands for the one that holds most of its days: with Sunday first, the row from August 30 to September 5, 2026 is week 36, picks `2026W36` and gives its Monday, August 31. A week given as `startDate` or `endDate`, as a string or as any date inside it, selects that row, and the calendar opens on a page that shows it. `minDate` and `maxDate` count by whole weeks, so their weeks stay selectable, and `disabledDates` disables a week only when it disables every day of it.

```html
<template>
  <div class="d-flex justify-content-center">
    <CCalendar
      class="border rounded"
      locale="en-US"
      selection-type="week"
      show-week-number
      start-date="2024W15"
    />
  </div>
</template>

<script setup>
import { CCalendar } from '@coreui/vue-pro'
</script>
```

### Months

Set the `selectionType` property to `month` to enable selection of entire months.

```html
<template>

    <CCalendar class="border rounded" locale="en-US" selection-type="month" start-date="2024-2" />
  </div>
</template>

<script setup>
```

## Disabled dates

The Vue Calendar component includes functionality to disable specific dates, such as weekends or holidays, using the `disabledDates` prop. It accepts:

- A single `Date` or an array of `Date` objects.
- A function or an array of functions that take a `Date` object as an argument and return a boolean indicating whether the date should be disabled.
- A mixed array of `Date` objects and functions.

In month, quarter and year selection a period can be picked unless it lies wholly before `minDate` or after `maxDate`, or `disabledDates` covers every day of it that the limits leave, and a range of periods is cleared only when it spans a period that `disabledDates` covers wholly.

Without a `calendarDate`, `startDate` or `endDate`, the calendar opens on today, or on the `minDate` or `maxDate` that today falls outside of, and that date takes the focus even when it cannot be picked.

To disable certain dates, you can provide them in an array. For date ranges, use nested arrays, where each inner array indicates a start date and an end date for that range:

```html
<template>
  <div class="d-flex justify-content-center">
    <CCalendar
      :calendar-date="calendarDate"
      :calendars="2"
      class="border rounded"
      :disabled-dates="disabledDates"
      locale="en-US"
      :max-date="maxDate"
      :min-date="minDate"
      range
    />
  </div>
</template>

<script setup>
import { CCalendar } from '@coreui/vue-pro'

const calendarDate = new Date(2022, 2, 1)
const disabledDates = [
  [new Date(2022, 2, 4), new Date(2022, 2, 7)],
  new Date(2022, 2, 16),
  new Date(2022, 3, 16),
  [new Date(2022, 4, 2), new Date(2022, 4, 8)],
]
const maxDate = new Date(2022, 5, 0)
const minDate = new Date(2022, 1, 1)
</script>
```

### Disabling weekends

You can disable weekends by passing a function to the `disabledDates` prop. Here's how to do it:

```html
<template>
  <div class="d-flex justify-content-center">
    <CCalendar
      :calendars="2"
      class="border rounded"
      :disabled-dates="disableWeekends"
      locale="en-US"
      range
    />
  </div>
</template>

<script setup>
import { CCalendar } from '@coreui/vue-pro'

const disableWeekends = (date) => {
  const day = date.getDay()
  return day === 0 || day === 6
}
</script>
```

In the example above:

- `disableWeekends` is a function that checks if a date falls on a Saturday (`6`) or a Sunday (`0`).
- The `disabledDates` prop is set to the `disableWeekends` function, which ensures that all weekends are disabled in the calendar.

This prop takes an array and applies custom logic to determine which dates should be disabled.

### Combining functions and specific dates

You can also combine specific dates and functions in the `disabledDates` array. For instance:

```html
<template>
  <div class="d-flex justify-content-center">
    <CCalendar
      :calendar-date="new Date(2024, 10, 1)"
      :calendars="2"
      class="border rounded"
      :disabled-dates="[disableWeekends, ...specificDates]"
      locale="en-US"
      range
    />
  </div>
</template>

<script setup>
import { CCalendar } from '@coreui/vue-pro'

const disableWeekends = (date) => {
  const day = date.getDay()
  return day === 0 || day === 6
}

const specificDates = [new Date(2024, 10, 25), new Date(2024, 11, 4), new Date(2024, 11, 12)]
</script>
```

In this example:

- `disableWeekends` disables weekends as before.
- `specificDates` is an array of specific dates to disable.
- The `disabledDates` prop combines both, allowing you to disable weekends and specific dates simultaneously.

## Locale

The CoreUI Vue Calendar allows users to display dates in non-English locales, making it suitable for international applications.

The navigation writes the month and the year in the order the locale does: the year first where the locale writes it first, as in Japanese, Chinese, Korean, Hungarian or Lithuanian, the month first as in English or Polish.

### Auto

By default, the Calendar component uses the browser's default locale. However, you can easily configure it to use a different locale supported by the JavaScript Internationalization API. This feature helps create inclusive and accessible applications for a diverse audience.

With server-side rendering, pass `locale` explicitly: by default the server writes the text in its own locale and the browser in the reader's, and Vue reports a hydration mismatch when the two differ.

```html
<template>
  <div class="d-flex justify-content-center">
    <CCalendar class="border rounded" />
  </div>
</template>

<script setup>
import { CCalendar } from '@coreui/vue-pro'
</script>
```

## Custom cell rendering

The Vue Calendar component lets you customize calendar cells with scoped slots, so you can render extra content, badges, pricing, or custom formatting directly inside each cell.

### Scoped slots

The component supports four scoped slots, one for each calendar view:

- `#dayCell` - Customize day cells in the days view
- `#monthCell` - Customize month cells in the months view
- `#quarterCell` - Customize quarter cells in the quarters view
- `#yearCell` - Customize year cells in the years view

Each slot receives a slot props object with the current cell state:

- `date` - a JavaScript `Date` object representing the cell date
- `isDisabled` - whether the cell is disabled
- `isInRange` - whether the cell is inside the selected range
- `isSelected` - whether the cell is selected; in a range only its start and end are, while `isInRange` covers them and every cell between
- `label` - the cell's full name (`Wednesday, August 12, 2026`, `August 2026`, `Q3 2026`, `2026`)

The `#dayCell` slot also receives:

- `isInCurrentMonth` - whether the day belongs to the currently displayed month
- `isToday` - whether the day is today, in its own month (the copy of today among an adjacent month's days is not)
- in day selection, a day among an adjacent month's days carries the range like the month's own days when `selectAdjacentDays` is on; without it the day only fills the grid, the range is not drawn on it and `isInRange` is `false`
- in day selection without `selectAdjacentDays`, a day among an adjacent month's days only fills the grid, so `isDisabled` is `true` and `isSelected` is `false` for it
- in week selection, `isDisabled`, `isInRange` and `isSelected` describe the week row the day sits in, since the row is what the calendar picks and draws; `isInCurrentMonth` and `isToday` still describe the day

Example:

```vue
<CCalendar>
  <template #dayCell="{ date, isSelected, isToday, label }">
    <div :class="{ 'fw-semibold': isSelected }">
      <span aria-hidden="true">{{ date.getDate() }}</span>
      <span class="visually-hidden">{{ label }}</span>
      <small v-if="isToday">Today</small>
    </div>
  </template>
</CCalendar>
```

A cell drawn by a slot gets no `aria-label` from the calendar, so its content is what a screen reader reads. Put `label` in it, for example in a `visually-hidden` span next to the short visible text marked `aria-hidden="true"`, as the pricing example below does.

### Navigation icon slots

Four more slots replace the navigation buttons' artwork, each called with no arguments: `#navPrevIcon` / `#navNextIcon` for the single-step buttons, `#navPrevDoubleIcon` / `#navNextDoubleIcon` for the double-step ones.

### Format options

You can combine custom cell slots with format props to control the default text produced by the calendar:

- `dayFormat` - controls day number formatting: `'numeric'` or `'2-digit'`
- `monthFormat` - controls month formatting: `'long'`, `'narrow'`, `'short'`, `'numeric'`, or `'2-digit'`
- `yearFormat` - controls the year cells of the years view: `'numeric'` or `'2-digit'`
- `weekdayFormat` - controls weekday formatting: number for character length, or `'long'`, `'narrow'`, `'short'`

These props use the JavaScript `Intl.DateTimeFormat` API and respect the current `locale`. They apply to the cells of the grid, not to the navigation above it, which writes months and years in full.

### Pricing calendar with custom cells

This example demonstrates a more advanced custom cell rendering setup. It uses scoped slots to display daily prices in the days view, monthly price ranges in the months view, and yearly ranges in the years view. The pricing data is fetched from an external API and cached to avoid duplicate requests.

```html
<template>
  <div class="d-flex justify-content-center">
    <CCalendar
      :calendar-date="calendarDate"
      :calendars="2"
      class="border rounded"
      locale="en-US"
      :max-date="new Date(2025, 11, 31)"
      :min-date="new Date(2022, 0, 1)"
      range
      @calendar-date-change="handleCalendarDateChange"
    >
      <template #dayCell="{ date, isInCurrentMonth, isSelected, label }">
        <div class="py-1">
          <div aria-hidden="true">{{ date.toLocaleDateString('en-US', { day: 'numeric' }) }}</div>
          <span class="visually-hidden">{{ label }}</span>
          <small
            :class="isSelected ? 'fg-reset' : !isInCurrentMonth ? 'fg-3 opacity-75' : 'fg-3'"
            style="font-size: 0.75rem"
          >
            {{ dayPrices[toISODate(date)] ? `$${dayPrices[toISODate(date)]}` : '-' }}
          </small>
        </div>
      </template>
      <template #monthCell="{ date, isSelected, label }">
        <div class="py-1">
          <div aria-hidden="true">{{ date.toLocaleDateString('en-US', { month: 'short' }) }}</div>
          <span class="visually-hidden">{{ label }}</span>
          <small :class="isSelected ? 'fg-reset' : 'fg-3'" style="font-size: 0.75rem">
            {{
              monthRanges[monthKey(date.getFullYear(), date.getMonth())]
                ? `$${monthRanges[monthKey(date.getFullYear(), date.getMonth())].min}-$${monthRanges[monthKey(date.getFullYear(), date.getMonth())].max}`
                : '-'
            }}
          </small>
        </div>
      </template>
      <template #yearCell="{ date, isSelected, label }">
        <div class="py-1">
          <div aria-hidden="true">{{ date.getFullYear() }}</div>
          <span class="visually-hidden">{{ label }}</span>
          <small :class="isSelected ? 'fg-reset' : 'fg-3'" style="font-size: 0.75rem">
            {{
              yearRanges[yearKey(date.getFullYear())]
                ? `$${yearRanges[yearKey(date.getFullYear())].min}-$${yearRanges[yearKey(date.getFullYear())].max}`
                : '-'
            }}
          </small>
        </div>
      </template>
    </CCalendar>
  </div>
</template>

<script setup>
import { ref } from 'vue'
import { CCalendar } from '@coreui/vue-pro'

const calendarDate = ref(new Date(2025, 0, 1))

const dayPrices = ref({})
const monthRanges = ref({})
const yearRanges = ref({})

const fetchedKeys = new Set()
const inFlightKeys = new Set()

const toISODate = (date) => date.toISOString().slice(0, 10)

const monthKey = (year, monthIndex) => `${year}-${String(monthIndex + 1).padStart(2, '0')}-01`

const yearKey = (year) => `${year}-01-01`

const getDateRangeForView = (date, view) => {
  const year = date.getFullYear()
  const month = date.getMonth()

  switch (view) {
    case 'months':
      return { startDate: new Date(year, 0, 1), endDate: new Date(year, 11, 31) }
    case 'years': {
      const startYear = Math.floor(year / 12) * 12
      return { startDate: new Date(startYear, 0, 1), endDate: new Date(startYear + 11, 11, 31) }
    }
    case 'days':
    default:
      return { startDate: new Date(year, month, 1), endDate: new Date(year, month + 2, 0) }
  }
}

const fetchPricingData = async (startDate, endDate, view, limit = 400) => {
  const start = toISODate(startDate)
  const end = toISODate(endDate)
  const requestKey = `${view}:${start}:${end}:${limit}`

  if (fetchedKeys.has(requestKey) || inFlightKeys.has(requestKey)) {
    return
  }

  inFlightKeys.add(requestKey)

  try {
    const response = await fetch(
      `https://apitest.coreui.io/demos/daily-rates.php?start_date=${start}&end_date=${end}&view=${view}&limit=${limit}`
    )
    const data = await response.json()

    fetchedKeys.add(requestKey)

    if (view === 'days') {
      dayPrices.value = { ...dayPrices.value, ...data }
      return
    }

    if (view === 'months') {
      monthRanges.value = { ...monthRanges.value, ...data }
      return
    }

    yearRanges.value = { ...yearRanges.value, ...data }
  } catch (error) {
    console.error('Error fetching pricing data:', error)
  } finally {
    inFlightKeys.delete(requestKey)
  }
}

const requestFor = async (date, view) => {
  const { startDate, endDate } = getDateRangeForView(date, view)
  await fetchPricingData(startDate, endDate, view)
}

const handleCalendarDateChange = async (date, view = 'days') => {
  calendarDate.value = date
  await requestFor(date, view)
}

onMounted(async () => {
  await requestFor(calendarDate.value, 'days')
})
</script>
```

## Accessibility

Keyboard navigation in the grid follows the [date picker dialog pattern](https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/dialog-modal/examples/datepicker-dialog/). The table is a `grid` of `gridcell` cells, which is what lets a cell report itself as selected: selected cells carry `aria-selected` (in week selection, the row), today carries `aria-current="date"`, a cell that cannot be picked carries `aria-disabled="true"` (a day outside `minDate` / `maxDate`, before year 1 or in `disabledDates`, a day among an adjacent month's days without `selectAdjacentDays`, and in week selection the row rather than its days), every day cell announces its full date with the weekday (`Wednesday, August 12, 2026`), and month, quarter and year cells are named by their text. With `range`, the grid of the view that picks the range is `aria-multiselectable`, and every day, week row or period between the two ends that can be picked carries `aria-selected` as well, so the ones in between are announced as selected; the months and years views of a day range only navigate, so there only the ends carry it. A cell drawn by a slot is named by its content; see [Scoped slots](#scoped-slots). In week selection the row that takes focus is named by the days it spans (`August 10 – 16, 2026`), after its week number when week numbers are shown (`Week 33, August 10 – 16, 2026`). Each grid is a composite with a single tab stop: <kbd>Tab</kbd> enters it once and leaves it, the keys below move inside it, and `tabindex="0"` sits on the selected date (in a range, an end the grid shows), else on the cell closest to the date the grid opens on, else wherever focus went last. Every cell that reaches into the days from the day of `minDate` to the day of `maxDate` can take the focus, times of day aside, also one that cannot be picked: the keys stop on it instead of skipping it, a screen reader announces it as unavailable, and <kbd>Enter</kbd> and <kbd>Space</kbd> do nothing there. Cells wholly outside those days, and in day selection the days of an adjacent month without `selectAdjacentDays`, carry no `tabindex`; a month, quarter or year counts as inside while any of its days is, and a week row while any day of the week it stands for is. When no panel has a cell that can take the focus, as when the calendar is given a page that lies wholly outside the limits, every grid itself takes the tab stop, also in markup rendered on the server, and the arrows move to the limit they point toward; a panel wholly outside the limits beside one that reaches into them has no tab stop of its own. A grid in which nothing can be picked, such as a page wholly outside the limits or one that `disabledDates` covers, points `aria-describedby` at a hidden element holding `ariaNothingToPickLabel` (`'Nothing on this page can be picked'`). The navigation buttons stay enabled at the limits: a page outside them can be shown, and it says so. Selectable cells and week rows are marked with `data-coreui-selectable`, which is the hook to use in your own CSS or scripts.

The month and year between the navigation arrows name the page the calendar shows, followed by a visually hidden `ariaNothingToPickLabel` when nothing on it can be picked. Turning a page is announced through [`announce()`](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/accessibility/screen-readers/#announcing-messages) in the polite live region of the page, or of the modal dialog around the calendar, such as the panel of a date picker: one message per panel that turned, naming the page, followed by `ariaNothingToPickLabel` when nothing on that page can be picked (`September 2026, Nothing on this page can be picked`). A day or a week row that holds focus already names its month and year, so a key that moves from it to another page names no page, and announces `ariaNothingToPickLabel` alone when nothing on the new page can be picked; another panel left with nothing to pick, by a turn or by a pick, is announced with its name. A month, quarter or year names only itself, so the page is announced from it as from a button. Nothing is announced while the calendar is hidden, and a newer turn cancels the messages of the previous one. In the years view the page is the range of years it shows, the same text as the grid's label. A pick is announced the same way, because focus stays on the cell and a screen reader does not read its `aria-selected` turning on: as `ariaSelectedDateAnnouncement` with the full name of what was picked (`Selected date: Wednesday, August 12, 2026`), and with `range` as `ariaSelectedRangeAnnouncement` whenever both ends are set after a pick, or as a date when they fall on the same day. The first pick of a range announces nothing. A date picker turns both messages off for the pick that closes its panel and names its toggle with the picked date instead, because a message added while focus goes back to the toggle is dropped by VoiceOver in Safari; a newer pick cancels a message that was not read yet. Activating the month or year button while it has focus opens the months or years view and moves focus to the month or year that panel showed, also when it cannot be picked, or to the panel's tab stop when it lies outside `minDate` / `maxDate`; holding <kbd>Enter</kbd> does not go on to pick it. In the years view the year button goes back to the view that picks the date; while it has focus, focus moves to the day, week, month or quarter that holds the start of the month the panel shows there, or to the panel's tab stop when that lies outside `minDate` / `maxDate`. The button is disabled when the years view is the one that picks (`selectionType="year"`). Picking a month or year in those views, with a click or with <kbd>Enter</kbd> / <kbd>Space</kbd>, opens the next view on that period, unless nothing in it can be picked, and moves focus to the first date of that panel inside `minDate` / `maxDate`, also when that date cannot be picked; when the panel lies wholly outside the limits, focus goes to the calendar's tab stop.

With `showWeekNumber`, each week number is a row header named with the locale's word for week and the number (`Week 36`, `Tydzień 36`), and the column header is that word, read by screen readers only unless `weekNumbersLabel` sets a visible one. In week selection the focused row's name starts with the same name, `Week 36, August 31 – September 6, 2026`. To name the week numbers yourself, give `ariaWeekNumberLabel` a function that takes the week number and returns its name (returning nothing keeps the default); keep the number in it, so a voice-control user can say what they see. The default puts the word before the number in every locale, so for a locale that writes it the other way round, such as `第36週`, pass the function.

### Keyboard support

| Key | Action |
| --- | --- |
| <kbd>Arrow Right</kbd> / <kbd>Arrow Left</kbd> | Move focus to the next / previous day; crossing the edge of the grid moves to the adjacent month |
| <kbd>Arrow Down</kbd> / <kbd>Arrow Up</kbd> | Move focus to the same day of the next / previous week |
| <kbd>Home</kbd> / <kbd>End</kbd> | Move focus to the first / last day of the week inside `minDate` / `maxDate`, into the previous / next month when the week starts or ends there |
| <kbd>Page Down</kbd> / <kbd>Page Up</kbd> | Move focus to the same day of the next / previous month, keeping the day number when the target month is long enough; a series of presses keeps the day it started from, so January 31 goes to February 28 and then March 31, also across a stop at `minDate` / `maxDate`; any other key or a click starts a new series |
| <kbd>Shift</kbd> + <kbd>Page Down</kbd> / <kbd>Shift</kbd> + <kbd>Page Up</kbd> | Move focus to the same day of the next / previous year, keeping the day of a series the same way; the other views turn as they do without Shift |
| <kbd>Tab</kbd> | Leave the grid; the calendar is one stop, so Tab never walks the dates |
| <kbd>Enter</kbd> / <kbd>Space</kbd> | Select the focused date; nothing happens on a date that cannot be picked |

The months, quarters, and years views answer to the same keys, with arrows moving by cell and row, <kbd>Home</kbd> / <kbd>End</kbd> moving to the first / last cell of the row, and <kbd>Page Down</kbd> / <kbd>Page Up</kbd> moving by year (by the twelve years of a page in the years view). A jump never lands outside `minDate` / `maxDate`: focus stops on the limit, also when that date cannot be picked.

With `selectionType="week"` the row is what gets picked, so it is the tab stop and the arrows move between rows; <kbd>Home</kbd> and <kbd>End</kbd> move to the first and last week of the month.

A key from the table pressed with <kbd>Alt</kbd>, <kbd>Ctrl</kbd> or <kbd>Cmd</kbd> is neither handled nor cancelled by the grid: focus stays where it is and the key stays free for the browser and assistive technology.

## API

Check out the documentation below for a comprehensive guide to all the props you can use with the components mentioned here.

- [&lt;CCalendar /&gt;](./api/#ccalendar)
