```html
        <CTableDataCell colspan="2">Larry the Bird</CTableDataCell>
        <CTableDataCell>@twitter</CTableDataCell>

import {
  CTable,
  CTableHead,
  CTableRow,
  CTableHeaderCell,
  CTableBody,
```

Starting from version **4.5.0** also this way.

### Captions

A `<CTableCaption>` functions like a heading for a table. It helps users with screen readers to find a table and understand what it's about and decide if they want to read it.

```html
<template>
  <CTable>
    <CTableCaption>List of users</CTableCaption>
    <CTableHead>
      <CTableRow>
        <CTableHeaderCell scope="col">#</CTableHeaderCell>
        <CTableHeaderCell scope="col">Class</CTableHeaderCell>
        <CTableHeaderCell scope="col">Heading</CTableHeaderCell>
        <CTableHeaderCell scope="col">Heading</CTableHeaderCell>
      </CTableRow>
    </CTableHead>
    <CTableBody>
      <CTableRow>
        <CTableHeaderCell scope="row">1</CTableHeaderCell>
        <CTableDataCell>Mark</CTableDataCell>
        <CTableDataCell>Otto</CTableDataCell>
        <CTableDataCell>@mdo</CTableDataCell>
      </CTableRow>
      <CTableRow>
        <CTableHeaderCell scope="row">2</CTableHeaderCell>
        <CTableDataCell>Jacob</CTableDataCell>
        <CTableDataCell>Thornton</CTableDataCell>
        <CTableDataCell>@fat</CTableDataCell>
      </CTableRow>
      <CTableRow>
        <CTableHeaderCell scope="row">3</CTableHeaderCell>
        <CTableDataCell>Larry</CTableDataCell>
        <CTableDataCell>the Bird</CTableDataCell>
        <CTableDataCell>@twitter</CTableDataCell>
      </CTableRow>
    </CTableBody>
  </CTable>
</template>

<script setup>
import {
  CTable,
  CTableCaption,
  CTableHead,
  CTableRow,
  CTableHeaderCell,
  CTableBody,
  CTableDataCell,
} from '@coreui/vue'
</script>
```

Starting from version **4.5.0** also this way.

```vue
<template>
  <CTable caption="List of users" :columns="columns" :items="items"  />
</template>
```

Add `captionTop` to put the caption on the top of the table.

```html
<template>
  <CTable caption-top>
    <CTableCaption>List of users</CTableCaption>
    <CTableHead>
      <CTableRow>
        <CTableHeaderCell scope="col">#</CTableHeaderCell>
        <CTableHeaderCell scope="col">Class</CTableHeaderCell>
        <CTableHeaderCell scope="col">Heading</CTableHeaderCell>
        <CTableHeaderCell scope="col">Heading</CTableHeaderCell>
      </CTableRow>
    </CTableHead>
    <CTableBody>
      <CTableRow>
        <CTableHeaderCell scope="row">1</CTableHeaderCell>
        <CTableDataCell>Mark</CTableDataCell>
        <CTableDataCell>Otto</CTableDataCell>
        <CTableDataCell>@mdo</CTableDataCell>
      </CTableRow>
      <CTableRow>
        <CTableHeaderCell scope="row">2</CTableHeaderCell>
        <CTableDataCell>Jacob</CTableDataCell>
        <CTableDataCell>Thornton</CTableDataCell>
        <CTableDataCell>@fat</CTableDataCell>
      </CTableRow>
      <CTableRow>
        <CTableHeaderCell scope="row">3</CTableHeaderCell>
        <CTableDataCell>Larry</CTableDataCell>
        <CTableDataCell>the Bird</CTableDataCell>
        <CTableDataCell>@twitter</CTableDataCell>
      </CTableRow>
    </CTableBody>
  </CTable>
</template>

<script setup>
import {
  CTable,
  CTableCaption,
  CTableHead,
  CTableRow,
  CTableHeaderCell,
  CTableBody,
  CTableDataCell,
} from '@coreui/vue'
</script>
```

It combines with the `caption` property the same way.

```vue
<template>
  <CTable caption="List of users" caption-top :columns="columns" :items="items"  />
</template>
```
## Responsive tables

Responsive tables allow tables to be scrolled horizontally with ease. Make any table responsive across all viewports by adding a `responsive` property. Or, pick a maximum breakpoint with which to have a responsive table up to by using `responsive="{-sm|-md|-lg|-xl|-2xl}"`.

```html

    <CTableHead>
      <CTableRow>

        <CTableHeaderCell scope="col">Heading</CTableHeaderCell>
        <CTableHeaderCell scope="col">Heading</CTableHeaderCell>
        <CTableHeaderCell scope="col">Heading</CTableHeaderCell>
        <CTableHeaderCell scope="col">Heading</CTableHeaderCell>
      </CTableRow>
    </CTableHead>
    <CTableBody>
      <CTableRow>
        <CTableHeaderCell scope="row">1</CTableHeaderCell>
        <CTableDataCell>Cell</CTableDataCell>
        <CTableDataCell>Cell</CTableDataCell>
        <CTableDataCell>Cell</CTableDataCell>
        <CTableDataCell>Cell</CTableDataCell>
        <CTableDataCell>Cell</CTableDataCell>
        <CTableDataCell>Cell</CTableDataCell>

        <CTableDataCell>Cell</CTableDataCell>
        <CTableDataCell>Cell</CTableDataCell>
        <CTableDataCell>Cell</CTableDataCell>
        <CTableDataCell>Cell</CTableDataCell>
```

## Stacked tables

A table that scrolls sideways is still a table; on a narrow screen it is often easier to read one record at a time. Add `.table-stacked{-sm|-md|-lg|-xl|-2xl}` to `<CTable>` to turn each row into a block below that breakpoint — the header is hidden from sight (it stays in the accessibility tree) and every cell carries its own label.

Two things are required: the `responsive` property, because that wrapper is the query container the class measures, and a `data-cell` attribute on every cell after the first, which supplies the label the hidden header would have given. The first cell is treated as the record's title and needs no label.

```html
<template>
  <CTable class="table-stacked-md" responsive>
    <CTableHead>
      <CTableRow>
        <CTableHeaderCell scope="col">Name</CTableHeaderCell>
        <CTableHeaderCell scope="col">Role</CTableHeaderCell>
        <CTableHeaderCell scope="col">Email</CTableHeaderCell>
      </CTableRow>
    </CTableHead>
    <CTableBody>
      <CTableRow>
        <CTableDataCell>Mark Otto</CTableDataCell>
        <CTableDataCell data-cell="Role">Maintainer</CTableDataCell>
        <CTableDataCell data-cell="Email">mark@example.com</CTableDataCell>
      </CTableRow>
      <CTableRow>
        <CTableDataCell>Jacob Thornton</CTableDataCell>
        <CTableDataCell data-cell="Role">Designer</CTableDataCell>
        <CTableDataCell data-cell="Email">jacob@example.com</CTableDataCell>
      </CTableRow>
    </CTableBody>
  </CTable>
</template>

<script setup>
import {
  CTable,
  CTableBody,
  CTableDataCell,
  CTableHead,
  CTableHeaderCell,
  CTableRow,
} from '@coreui/vue'
</script>
```

> Because the breakpoint is read from the responsive wrapper rather than the window, a stacked table inside a narrow column stacks there while the same markup in the main content area stays a table.

# Vue Table Component API

> Explore the API reference for the Vue Table component and discover how to effectively utilize its props for customization.

## CTable

```jsx
import { CTable } from '@coreui/vue'
```

### Props

| Name | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `align` | `string` | - | Set the vertical aligment. |
| `borderColor` | `Color` | - | Sets the border color of the component to one of CoreUI’s themed colors. |
| `bordered` | `boolean` | - | Add borders on all sides of the table and cells. |
| `borderless` | `boolean` | - | Remove borders on all sides of the table and cells. |
| `caption` | `string` | - | The table caption. |
| `captionTop` | `boolean` | - | Put the caption on the top of the table. |
| `card` | `boolean` | - | Wrap the table in a card's border and corner radius, clipping its cells and dropping the borders that would stack on the frame. |
| `color` | `Color` | - | Sets the color context of the component to one of CoreUI’s themed colors. |
| `columns` | `(Column \| string)[]` | - | Prop for table columns configuration. If prop is not defined, table will display columns based on the first item keys, omitting keys that begins with underscore (e.g. '_props') In columns prop each array item represents one column. Item might be specified in two ways: String: each item define column name equal to item value. Object: item is object with following keys available as column configuration: - key (required)(String) - define column name equal to item key. - label (String) - define visible label of column. If not defined, label will be generated automatically based on column name, by converting kebab-case and snake_case to individual words and capitalization of each word. - _props (Object) - adds classes to all cels in column, ex. _props: { scope: 'col', className: 'custom-class' }, - _style (Object) - adds styles to the column header (useful for defining widths) |
| `footer` | `(FooterItem \| string)[]` | - | Array of objects or strings, where each element represents one cell in the table footer. Example items: ['FooterCell', 'FooterCell', 'FooterCell'] or [{ label: 'FooterCell', _props: { color: 'success' }, ...] |
| `hover` | `boolean` | - | Enable a hover state on table rows within a `<CTableBody>`. |
| `items` | `Item[]` | - | Array of objects, where each object represents one item - row in table. Additionally, you can add style classes to each row by passing them by '_props' key and to single cell by '_cellProps'. Example item: { name: 'John' , age: 12, _props: { color: 'success' }, _cellProps: { age: { className: 'fw-bold'}}} |
| `responsive` | `boolean\|string` | - |  |
| `small` | `boolean` | - | Make table more compact by cutting all cell `padding` in half. |
| `striped` | `boolean` | - | Add zebra-striping to any table row within the `<CTableBody>`. |
| `stripedColumns` | `boolean` | - | Add zebra-striping to any table column. |
| `tableFootProps` | `object` | - | Properties that will be passed to the table footer component. Properties to [CTableFoot](#ctablefoot) component. |
| `tableHeadProps` | `object` | - | Properties that will be passed to the table head component. Properties to [CTableHead](#ctablehead) component. |
| `theme` | `Color` | - | Sets the color context of the component to one of CoreUI’s themed colors. |

# Vue Table Component Styling

> Learn how to customize the Vue Table component with CSS classes, variables, and Sass for flexible styling and seamless integration into your design.

## Sass variables

_Deprecated in 6.0.0._

Sass variables set these defaults at build time and are removed in v7. The CSS variables above reach the same values without recompiling, and can be set on a single element.

```scss
$table-striped-order:         odd !default;
$table-striped-columns-order: even !default;
```

## Sass loops

```scss
// Which theme colours get a .table-* variant. The values come from the theme
// tokens now, so this is a list of names rather than a map of shifted colours.
$table-variants: map.keys($theme-colors) !default;
```


---

# Vue Bootstrap Table Component

> Learn how to use CoreUI’s Vue Table component with Bootstrap styles for flexible, framework-consistent UI.

## How to use Vue Table Component

Due to the widespread use of `<CTable>` elements across third-party widgets like calendars and date pickers, CoreUI's tables are **opt-in**. All table styles are not inherited in CoreUI, meaning any nested tables can be styled independent from the parent.

Using the most basic table CoreUI, here's how `<CTable>`-based tables look in CoreUI.

```html
<template>
  <CTable :columns="columns" :items="items" />
</template>

<script setup>
import { CTable } from '@coreui/vue'
const columns = [
  {
    key: 'id',
    label: '#',
    _props: { scope: 'col' },
  },
  {
    key: 'class',
    _props: { scope: 'col' },
  },
  {
    key: 'heading_1',
    label: 'Heading',
    _props: { scope: 'col' },
  },
  {
    key: 'heading_2',
    label: 'Heading',
    _props: { scope: 'col' },
  },
]
const items = [
  {
    id: 1,
    class: 'Mark',
    heading_1: 'Otto',
    heading_2: '@mdo',
    _cellProps: { id: { scope: 'row' } },
  },
  {
    id: 2,
    class: 'Jacob',
    heading_1: 'Thornton',
    heading_2: '@fat',
    _cellProps: { id: { scope: 'row' } },
  },
  {
    id: 3,
    class: 'Larry the Bird',
    heading_2: '@twitter',
    _cellProps: { id: { scope: 'row' }, class: { colSpan: 2 } },
  },
]
</script>
```
In version **4.5.0** we introduced a new way to create a table, similarly to our [Smart Table component](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/components/smart-table/).

```vue
<template>
  <CTable :columns="columns" :items="items" />
</template>
```

You can also put all table components together manually as hitherto.

```vue
<CTable>
  <CTableHead>
    <CTableRow>
      <CTableHeaderCell scope="col">#</CTableHeaderCell>
      <CTableHeaderCell scope="col">Class</CTableHeaderCell>
      <CTableHeaderCell scope="col">Heading</CTableHeaderCell>
      <CTableHeaderCell scope="col">Heading</CTableHeaderCell>
    </CTableRow>
  </CTableHead>
  <CTableBody>
    <CTableRow>
      <CTableHeaderCell scope="row">1</CTableHeaderCell>
      <CTableDataCell>Mark</CTableDataCell>
      <CTableDataCell>Otto</CTableDataCell>
      <CTableDataCell>@mdo</CTableDataCell>
    </CTableRow>
    <CTableRow>
      <CTableHeaderCell scope="row">2</CTableHeaderCell>
      <CTableDataCell>Jacob</CTableDataCell>
      <CTableDataCell>Thornton</CTableDataCell>
      <CTableDataCell>@fat</CTableDataCell>
    </CTableRow>
    <CTableRow>
      <CTableHeaderCell scope="row">3</CTableHeaderCell>
      <CTableDataCell colspan="2">Larry the Bird</CTableDataCell>
      <CTableDataCell>@twitter</CTableDataCell>
    </CTableRow>
  </CTableBody>
</CTable>
```

### Active tables

Highlight a table row or cell by adding a `active` property.

```html

</template>

<script setup>
import { CTable } from '@coreui/vue'
const columnsActiveTableExample = [
  {
    key: 'id',
    label: '#',
    _props: { scope: 'col' },
  },
  {
    key: 'class',
    _props: { scope: 'col' },
  },
  {
    key: 'heading_1',
    label: 'Heading',
    _props: { scope: 'col' },
  },
  {
    key: 'heading_2',
    label: 'Heading',
    _props: { scope: 'col' },
  },
]
const itemsActiveTableExample = [
  {
    id: 1,
    class: 'Mark',
    heading_1: 'Otto',
    heading_2: '@mdo',
    _props: { active: true },
    _cellProps: { id: { scope: 'row' } },
  },
  {
    id: 2,
    class: 'Jacob',
    heading_1: 'Thornton',
    heading_2: '@fat',
    _cellProps: { id: { scope: 'row' } },

  {
    id: 3,
    class: 'Larry the Bird',
    heading_2: '@twitter',
    _cellProps: { id: { scope: 'row' }, class: { active: true, colSpan: 2 } },

]
</script>
```

## Card-like tables

Need a bordered, rounded table without nesting it in a [card](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/components/card/)? Wrap the table and clip the corners.

### With utilities

Compose [border](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/utilities/border/), [border radius](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/utilities/border-radius/), and [overflow](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/utilities/overflow/) utilities. Drop the table's bottom margin with `.mb-0`.

```html
<template>
  <div class="border rounded overflow-hidden">
    <CTable class="mb-0" striped :columns="columns" :items="items" />
  </div>
</template>

const columns = [
  {
    key: 'id',
    label: '#',
    _props: { scope: 'col' },
  },
  {
    key: 'class',
    _props: { scope: 'col' },
  },
  {
    key: 'heading_1',
    label: 'Heading',
    _props: { scope: 'col' },
  },
  {
    key: 'heading_2',
    label: 'Heading',
    _props: { scope: 'col' },
  },
]
const items = [
  {
    id: 1,
    class: 'Mark',
    heading_1: 'Otto',
    heading_2: '@mdo',
    _cellProps: { id: { scope: 'row' } },
  },
  {
    id: 2,
    class: 'Jacob',
    heading_1: 'Thornton',
    heading_2: '@fat',
    _cellProps: { id: { scope: 'row' } },
  },
  {
    id: 3,
    class: 'Larry the Bird',
    heading_2: '@twitter',
    _cellProps: { id: { scope: 'row' }, class: { colSpan: 2 } },
  },
]
</script>
```

### With `card`

Add the `card` property for the card look in one step. The table gets the default border and corner radius of a [card](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/components/card/), and a `.theme-*` class on an ancestor colours the frame the way it colours a card. The cells are clipped, and the borders that would stack on the frame go: the last row's bottom border and the outer borders of a `bordered` table. A caption at the bottom keeps the line above it.

```html
<template>
  <CTable card hover :columns="columns" :items="items" />
</template>

<script setup>
import { CTable } from '@coreui/vue'
const columns = [
  {
    key: 'id',
    label: '#',
    _props: { scope: 'col' },
  },
  {
    key: 'class',
    _props: { scope: 'col' },
  },
  {
    key: 'heading_1',
    label: 'Heading',
    _props: { scope: 'col' },
  },
  {
    key: 'heading_2',
    label: 'Heading',
    _props: { scope: 'col' },
  },
]
const items = [
  {
    id: 1,
    class: 'Mark',
    heading_1: 'Otto',
    heading_2: '@mdo',
    _cellProps: { id: { scope: 'row' } },
  },
  {
    id: 2,
    class: 'Jacob',
    heading_1: 'Thornton',
    heading_2: '@fat',
    _cellProps: { id: { scope: 'row' } },
  },
  {
    id: 3,
    class: 'Larry the Bird',
    heading_2: '@twitter',
    _cellProps: { id: { scope: 'row' }, class: { colSpan: 2 } },
  },
]
</script>
```

Combine it with `responsive` when the table can overflow; both land on the same wrapper.

> ##### Clipping
> 
> `card` clips everything at the rounded edge: a dropdown menu opened from a cell, the focus ring of a control in an edge cell, and columns wider than the frame. Render menus outside the table with the dropdown's [`teleport`](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/components/dropdown/api/#cdropdown) property, and add `responsive` when the table can be wider than its container.

## Table group dividers

Add a thicker, darker border between table groups—`<CTableHead>`, `<CTableBody>`, and `<CTableFoot>`—with `.table-group-divider`. Customize the color by changing the `border-top-color` (which we don't currently provide a utility class for at this time).

```html
<template>
  <CTable>
    <CTableHead>
      <CTableRow>
        <CTableHeaderCell scope="col">#</CTableHeaderCell>
        <CTableHeaderCell scope="col">First</CTableHeaderCell>
        <CTableHeaderCell scope="col">Last</CTableHeaderCell>
        <CTableHeaderCell scope="col">Handle</CTableHeaderCell>
      </CTableRow>
    </CTableHead>
    <CTableBody class="table-group-divider">
      <CTableRow>
        <CTableHeaderCell scope="row">1</CTableHeaderCell>
        <CTableDataCell>Mark</CTableDataCell>
        <CTableDataCell>Otto</CTableDataCell>
        <CTableDataCell>@mdo</CTableDataCell>
      </CTableRow>
      <CTableRow>
        <CTableHeaderCell scope="row">2</CTableHeaderCell>
        <CTableDataCell>Jacob</CTableDataCell>
        <CTableDataCell>Thornton</CTableDataCell>
        <CTableDataCell>@fat</CTableDataCell>
      </CTableRow>
      <CTableRow>
        <CTableHeaderCell scope="row">3</CTableHeaderCell>
        <CTableDataCell :colspan="2">Larry the Bird</CTableDataCell>
        <CTableDataCell>@twitter</CTableDataCell>
      </CTableRow>
    </CTableBody>
  </CTable>
</template>

<script setup>
import {
  CTable,
  CTableBody,
  CTableDataCell,
  CTableHead,
  CTableHeaderCell,
  CTableRow,
} from '@coreui/vue'
</script>
```

## Vertical alignment

Table cells of `<CTableHead>` are always vertical aligned to the bottom. Table cells in `<CTableBody>` inherit their alignment from `<CTable>` and are aligned to the the top by default. Use the align property to re-align where needed.

```html
<template>
  <CTable align="middle" reponsive>
    <CTableHead>
      <CTableRow>
        <CTableHeaderCell scope="col" class="w-25">Heading 1</CTableHeaderCell>
        <CTableHeaderCell scope="col" class="w-25">Heading 2</CTableHeaderCell>
        <CTableHeaderCell scope="col" class="w-25">Heading 3</CTableHeaderCell>
        <CTableHeaderCell scope="col" class="w-25">Heading 4</CTableHeaderCell>
      </CTableRow>
    </CTableHead>
    <CTableBody>
      <CTableRow>
        <CTableDataCell
          >This cell inherits <code>vertical-align: middle;</code> from the table</CTableDataCell
        >
        <CTableDataCell
          >This cell inherits <code>vertical-align: middle;</code> from the table</CTableDataCell
        >
        <CTableDataCell
          >This cell inherits <code>vertical-align: middle;</code> from the table</CTableDataCell
        >
        <CTableDataCell
          >This here is some placeholder text, intended to take up quite a bit of vertical space, to
          demonsCTableRowate how the vertical alignment works in the preceding
          cells.</CTableDataCell
        >
      </CTableRow>
```

## Nesting

Border styles, active styles, and table variants are not inherited by nested tables.

```html
<template>
  <CTable striped>
    <CTableHead>
      <CTableRow>
        <CTableHeaderCell scope="col">#</CTableHeaderCell>
        <CTableHeaderCell scope="col">Class</CTableHeaderCell>
        <CTableHeaderCell scope="col">Heading</CTableHeaderCell>
        <CTableHeaderCell scope="col">Heading</CTableHeaderCell>
      </CTableRow>
    </CTableHead>
    <CTableBody>
      <CTableRow>
        <CTableHeaderCell scope="row">1</CTableHeaderCell>
        <CTableDataCell>Mark</CTableDataCell>
        <CTableDataCell>Otto</CTableDataCell>
        <CTableDataCell>@mdo</CTableDataCell>
      </CTableRow>
      <CTableRow>
        <CTableHeaderCell colspan="4">
          <CTable>
            <CTableHead>
              <CTableRow>
                <CTableHeaderCell scope="col">Header</CTableHeaderCell>
                <CTableHeaderCell scope="col">Header</CTableHeaderCell>
                <CTableHeaderCell scope="col">Header</CTableHeaderCell>
              </CTableRow>
            </CTableHead>
            <CTableBody>
              <CTableRow>
                <CTableHeaderCell scope="row">A</CTableHeaderCell>
                <CTableDataCell>First</CTableDataCell>
                <CTableDataCell>Last</CTableDataCell>
              </CTableRow>
              <CTableRow>
                <CTableHeaderCell scope="row">B</CTableHeaderCell>
                <CTableDataCell>First</CTableDataCell>
                <CTableDataCell>Last</CTableDataCell>
              </CTableRow>
              <CTableRow>
                <CTableHeaderCell scope="row">C</CTableHeaderCell>
                <CTableDataCell>First</CTableDataCell>
                <CTableDataCell>Last</CTableDataCell>
              </CTableRow>
            </CTableBody>
          </CTable>
        </CTableHeaderCell>
      </CTableRow>
      <CTableRow>
        <CTableHeaderCell scope="row">3</CTableHeaderCell>
        <CTableDataCell colspan="2">Larry the Bird</CTableDataCell>
        <CTableDataCell>@twitter</CTableDataCell>
      </CTableRow>
    </CTableBody>
  </CTable>
</template>

<script setup>
import {
  CTable,
  CTableHead,
  CTableRow,
  CTableHeaderCell,
  CTableBody,
  CTableDataCell,
} from '@coreui/vue'
</script>
```

## Anatomy

### Table head

Similar to tables and dark tables, use the modifier prop `color="secondary"` or `color="inverse"` to make `<CTableHead>`s appear light or dark gray.

```html
<template>
  <CTable>
    <CTableHead theme="secondary">
      <CTableRow>
        <CTableHeaderCell scope="col">#</CTableHeaderCell>
        <CTableHeaderCell scope="col">Class</CTableHeaderCell>
        <CTableHeaderCell scope="col">Heading</CTableHeaderCell>
        <CTableHeaderCell scope="col">Heading</CTableHeaderCell>
      </CTableRow>
    </CTableHead>
    <CTableBody>
      <CTableRow>
        <CTableHeaderCell scope="row">1</CTableHeaderCell>
        <CTableDataCell>Mark</CTableDataCell>
        <CTableDataCell>Otto</CTableDataCell>
        <CTableDataCell>@mdo</CTableDataCell>
      </CTableRow>
      <CTableRow>
        <CTableHeaderCell scope="row">2</CTableHeaderCell>
        <CTableDataCell>Jacob</CTableDataCell>
        <CTableDataCell>Thornton</CTableDataCell>
        <CTableDataCell>@fat</CTableDataCell>
      </CTableRow>
      <CTableRow>
        <CTableHeaderCell scope="row">3</CTableHeaderCell>
        <CTableDataCell>Larry</CTableDataCell>
        <CTableDataCell>the Bird</CTableDataCell>
        <CTableDataCell>@twitter</CTableDataCell>
      </CTableRow>
    </CTableBody>
  </CTable>
</template>

<script setup>
import {
  CTable,
  CTableHead,
  CTableRow,
  CTableHeaderCell,
  CTableBody,
  CTableDataCell,
} from '@coreui/vue'
</script>
```

If you generate a table using the new method incorporated in version **4.5.0**, you have to use tableHeadProps property to pass properties to the table header component.

```vue
<template>
  <CTable :columns="columns" :items="items" :tableHeadProps="{ color: 'light' }" />
</template>
```

```html
<template>
  <CTable>
    <CTableHead theme="inverse">
      <CTableRow>
        <CTableHeaderCell scope="col">#</CTableHeaderCell>
        <CTableHeaderCell scope="col">Class</CTableHeaderCell>

        <CTableHeaderCell scope="col">Heading</CTableHeaderCell>

    </CTableHead>

      <CTableRow>
        <CTableHeaderCell scope="row">1</CTableHeaderCell>

        <CTableDataCell>@twitter</CTableDataCell>

import {
  CTable,
  CTableHead,
  CTableRow,
  CTableHeaderCell,
  CTableBody,
```

Starting from version **4.5.0** also this way.

### Captions

A `<CTableCaption>` functions like a heading for a table. It helps users with screen readers to find a table and understand what it's about and decide if they want to read it.

```html
<template>
  <CTable>
    <CTableCaption>List of users</CTableCaption>
    <CTableHead>
      <CTableRow>
        <CTableHeaderCell scope="col">#</CTableHeaderCell>
        <CTableHeaderCell scope="col">Class</CTableHeaderCell>
        <CTableHeaderCell scope="col">Heading</CTableHeaderCell>
        <CTableHeaderCell scope="col">Heading</CTableHeaderCell>
      </CTableRow>
    </CTableHead>
    <CTableBody>
      <CTableRow>
        <CTableHeaderCell scope="row">1</CTableHeaderCell>
        <CTableDataCell>Mark</CTableDataCell>
        <CTableDataCell>Otto</CTableDataCell>
        <CTableDataCell>@mdo</CTableDataCell>
      </CTableRow>
      <CTableRow>
        <CTableHeaderCell scope="row">2</CTableHeaderCell>
        <CTableDataCell>Jacob</CTableDataCell>
        <CTableDataCell>Thornton</CTableDataCell>
        <CTableDataCell>@fat</CTableDataCell>
      </CTableRow>
      <CTableRow>
        <CTableHeaderCell scope="row">3</CTableHeaderCell>
        <CTableDataCell>Larry</CTableDataCell>
        <CTableDataCell>the Bird</CTableDataCell>
        <CTableDataCell>@twitter</CTableDataCell>
      </CTableRow>
    </CTableBody>
  </CTable>
</template>

<script setup>
import {
  CTable,
  CTableCaption,
  CTableHead,
  CTableRow,
  CTableHeaderCell,
  CTableBody,
  CTableDataCell,
} from '@coreui/vue'
</script>
```

Starting from version **4.5.0** also this way.

```vue
<template>
  <CTable caption="List of users" :columns="columns" :items="items"  />
</template>
```

Add `captionTop` to put the caption on the top of the table.

```html
<template>
  <CTable caption-top>
    <CTableCaption>List of users</CTableCaption>
    <CTableHead>
      <CTableRow>
        <CTableHeaderCell scope="col">#</CTableHeaderCell>
        <CTableHeaderCell scope="col">Class</CTableHeaderCell>
        <CTableHeaderCell scope="col">Heading</CTableHeaderCell>
        <CTableHeaderCell scope="col">Heading</CTableHeaderCell>
      </CTableRow>
    </CTableHead>
    <CTableBody>
      <CTableRow>
        <CTableHeaderCell scope="row">1</CTableHeaderCell>
        <CTableDataCell>Mark</CTableDataCell>
        <CTableDataCell>Otto</CTableDataCell>
        <CTableDataCell>@mdo</CTableDataCell>
      </CTableRow>
      <CTableRow>
        <CTableHeaderCell scope="row">2</CTableHeaderCell>
        <CTableDataCell>Jacob</CTableDataCell>
        <CTableDataCell>Thornton</CTableDataCell>
        <CTableDataCell>@fat</CTableDataCell>
      </CTableRow>
      <CTableRow>
        <CTableHeaderCell scope="row">3</CTableHeaderCell>
        <CTableDataCell>Larry</CTableDataCell>
        <CTableDataCell>the Bird</CTableDataCell>
        <CTableDataCell>@twitter</CTableDataCell>
      </CTableRow>
    </CTableBody>
  </CTable>
</template>

<script setup>
import {
  CTable,
  CTableCaption,
  CTableHead,
  CTableRow,
  CTableHeaderCell,
  CTableBody,
  CTableDataCell,
} from '@coreui/vue'
</script>
```

It combines with the `caption` property the same way.

```vue
<template>
  <CTable caption="List of users" caption-top :columns="columns" :items="items"  />
</template>
```
## Responsive tables

Responsive tables allow tables to be scrolled horizontally with ease. Make any table responsive across all viewports by adding a `responsive` property. Or, pick a maximum breakpoint with which to have a responsive table up to by using `responsive="{-sm|-md|-lg|-xl|-2xl}"`.

```html

    <CTableHead>

        <CTableHeaderCell scope="col">Heading</CTableHeaderCell>

        <CTableHeaderCell scope="col">Heading</CTableHeaderCell>
      </CTableRow>
    </CTableHead>
    <CTableBody>
      <CTableRow>
        <CTableHeaderCell scope="row">1</CTableHeaderCell>
        <CTableDataCell>Cell</CTableDataCell>
        <CTableDataCell>Cell</CTableDataCell>

        <CTableDataCell>Cell</CTableDataCell>
        <CTableDataCell>Cell</CTableDataCell>

        <CTableDataCell>Cell</CTableDataCell>
        <CTableDataCell>Cell</CTableDataCell>
        <CTableDataCell>Cell</CTableDataCell>
```

## Stacked tables

A table that scrolls sideways is still a table; on a narrow screen it is often easier to read one record at a time. Add `.table-stacked{-sm|-md|-lg|-xl|-2xl}` to `<CTable>` to turn each row into a block below that breakpoint — the header is hidden from sight (it stays in the accessibility tree) and every cell carries its own label.

Two things are required: the `responsive` property, because that wrapper is the query container the class measures, and a `data-cell` attribute on every cell after the first, which supplies the label the hidden header would have given. The first cell is treated as the record's title and needs no label.

```html
<template>
  <CTable class="table-stacked-md" responsive>
    <CTableHead>
      <CTableRow>
        <CTableHeaderCell scope="col">Name</CTableHeaderCell>
        <CTableHeaderCell scope="col">Role</CTableHeaderCell>
        <CTableHeaderCell scope="col">Email</CTableHeaderCell>
      </CTableRow>
    </CTableHead>
    <CTableBody>
      <CTableRow>
        <CTableDataCell>Mark Otto</CTableDataCell>
        <CTableDataCell data-cell="Role">Maintainer</CTableDataCell>
        <CTableDataCell data-cell="Email">mark@example.com</CTableDataCell>
      </CTableRow>
      <CTableRow>
        <CTableDataCell>Jacob Thornton</CTableDataCell>
        <CTableDataCell data-cell="Role">Designer</CTableDataCell>
        <CTableDataCell data-cell="Email">jacob@example.com</CTableDataCell>
      </CTableRow>
    </CTableBody>
  </CTable>
</template>

<script setup>
import {
  CTable,
  CTableBody,
  CTableDataCell,
  CTableHead,
  CTableHeaderCell,
  CTableRow,
} from '@coreui/vue'
</script>
```

> Because the breakpoint is read from the responsive wrapper rather than the window, a stacked table inside a narrow column stacks there while the same markup in the main content area stays a table.

# Vue Toast Component

> Push notifications to your visitors with a toast, a lightweight and easily customizable alert message.

Vue toasts are lightweight notifications designed to mimic the push notifications that have been popularized by mobile and desktop operating systems. They’re built with flexbox, so they’re easy to align and position.

## Overview

Things to know when using the toast plugin:

- Toasts are opt-in for performance reasons, so **you must initialize them yourself**.
- Toasts will automatically hide if you do not specify `autohide: false`.

## Examples

### Basic

To encourage extensible and predictable toasts, we recommend a header and body. Toast headers use `display: flex`, allowing easy alignment of content thanks to our margin and flexbox utilities.

Toasts are as flexible as you need and have very little required markup. At a minimum, we require a single element to contain your "toasted" content and strongly encourage a dismiss button.

```html
<template>
  <CToast :autohide="false" visible>
    <CToastHeader close-button>
      <svg
        class="rounded me-3"
        width="20"
        height="20"
        xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"
        preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid slice"
        focusable="false"
        role="img"
      >
        <rect width="100%" height="100%" fill="#007aff"></rect>
      </svg>
      <span class="me-auto fw-bold">CoreUI for Vue.js</span>
      <small>7 min ago</small>
    </CToastHeader>
    <CToastBody>Hello, world! This is a toast message.</CToastBody>
  </CToast>
</template>

<script setup>
import { CToast, CToastHeader, CToastBody } from '@coreui/vue'
</script>
```

### Translucent

Add the `translucent` property to let the background through the toast and blur it. The header thins out with it, so the whole toast reads as one surface.

```html
<template>
  <CToast :autohide="false" translucent visible>
    <CToastHeader close-button>
      <svg
        class="rounded me-3"
        width="20"
        height="20"

        preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid slice"
        focusable="false"
        role="img"
      >
        <rect width="100%" height="100%" fill="#007aff"></rect>
      </svg>
      <span class="me-auto fw-bold">CoreUI for Vue.js</span>
      <small>7 min ago</small>
    </CToastHeader>
    <CToastBody>Hello, world! This is a toast message.</CToastBody>
  </CToast>
</template>

<script setup>
import { CToast, CToastHeader, CToastBody } from '@coreui/vue'
</script>
```

### Stacking

You can stack toasts by wrapping them in a toast container, which will vertically add some spacing.

```html
<template>

        >

          preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid slice"
          focusable="false"
          role="img"
        >
          <rect width="100%" height="100%" fill="#007aff"></rect>
        </svg>
        <span class="me-auto fw-bold">CoreUI for Vue.js</span>
        <small>7 min ago</small>
      </CToastHeader>
      <CToastBody>Hello, world! This is a toast message.</CToastBody>
    </CToast>
  </CToaster>
</template>

<script setup>
import { CToaster, CToast, CToastHeader, CToastBody } from '@coreui/vue'
</script>
```

### Custom content

Customize your toasts by removing sub-components, tweaking them with [utilities](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/utilities/api/), or by adding your own markup. Here we've created a simpler toast by removing the default `<CToastHeader>`, adding a custom hide icon from [CoreUI Icons](https://coreui.io/icons/), and using some [flexbox utilities](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/utilities/flex/) to adjust the layout.

```html
<template>
  <CToast :autohide="false" class="align-items-center" visible>
    <div class="d-flex">
      <CToastBody>Hello, world! This is a toast message.</CToastBody>
      <CToastClose class="me-3 m-auto" />
    </div>
  </CToast>
</template>

<script setup>
import { CToast, CToastBody, CToastClose } from '@coreui/vue'
</script>
```

Alternatively, you can also add additional controls and components to toasts.

```html
<template>
  <CToast :autohide="false" class="align-items-center" visible>
    <CToastBody>
      Hello, world! This is a toast message.
      <div class="mt-3 pt-3 border-top">
        <CButton type="button" theme="primary" size="sm"> Take action </CButton>
        <CToastClose as="CButton" color="secondary" size="sm" class="ms-1">Close</CToastClose>
      </div>
    </CToastBody>
  </CToast>
</template>

<script setup>
import { CToast, CToastBody, CButton, CToastClose } from '@coreui/vue'
</script>
```

### Color schemes

Building on the above example, you can create different toast color schemes with our [color](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/utilities/colors/) and [background](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/utilities/background/) utilities. Here we've set `color="primary"` and added `.fg-white` class to the `<Ctoast>`, and then set `white` property to our close button. For a crisp edge, we remove the default border with `.border-0`.

```html
<template>
  <CToast :autohide="false" theme="primary" class="fg-white align-items-center" visible>
    <div class="d-flex">
      <CToastBody>Hello, world! This is a toast message.</CToastBody>
      <CToastClose class="me-3 m-auto" white />
    </div>
  </CToast>
</template>

<script setup>
import { CToast, CToastBody, CToastClose } from '@coreui/vue'
</script>
```

## Toaster

_Added in 6.0.0._

`createToaster()` creates a store of toasts that lives outside the component tree, and `` renders a `<CToast>` for every entry, keyed by id — so a toast can be added from anywhere, without any markup up front. See the [toaster](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/components/toaster/) for the store API, the visible-toasts limit, stacking, motion and the live regions it announces through.

## Placement

Place toasts with the `<CToaster>` component. Its `placement` property renders one of the nine `.toast-container-{placement}` classes that fix the container to a corner or an edge of the viewport — `placement="top-end"` pins them to the upper right corner, a common spot for notifications. A `<CToaster>` bound to a store takes the placement from `createToaster()` unless the property overrides it. Toasts in the same toaster stack automatically. To show only ever one toast, you can position a single `<CToast>` yourself with our [position utilities](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/utilities/position/).

```html
<template>
  <CButton theme="primary" @click="toasts.push(toasts.length + 1)">Send a toast</CButton>
  <CToaster class="p-4" placement="top-end">
    <CToast v-for="key in toasts" :key="key" visible>
      <CToastHeader close-button>
        <span class="me-auto fw-bold">CoreUI for Vue.js</span>
        <small>Just now</small>
      </CToastHeader>
      <CToastBody>Pinned to the upper right corner.</CToastBody>
    </CToast>
  </CToaster>
</template>

<script setup>
import { ref } from 'vue'
import { CButton, CToast, CToastBody, CToaster, CToastHeader } from '@coreui/vue'

const toasts = ref([])
</script>
```

## Usage with v-model

Bind `v-model:show` and the toast keeps its visibility in step with your state — dismissing it writes `false` back, so the value never drifts from what is on screen.

```html
<template>
  <CButton theme="primary" @click="show = true">Show toast</CButton>
  <p class="mt-4">
    Visible: <strong>{{ show }}</strong>
  </p>
  <CToaster class="p-4" placement="top-end">
    <CToast v-model:show="show">
      <CToastHeader close-button>
        <span class="me-auto fw-bold">CoreUI for Vue.js</span>
      </CToastHeader>
      <CToastBody>Closing this toast writes back to your state.</CToastBody>
    </CToast>
  </CToaster>
</template>

<script setup>
import { ref } from 'vue'
import { CButton, CToast, CToastBody, CToaster, CToastHeader } from '@coreui/vue'

const show = ref(false)
</script>
```

## Accessibility

Toasts are meant to be brief interruptions for your visitors or users. To assist those using screen readers and similar assistive technologies, `<CToast>` renders as an [`aria-live` region](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Accessibility/ARIA/ARIA_Live_Regions) with `role="alert"`, `aria-live="assertive"` and `aria-atomic="true"`. Screen readers announce changes to a live region — showing or updating a toast — without moving focus or interrupting the user, and `aria-atomic="true"` makes the whole toast announce as one unit rather than only the part that changed. If the information is critical to the process, such as a list of form errors, use the [alert component](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/components/alert/) instead.

Adjust `role` and `aria-live` to the content: the defaults suit important messages like errors, while a less urgent notification should carry `role="status"` and `aria-live="polite"`. A toast rendered by a [toaster](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/components/toaster/#accessibility) carries neither: the store announces it through the [live regions of the page](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/accessibility/screen-readers/#announcing-messages), and `priority` picks the polite or the assertive one.

The live region has to exist in the markup *before* the toast is generated for assistive technologies to announce it reliably. `<CToast>` mounts its element only when shown, so for critical messages keep a permanently rendered wrapper carrying the `aria-live` attribute around your toasts, or use the [toaster](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/components/toaster/#accessibility), which announces through the live regions of the page and needs no wrapper.

- [&lt;CToaster /&gt;](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/components/toaster/api/#ctoaster)

# Vue Toast Component API

> Explore the API reference for the Vue Toast component and discover how to effectively utilize its props for customization.

## CToast

```jsx
import { CToast } from '@coreui/vue'
```

### Props

| Name | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `animation` | `boolean` | `true` | Apply a CSS fade transition to the toast. |
| `autohide` | `boolean` | `true` | Auto hide the toast. |
| `color` | `Color` | - | Sets the color context of the component to one of CoreUI’s themed colors. |
| `delay` | `number` | `5000` | Delay hiding the toast (ms). |
| `show` | `boolean` | `undefined` | Control the visibility. When set, the toast renders what `show` says and internal gestures only emit `update:show` — nothing closes until the parent flips the prop. Supports the `v-model:show` binding. |
| `theme` | `Color` | - | Sets the color context of the component to one of CoreUI’s themed colors. |
| `translucent` | `boolean` | - | Let the background through the toast and blur it. |
| `visible` | `boolean` | `undefined` | Toggle the visibility of component. |

### Events

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `close` | Callback fired when the component requests to be closed. |
| `show` | Callback fired when the component requests to be shown. |
| `update:show` | Emit the requested visibility to support the `v-model:show` binding. |

## CToastBody

```jsx
import { CToastBody } from '@coreui/vue'
```

## CToastClose

```jsx
import { CToastClose } from '@coreui/vue'
```

### Props

| Name | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `as` | - | - | Component used for the root node. Either a string to use a HTML element or a component. |

### Events

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `close` | Event called before the dissmiss animation has started. |

## CToastHeader

```jsx
import { CToastHeader } from '@coreui/vue'
```

### Props

| Name | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `ariaCloseLabel` | `string` | - | Sets the `aria-label` of the close button. |
| `closeButton` | `boolean` | - | Automatically add a close button to the header. |

# Vue Toast Component Styling

> Learn how to customize the Vue Toast component with CSS classes, variables, and Sass for flexible styling and seamless integration into your design.

## CSS variables

Vue toasts use local CSS variables on `.toast` for enhanced real-time customization. Values for the CSS variables are set via Sass, so Sass customization is still supported, too.

```scss
$toast-tokens: defaults(
  (
    --cui-toast-zindex: var(--cui-z-toast),
    --cui-toast-padding-x: .75rem,
    --cui-toast-padding-y: .5rem,
    --cui-toast-spacing: #{$container-padding-x},
    --cui-toast-max-width: #{350px},
    --cui-toast-color: var(--cui-fg-body),
    --cui-toast-bg: #{$toast-background-color},
    --cui-toast-border-width: var(--cui-border-width),
    --cui-toast-border-color: #{$toast-border-color},
    --cui-toast-border-radius: var(--cui-radius-7),
    --cui-toast-box-shadow: var(--cui-box-shadow),
    --cui-toast-header-color: var(--cui-fg-3),
    --cui-toast-header-bg: #{$toast-background-color},
    --cui-toast-header-border-color: #{$toast-border-color},
    --cui-toast-font-size: .875rem,
    --cui-toast-slide: .5rem,
    --cui-toast-transition-property: #{"opacity, translate, display"},
    --cui-toast-transition-duration: #{.3s},
    --cui-toast-transition-timing: #{ease-out},
  ),
  $toast-tokens
);
```

### How to use CSS variables

```vue
<template>
  <CToast :style="vars">...</CToast>
</template>

<script setup>
const vars = {
  '--cui-toast-color': '#333',
  '--cui-toast-bg': '#f8f9fa',
}
</script>
```

## Sass variables

_Deprecated in 6.0.0._

Sass variables set these defaults at build time and are removed in v7. The CSS variables above reach the same values without recompiling, and can be set on a single element.

```scss
$toast-background-color:            var(--cui-bg-body) !default;
$toast-border-color:                var(--cui-border-color-translucent) !default;
```

```html
    <CToastBody>
      Hello, world! This is a toast message.
      <div class="mt-3 pt-3 border-top">
        <CButton type="button" theme="primary" size="sm"> Take action </CButton>
        <CToastClose as="CButton" color="secondary" size="sm" class="ms-1">Close</CToastClose>
      </div>
    </CToastBody>
  </CToast>
</template>

<script setup>
import { CToast, CToastBody, CButton, CToastClose } from '@coreui/vue'
</script>
```

### Color schemes

Building on the above example, you can create different toast color schemes with our [color](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/utilities/colors/) and [background](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/utilities/background/) utilities. Here we've set `color="primary"` and added `.fg-white` class to the `<Ctoast>`, and then set `white` property to our close button. For a crisp edge, we remove the default border with `.border-0`.

```html
<template>
  <CToast :autohide="false" theme="primary" class="fg-white align-items-center" visible>
    <div class="d-flex">
      <CToastBody>Hello, world! This is a toast message.</CToastBody>
      <CToastClose class="me-3 m-auto" white />
    </div>
  </CToast>
</template>

<script setup>
import { CToast, CToastBody, CToastClose } from '@coreui/vue'
</script>
```


---

# Vue Toaster Component

> Create toast notifications from anywhere in a Vue app with the CoreUI Toaster: a store keyed by id with add, update, close and promise, a placed container, a visible-toasts limit and screen-reader priority.

## Overview

_Added in 6.0.0._

`createToaster()` creates a store of [toasts](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/components/toast/) that lives outside the component tree, so a toast can be added from anywhere — a composable, a Pinia action, a fetch wrapper — without any markup up front. `` renders a `<CToast>` for every entry, keyed by id, and one pair serves the whole app: `add()` returns the id, `update()` rewrites a toast in place, `close()` hides one or all of them, and `promise()` follows an asynchronous operation through its loading, success and error states.

```ts
import { createToaster } from '@coreui/vue'

export const toaster = createToaster({ placement: 'top-end', limit: 3 })

const id = toaster.add({ title: 'Saved', description: 'Your changes are live.', theme: 'success' })
toaster.update(id, { description: 'Done' })
toaster.close(id)
```

The store carries the placement, so `` needs nothing else; the container is a `region` landmark named `Notifications`, and users of assistive technology can navigate to it.

## Live example

Two toasters, each with its container in a top corner of the viewport: a list on the end side and a [stack](#stacking) on the start side. Every other example on this page renders its container inside the example, so its toasts stay put.

```html
<template>
  <CButton theme="primary" @click="addToast">Add a toast</CButton>
  <CButton theme="secondary" @click="addToStack">Add to the stack</CButton>
  <CToaster :toaster="toaster" />
  <CToaster :toaster="stacked" />
</template>

<script setup>
import { CButton, CToaster, createToaster } from '@coreui/vue'

const toaster = createToaster({ placement: 'top-end' })
const stacked = createToaster({ placement: 'top-start', stack: true, limit: 6 })

const addToast = () => {
  toaster.add({
    title: 'CoreUI for Vue.js',
    description: 'Hello, world! This is a toast message.',
  })
}

const addToStack = () => {
  stacked.add({
    title: 'CoreUI for Vue.js',
    description: 'Hello, world! This one joins a stack.',
  })
}
</script>
```

## Title, description and theme

A toast is a plain options object. `title` renders the header with a close button, `description` the body; a toast without a title puts the close button in the body. `theme` adds the `theme-{color}` class, `priority: 'high'` has screen readers announce it right away, `timeout` overrides the toaster's default (`0` keeps the toast until it is closed) and `dismissible: false` drops the close button.

```html
<template>
  <div class="hstack gap-3 flex-wrap mb-4">
    <CButton theme="primary" @click="addTitled">Title and description</CButton>
    <CButton theme="secondary" @click="addDescription">Description only</CButton>
    <CButton theme="danger" @click="addThemed">Themed, high priority</CButton>
    <CButton theme="secondary" variant="outline" @click="addSticky">Not dismissible</CButton>
  </div>
  <CToaster :toaster="toaster" class="position-static" />
</template>

<script setup>
import { CButton, CToaster, createToaster } from '@coreui/vue'

const toaster = createToaster({ timeout: 0 })

const addTitled = () => toaster.add({ title: 'Saved', description: 'Your changes are live.' })

const addDescription = () => toaster.add({ description: 'Copied to the clipboard' })

const addThemed = () =>
  toaster.add({
    title: 'Payment failed',
    description: 'The card was declined.',
    theme: 'danger',
    priority: 'high',
  })

const addSticky = () =>
  toaster.add({
    title: 'Read me',
    description: 'This one stays until you close it.',
    dismissible: false,
    timeout: 0,
  })
</script>
```

`title` and `description` take a string or a `VNode`; for a body of your own pass `render: (toast) => VNode` and the toast object — `id`, `data`, `updateKey` and every option — is yours to read. Components rendered inside a `<CToaster>` reach the store with `useToaster()`.

## Updating a toast

Passing an `id` that already exists updates that toast instead of adding a second one, and bumps its `updateKey`, so a "Draft saved" toast clicked twice stays a single toast. `update()` does the same for a toast whose id you kept, and accepts a function of the current toast when the change depends on it: `toaster.update(id, (previous) => ({ description: previous.data.step + 1 }))`. A toast that is already closing is not reused: adding its `id` again removes it at once and adds a new toast, which takes the newest place in the container.

```html
<template>
  <div class="hstack gap-3 flex-wrap mb-4">
    <CButton theme="primary" @click="saveDraft">Save draft</CButton>
    <CButton theme="secondary" @click="upload">Upload with progress</CButton>
  </div>
  <CToaster :toaster="toaster" class="position-static" />
</template>

<script setup>
import { CButton, CToaster, createToaster } from '@coreui/vue'

const toaster = createToaster({ timeout: 0 })
let saves = 0

const saveDraft = () => {
  saves += 1
  toaster.add({
    id: 'draft',
    title: 'Draft saved',
    description: `Saved ${saves} time${saves === 1 ? '' : 's'}`,
  })
}

const upload = () => {
  const id = toaster.add({ title: 'Uploading…', description: '0 %' })
  let progress = 0

  const interval = setInterval(() => {
    progress += 25
    toaster.update(id, { description: `${progress} %` })

    if (progress === 100) {
      clearInterval(interval)
      toaster.update(id, { title: 'Uploaded', theme: 'success' })
    }
  }, 500)
}
</script>
```

## Promises

`promise()` adds a toast in the `loading` state and updates it when the promise settles: `success` receives the resolved value, `error` the rejection. Each state is a description string, a full options object, or a function returning either.

```html
<template>
  <CButton theme="primary" class="mb-4" @click="save">Save</CButton>
  <CToaster :toaster="toaster" class="position-static" />
</template>

<script setup>
import { CButton, CToaster, createToaster } from '@coreui/vue'

const toaster = createToaster({ timeout: 0 })

const save = () => {
  const request = new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    setTimeout(
      () => (Math.random() > 0.3 ? resolve('3 files') : reject(new Error('Network error'))),
      2000
    )
  })

  toaster
    .promise(request, {
      loading: 'Saving…',
      success: (files) => `Saved ${files}`,
      error: (error) => ({ title: 'Not saved', description: error.message, priority: 'high' }),
    })
    .catch(() => {})
}
</script>
```

## Action

`action` renders a button in the body; its `onClick` receives the click event and the toast object, so an undo can rewrite the same toast.

```html
<template>
  <CButton theme="primary" class="mb-4" @click="archive">Archive message</CButton>
  <CToaster :toaster="toaster" class="position-static" />
</template>

<script setup>
import { CButton, CToaster, createToaster } from '@coreui/vue'

const toaster = createToaster({ timeout: 0 })

const archive = () =>
  toaster.add({
    description: 'Message archived',
    action: {
      label: 'Undo',
      onClick: (event, toast) =>
        toaster.update(toast.id, { description: 'Message restored', action: null }),
    },
  })
</script>
```

## Limit

`limit` caps how many toasts are visible at once. The newest stay on screen; older ones sink away from the edge and fade, remain in the DOM with `inert` and `data-coreui-limited`, and rise back in as the visible ones go away. `limit: 0` shows everything.

```html
<template>
  <div class="hstack gap-3 mb-4">
    <CButton theme="primary" @click="addToast">Add a toast</CButton>
    <CButton theme="secondary" variant="outline" @click="toaster.close()">Close all</CButton>
  </div>
  <CToaster :toaster="toaster" class="position-static" />
</template>

<script setup>
import { CButton, CToaster, createToaster } from '@coreui/vue'

const toaster = createToaster({ limit: 2, timeout: 0 })
let count = 0

const addToast = () => {
  count += 1
  toaster.add({ title: `Toast ${count}`, description: 'Only two stay visible.' })
}
</script>
```

## Stacking

With `stack: true` the toasts sit on top of each other: the newest in front at full size, the ones behind it scaled down by `--cui-toast-stack-scale` per step and receding towards a vanishing depth. The first toast behind peeks out by `--cui-toast-stack-peek` and every further one by that strip times the scale ratio, so the corners of the stack line up like a deck of cards seen in perspective. Only the front toast's timer runs; the ones behind wait their turn and start counting when they reach the front, so the stack empties from the front. A toast that leaves from behind — closed by id, or pushed over the limit — fades where it is instead of sliding out from under the deck. Hovering or focusing the container spreads the stack into a list; leaving it folds the stack back. The stack takes the place of the flow layout; `limit` decides how many toasts it holds. Folded, the deck shows the front toast and two behind it (`--cui-toast-stack-visible`); spreading it reveals every toast within the limit.

```html
<template>
  <div class="hstack gap-3 mb-4">
    <CButton theme="primary" @click="addToast">Add a toast</CButton>
    <CButton theme="secondary" variant="outline" @click="toaster.close()">Close all</CButton>
  </div>
  <CToaster :toaster="toaster" class="position-relative" />
</template>

<script setup>
import { CButton, CToaster, createToaster } from '@coreui/vue'

const toaster = createToaster({ stack: true, limit: 0, timeout: 0 })
let count = 0

const addToast = () => {
  count += 1
  toaster.add({
    title: `Toast ${count}`,
    description: count % 2 ? 'Hover or focus the stack to spread it out.' : 'A shorter one.',
  })
}
</script>
```

`<CToaster>` keeps the geometry in tokens the CSS reads: `--cui-toast-stack-index`, `--cui-toast-stack-before` (the height of the toasts in front) and `--cui-toast-height` on each toast, `--cui-toast-stack-count`, `--cui-toast-stack-front-height` and `--cui-toast-stack-heights` on the container. Style the stack by these — the `data-coreui-stack-index` and `data-coreui-stack-hidden` attributes mark a toast's place in it.

A stack works in every placement: it grows away from the edge it is pinned to, so at the bottom the newest toast is the lowest one and the stack peeks upward.

```html
<template>
  <div class="d-grid gap-3" style="grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr); max-width: 30rem">
    <CButton
      v-for="placement in placements"
      :key="placement"
      theme="secondary"
      variant="outline"
      @click="addToast(placement)"
    >
      {{ placement }}
    </CButton>
  </div>
  <CToaster v-for="placement in placements" :key="placement" :toaster="stacks[placement]" />
</template>

<script setup>
import { CButton, CToaster, createToaster } from '@coreui/vue'

const placements = [
  'top-start',
  'top-center',
  'top-end',
  'middle-start',
  'middle-center',
  'middle-end',
  'bottom-start',
  'bottom-center',
  'bottom-end',
]

const stacks = Object.fromEntries(
  placements.map((placement) => [placement, createToaster({ placement, stack: true, limit: 0 })])
)

const addToast = (placement) => {
  const toaster = stacks[placement]

  toaster.add({
    title: `${placement} · ${toaster.getToasts().length + 1}`,
    description: 'Hover the stack to spread it.',
  })
}
</script>
```

## Motion

A toast slides in from beyond the container's edge while it fades in — from the side in the `start` and `end` placements, from above in `top-center` and from below in `bottom-center` — and leaves the way it came, so the entry and the exit read as one gesture. `middle-center` sits in the middle of the screen with no edge to come from, so its toasts only fade. While a toast leaves, the ones behind it glide into the freed space; when a new one arrives, they make room the same way. `enter` picks another edge for the entry and `leave` for the exit — a `top-end` toaster can drop its toasts in from above and still send them out sideways — and a toast outside a placed container slides by `--cui-toast-slide` instead. `start` and `end` are logical: they follow the direction the container sits in, so under `dir="rtl"` they change sides along with the placement. All of it respects `prefers-reduced-motion`.

```ts
const toaster = createToaster({ placement: 'top-end', enter: 'top', leave: 'end' })
```

### Instant

A toast with `instant: true` skips all of it — no slide, no fade, no glide of its neighbours, no stack transition — and so does every toast when the user prefers reduced motion: the stylesheet emits no transitions under `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` and the toaster skips its position animations, so toasts appear, move and vanish in place.

```html
<template>
  <div class="hstack gap-3 mb-4">
    <CButton theme="primary" @click="addInstant">Add an instant toast</CButton>
    <CButton theme="secondary" @click="addAnimated">Add an animated toast</CButton>
  </div>
  <CToaster :toaster="toaster" class="position-static" />
</template>

<script setup>
import { CButton, CToaster, createToaster } from '@coreui/vue'

const toaster = createToaster({ timeout: 3000 })

const addInstant = () =>
  toaster.add({ title: 'Instant', description: 'No slide, no fade, no glide.', instant: true })

const addAnimated = () =>
  toaster.add({ title: 'Animated', description: 'Slides in and glides the others.' })
</script>
```

## Placement

`placement` pins the container to the viewport with one of the nine [`.toast-container-{block}-{inline}`](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/components/toast/#placement) classes: `top`, `middle` or `bottom` × `start`, `center` or `end`. In the `top` placements a new toast is inserted first, in the others last, so the newest always sits closest to the edge. The `placement` property of `<CToaster>` overrides the store's for that container.

Each button below adds a toast through a toaster placed at that spot, so you can see where a toast enters from: from the side in the `start` and `end` columns, from above in `top-center` and from below in `bottom-center`, while `middle-center` fades in place.

```html
<template>
  <div class="d-grid gap-3" style="grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr); max-width: 30rem">
    <CButton
      v-for="placement in placements"
      :key="placement"
      theme="secondary"
      variant="outline"
      @click="addToast(placement)"
    >
      {{ placement }}
    </CButton>
  </div>
  <CToaster v-for="placement in placements" :key="placement" :toaster="toasters[placement]" />
</template>

<script setup>
import { CButton, CToaster, createToaster } from '@coreui/vue'

const placements = [
  'top-start',
  'top-center',
  'top-end',
  'middle-start',
  'middle-center',
  'middle-end',
  'bottom-start',
  'bottom-center',
  'bottom-end',
]

const toasters = Object.fromEntries(
  placements.map((placement) => [placement, createToaster({ placement })])
)

const addToast = (placement) =>
  toasters[placement].add({ title: placement, description: 'Slides in from the nearest edge.' })
</script>
```

Render the container where you want the toasts to land — a `position-static` or `position-relative` class keeps it inside the layout instead of pinning it to the viewport:

```vue
<CToaster :toaster="toaster" class="position-static" />
```

## Accessibility

The container is a `region` landmark named by `ariaLabel` (`Notifications` by default), so screen-reader users can jump to it through landmark navigation. Every toast is read through [`announce()`](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/accessibility/screen-readers/#announcing-messages) when it is added or updated: the string parts of its `title` and `description` go to the polite live region of the page, or to the assertive one with `priority: 'high'`, as a message of their own, so toasts raised together are each announced instead of the last one overwriting the others. The store sends the message once and it belongs to the page, not to `<CToaster>`, so a container mounted again on the same store, for example after a route change, does not add the messages of older toasts again, a toast added together with a route change is announced once, and while a modal dialog is open the message goes to a region inside the dialog. Updating or removing a toast takes its message out of the region. Only that text is announced, never the close button or the action, and the toast element itself carries no live role. A toast added while a modal dialog plays its closing transition, or from the modal's `close` event, is announced on the page half a second after the dialog has closed, once the page is back for the screen reader; [Announcing messages](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/accessibility/screen-readers/#announcing-messages) has the measurements. The close button `<CToaster>` renders is named by `ariaCloseLabel` (`Close` by default); set it once for the whole toaster in a translated interface, and name the close button of a `render` body yourself. `normal`, the default, waits until the user is idle, unless the toast is added together with a `high` one, which takes both to the assertive region; keep `high` for the few messages that should interrupt, such as a failed save (WCAG 4.1.3 Status Messages).

Auto-hiding is a time limit on reading, which WCAG 2.2.1 Timing Adjustable asks you to let the user turn off, adjust or extend. Timers stop while the pointer or focus is inside the container (`pauseOnHover`), so a spread stack or a toast being read does not disappear mid-way, and the default `timeout` is the toaster's to set for the whole app. A toast with an action, or one the user must act on, should not hide on its own: give it `timeout: 0`, so keyboard and screen-reader users can reach the button. Toasts never take focus.

## Usage

Create a toaster once, outside the component tree, and export it; every toast in the app goes through it. Mount one `<CToaster>` for it — in the app shell, so it survives route changes.

```ts
// toaster.ts
import { createToaster } from '@coreui/vue'

export const toaster = createToaster({ placement: 'bottom-end', limit: 3 })
```

```vue
<template>
  <RouterView />
  <CToaster :toaster="toaster" />
</template>

<script setup>
import { CToaster } from '@coreui/vue'
import { toaster } from './toaster'
</script>
```

`useToaster()` returns the store to any component rendered inside a `<CToaster>`, so a custom body can close or update the toast it belongs to.

### Options

Options of `createToaster()`.

| Name | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `ariaCloseLabel` | string | `'Close'` | Accessible name of the close button `<CToaster>` renders in every toast; a `render` body names its own. |
| `ariaLabel` | string | `'Notifications'` | Accessible name of the container's `region` landmark. |
| `enter` | string | `'auto'` | Edge a toast slides in from: `'start'`, `'end'`, `'top'` or `'bottom'`. `'start'` and `'end'` are logical and follow the direction the container sits in. `'auto'` follows the placement — the side in the `start` and `end` columns, above in `top-center`, below in `bottom-center`, and no slide at all in `middle-center`. |
| `leave` | string | `'auto'` | Edge a toast slides out to, taking the same values as `enter`. `'auto'` is the edge it came in from. |
| `limit` | number | `3` | How many toasts stay visible; the oldest beyond it are hidden and `inert` until a slot frees. `0` disables the limit. |
| `pauseOnHover` | boolean | `true` | Pause every toast's timer while the pointer or focus is inside the container, and resume when it leaves. Each toast still pauses on its own hover. |
| `placement` | string | `'top-end'` | Corner or edge of the viewport for the container: `top`, `middle` or `bottom` × `start`, `center` or `end`. Toasts in the `top` placements are inserted first, in the others last, so the newest always sits closest to the edge. |
| `stack` | boolean | `false` | Stack the toasts on top of each other, newest in front, and spread them out on hover or focus. |
| `timeout` | number | `5000` | Default time (ms) before a toast hides. `0` keeps toasts until they are closed. |

### Toast options

Options of `add()`, `update()` and the toast objects `getToasts()` returns.

| Name | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `action` | object, null | — | `{ label, onClick(event, toast) }` renders a button in the body. |
| `class` | string | — | Extra classes on the `.toast`. |
| `data` | object | — | Anything you want to read back from the toast object later, e.g. in `update(id, (previous) => …)`. |
| `description` | string, VNode | — | Body of the toast. |
| `dismissible` | boolean | `true` | Render the close button. |
| `id` | string | generated | Stable id; adding with an existing id updates that toast in place, unless it is already closing, in which case a new toast replaces it. |
| `instant` | boolean | `false` | Skip the fade (`.toast-instant`). |
| `onClose` | function | — | Called when the toast starts hiding, with the toast object. |
| `onRemove` | function | — | Called after the toast left the DOM, with the toast object. |
| `priority` | string | `'normal'` | Which live region announces the toast, as in [`announce()`](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/accessibility/screen-readers/#announcing-messages): `'normal'` the polite one, `'high'` the assertive one, which also takes the normal toasts added together with it. |
| `render` | function | — | `(toast) => VNode` renders the body of the toast yourself, instead of the header and body built from `title`, `description` and `action`. |
| `theme` | string | — | Adds `theme-{color}`. |
| `timeout` | number | toaster's `timeout` | Time (ms) before this toast hides; `0` keeps it. |
| `title` | string, VNode | — | Header of the toast, with the close button next to it. |
| `translucent` | boolean | `false` | Adds `.toast-translucent`. |

A toast object in the store carries `id`, `updateKey`, `limited`, `open` and `order` next to the options it was created with.

### Methods

| Method | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `add(options)` | Adds a toast and returns its id. With an `id` that already exists it behaves like `update`, unless that toast is already closing. |
| `update(id, options)` | Rewrites the toast in place and increments its `updateKey`. `options` may be a function receiving the current toast object and returning the changes. |
| `close(id?)` | Hides the toast, which removes it from the store once the fade ends. Without an id, hides every toast. |
| `remove(id)` | Drops the toast from the store at once, without the exit transition. `<CToaster>` calls it when a toast finished hiding. |
| `promise(promise, { loading, success, error })` | Adds a toast in the `loading` state and updates it when the promise settles: `success` gets the resolved value, `error` the rejection. Each state is a description string or a full options object, or a function returning either. Returns the promise. |
| `pause()` / `resume()` | Stop and restart every toast's timer; `pauseOnHover` calls these for the container. |
| `getToasts()` | The toast objects in render order. |
| `toasts` | The reactive `shallowRef` behind `getToasts()`, to read the toasts in a computed of your own. |

### Events

The store reports through the callbacks of a toast — `onClose` when it starts hiding, `onRemove` once it left the DOM — and every rendered toast still emits the [`<CToast>` events](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/components/toast/api/#ctoast) on its own component.

## Customizing

### CSS variables

`<CToaster>` renders regular toasts, so their tokens apply — see the [toast CSS variables](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/components/toast/styling/#css-variables). Four are its own: `--cui-toast-container-inset` on the container sets the distance from the viewport edge, `--cui-toast-translate` on the container is where a toast enters from and leaves to, overridden separately by `--cui-toast-enter-translate` and `--cui-toast-leave-translate` (the `enter` and `leave` options write those; set them yourself for any other offset), `--cui-toast-inline-sign` on the container is the `1` or `-1` those inline offsets are multiplied by, which is how `start` and `end` follow the direction, and `--cui-toast-limited-translate` on a toast sets where a toast over the limit sinks to.

```scss
--cui-toast-zindex: var(--cui-z-toast);
--cui-toast-container-inset: #{var(--cui-spacer-5)};
--cui-toast-inline-sign: 1;
--cui-toast-max-width: #{350px};
--cui-toast-spacing: #{$container-padding-x};
--cui-toast-transition-duration: #{.3s};
--cui-toast-transition-timing: #{ease-out};
```

The stack's peek, scale step and folded count are tokens on `.toast-container-stack`:

```scss
.toast-container-stack {
  --cui-toast-stack-peek: .75rem;
  --cui-toast-stack-scale: .1;
  // Every toast behind is scaled by the same ratio again and pushed towards a vanishing depth,
  // so the corners of the stack line up and each strip is the previous one times the ratio
  --cui-toast-stack-visible: 3;
  --cui-toast-stack-ratio: calc(1 - var(--cui-toast-stack-scale));
  --cui-toast-stack-depth: calc(var(--cui-toast-stack-front-height) + var(--cui-toast-stack-peek) / var(--cui-toast-stack-scale));
  --cui-toast-stack-last: calc(min(var(--cui-toast-stack-count), var(--cui-toast-stack-visible)) - 1);

  width: var(--cui-toast-max-width);
  max-width: 100%;
  height: calc(var(--cui-toast-stack-depth) * (1 - pow(var(--cui-toast-stack-ratio), var(--cui-toast-stack-last))) + var(--cui-toast-stack-front-height) * pow(var(--cui-toast-stack-ratio), var(--cui-toast-stack-last)));
  pointer-events: auto;
  @include transition-props(height, var(--cui-toast-transition-duration), var(--cui-toast-transition-timing));

  > .toast {
    position: absolute;
    inset-block-start: calc(var(--cui-toast-stack-depth) * (1 - pow(var(--cui-toast-stack-ratio), var(--cui-toast-stack-index))));
    inset-inline: 0;
    z-index: calc(var(--cui-toast-stack-count) - var(--cui-toast-stack-index));
    height: var(--cui-toast-stack-front-height);
    margin-block-end: 0;
    overflow: hidden;
    transform-origin: top center;
    scale: pow(var(--cui-toast-stack-ratio), var(--cui-toast-stack-index));

    &:not(.toast-instant) {
      @include transition-props(
        #{"opacity, translate, display, inset-block-start, height, scale"},
        var(--cui-toast-transition-duration),
        var(--cui-toast-transition-timing),
        allow-discrete
      );

      > * {
        @include transition-props(opacity, var(--cui-toast-transition-duration), var(--cui-toast-transition-timing));
      }
    }
  }

  > .toast:not([data-coreui-stack-index="0"]) {
    --cui-toast-leave-translate: 0 0;
    --cui-toast-limited-translate: 0 0;

    > * {
      opacity: 0;
    }
  }

  > .toast[data-coreui-stack-hidden] {
    pointer-events: none;
    opacity: 0;
  }

  &:is(:hover, :focus-within) {
    height: calc(var(--cui-toast-stack-heights) + (var(--cui-toast-stack-count) - 1) * var(--cui-toast-spacing));

    > .toast {
      inset-block-start: calc(var(--cui-toast-stack-before) + var(--cui-toast-stack-index) * var(--cui-toast-spacing));
      height: var(--cui-toast-height);
      scale: 1;

      > * {
        opacity: 1;
      }
    }

    > .toast[data-coreui-stack-hidden]:not([data-coreui-limited]) {
      pointer-events: auto;
      opacity: 1;
    }
  }
}

.toast-container-bottom-start.toast-container-stack,
.toast-container-bottom-center.toast-container-stack,
.toast-container-bottom-end.toast-container-stack {
  > .toast {
    inset-block-start: auto;
    inset-block-end: calc(var(--cui-toast-stack-depth) * (1 - pow(var(--cui-toast-stack-ratio), var(--cui-toast-stack-index))));
    transform-origin: bottom center;

    &:not(.toast-instant) {
      @include transition-props(
        #{"opacity, translate, display, inset-block-end, height, scale"},
        var(--cui-toast-transition-duration),
        var(--cui-toast-transition-timing),
        allow-discrete
      );
    }
  }

  &:is(:hover, :focus-within) > .toast {
    inset-block-end: calc(var(--cui-toast-stack-before) + var(--cui-toast-stack-index) * var(--cui-toast-spacing));
  }
}
```

# Vue Toaster Component API

```jsx
import { CToaster } from '@coreui/vue'
```

### Props

| Name | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `placement` | `string` | - | Describes the placement of component. Overrides the placement of the `toaster` store. |
| `toaster` | `Toaster` | - | The store created with `createToaster()`. When set, the component renders a `<CToast>` for every toast in the store and provides the store to `useToaster()`. |

# Vue Bootstrap Toaster Component

> Learn how to use CoreUI’s Vue Toaster component with Bootstrap styles for flexible, framework-consistent UI.

## Overview

`createToaster()` keeps the toasts of the whole app in one store and `` renders them, so a toast can be added from anywhere without any markup up front. See the [toaster](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/components/toaster/) for the full API.

```html
<template>
  <CButton theme="primary" @click="addToast">Add a toast</CButton>
  <CButton theme="secondary" @click="addToStack">Add to the stack</CButton>
  <CToaster :toaster="toaster" />
  <CToaster :toaster="stacked" />
</template>

<script setup>
import { CButton, CToaster, createToaster } from '@coreui/vue'

const toaster = createToaster({ placement: 'top-end' })
const stacked = createToaster({ placement: 'top-start', stack: true, limit: 6 })

const addToast = () => {
  toaster.add({
    title: 'CoreUI for Vue.js',
    description: 'Hello, world! This is a toast message.',
  })
}

const addToStack = () => {
  stacked.add({
    title: 'CoreUI for Vue.js',
    description: 'Hello, world! This one joins a stack.',
  })
}
</script>
```

## Title, description and theme

```html
<template>
  <div class="hstack gap-3 flex-wrap mb-4">
    <CButton theme="primary" @click="addTitled">Title and description</CButton>
    <CButton theme="secondary" @click="addDescription">Description only</CButton>
    <CButton theme="danger" @click="addThemed">Themed, high priority</CButton>
    <CButton theme="secondary" variant="outline" @click="addSticky">Not dismissible</CButton>
  </div>
  <CToaster :toaster="toaster" class="position-static" />
</template>

<script setup>
import { CButton, CToaster, createToaster } from '@coreui/vue'

const toaster = createToaster({ timeout: 0 })

const addTitled = () => toaster.add({ title: 'Saved', description: 'Your changes are live.' })

const addDescription = () => toaster.add({ description: 'Copied to the clipboard' })

const addThemed = () =>
  toaster.add({
    title: 'Payment failed',
    description: 'The card was declined.',
    theme: 'danger',
    priority: 'high',
  })

const addSticky = () =>
  toaster.add({
    title: 'Read me',
    description: 'This one stays until you close it.',
    dismissible: false,
    timeout: 0,
  })
</script>
```

## Stacking

```html
<template>
  <div class="hstack gap-3 mb-4">
    <CButton theme="primary" @click="addToast">Add a toast</CButton>
    <CButton theme="secondary" variant="outline" @click="toaster.close()">Close all</CButton>
  </div>
  <CToaster :toaster="toaster" class="position-relative" />
</template>

<script setup>
import { CButton, CToaster, createToaster } from '@coreui/vue'

const toaster = createToaster({ stack: true, limit: 0, timeout: 0 })
let count = 0

const addToast = () => {
  count += 1
  toaster.add({
    title: `Toast ${count}`,
    description: count % 2 ? 'Hover or focus the stack to spread it out.' : 'A shorter one.',
  })
}
</script>
```
