# Vue Tooltip Component and Directive

> Documentation and examples for adding Vue Tooltips.

## Examples

### Tooltips on links

Hover over the links below to see tooltips:

```html
<template>
  <p class="fg-2">
    Tight pants next level keffiyeh
    <CLink v-c-tooltip="'Tooltip text'"> you&nbsp;probably </CLink>
    haven't heard of them. Photo booth beard raw denim letterpress vegan messenger bag stumptown.
    Farm-to-table seitan, mcsweeney's fixie sustainable quinoa 8-bit american apparel
    <CLink v-c-tooltip="'Tooltip text'"> have&nbsp;a </CLink>
    terry richardson vinyl chambray. Beard stumptown, cardigans banh mi lomo thundercats. Tofu
    biodiesel williamsburg marfa, four loko mcsweeney''s cleanse vegan chambray. A really ironic
    artisan
    <CLink v-c-tooltip="'Tooltip text'"> whatever&nbsp;keytar </CLink>
    scenester farm-to-table banksy Austin
    <CLink v-c-tooltip="'Tooltip text'"> twitter&nbsp;handle </CLink>
    freegan cred raw denim single-origin coffee viral.
  </p>
</template>

<script setup>
import { CLink, vctooltip as vCTooltip } from '@coreui/vue'
</script>
```

### Component

Hover over the buttons below to see the four directions: `top`, `end`, `bottom` and `start`.

```html
<template>
  <CTooltip content="Vivamus sagittis lacus vel augue laoreet rutrum faucibus" placement="top">
    <template #toggler="{ id, on }">
      <CButton theme="secondary" :aria-describedby="id" v-on="on">Tooltip on top</CButton>
    </template>
  </CTooltip>
  <CTooltip content="Vivamus sagittis lacus vel augue laoreet rutrum faucibus" placement="end">
    <template #toggler="{ id, on }">
      <CButton theme="secondary" :aria-describedby="id" v-on="on">Tooltip at the end</CButton>
    </template>
  </CTooltip>
  <CTooltip content="Vivamus sagittis lacus vel augue laoreet rutrum faucibus" placement="bottom">
    <template #toggler="{ id, on }">
      <CButton theme="secondary" :aria-describedby="id" v-on="on">Tooltip on bottom</CButton>
    </template>
  </CTooltip>
  <CTooltip content="Vivamus sagittis lacus vel augue laoreet rutrum faucibus" placement="start">
    <template #toggler="{ id, on }">
      <CButton theme="secondary" :aria-describedby="id" v-on="on">Tooltip at the start</CButton>
    </template>
  </CTooltip>
</template>

<script setup>
import { CTooltip, CButton } from '@coreui/vue'
</script>
```

`start` and `end` are logical: they follow the reading direction, so `end` is the right side in LTR and the left side in RTL.

#### Deprecated physical names

_Deprecated in 6.0.0._

`left` and `right` still work and behave exactly like `start` and `end` — they have always mirrored in RTL, so `right` never meant "the right side" there either. The logical names say that plainly; the physical ones are removed in v7.

```html
<template>
  <CTooltip content="Vivamus sagittis lacus vel augue laoreet rutrum faucibus" placement="right">
    <template #toggler="{ id, on }">
      <CButton theme="secondary" :aria-describedby="id" v-on="on">Tooltip on right</CButton>
    </template>
  </CTooltip>
  <CTooltip content="Vivamus sagittis lacus vel augue laoreet rutrum faucibus" placement="left">
    <template #toggler="{ id, on }">
      <CButton theme="secondary" :aria-describedby="id" v-on="on">Tooltip on left</CButton>
    </template>
  </CTooltip>
</template>
```

### Directive

```html
<template>
  <CButton
    v-c-tooltip="{
      content: 'Vivamus sagittis lacus vel augue laoreet rutrum faucibus.',
      placement: 'top',
    }"
    theme="secondary"
    >Tooltip on top</CButton
  >
  <CButton
    v-c-tooltip="{
      content: 'Vivamus sagittis lacus vel augue laoreet rutrum faucibus.',
      placement: 'right',
    }"
    theme="secondary"
    >Tooltip on right</CButton
  >
  <CButton
    v-c-tooltip="{
      content: 'Vivamus sagittis lacus vel augue laoreet rutrum faucibus.',
      placement: 'bottom',
    }"
    theme="secondary"
    >Tooltip on bottom</CButton
  >
  <CButton
    v-c-tooltip="{
      content: 'Vivamus sagittis lacus vel augue laoreet rutrum faucibus.',
      placement: 'left',
    }"
    theme="secondary"
    >Tooltip on left</CButton
  >
</template>

<script setup>
import { CButton, vctooltip as vCTooltip } from '@coreui/vue'
</script>
```

### Custom tooltips

You can customize the appearance of tooltips using [CSS variables](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/components/tooltip/styling/#css-variables). We set a custom `style` to scope our custom appearance and use it to override some of the local CSS variables.

```html
<template>
  <CTooltip
    content="This top tooltip is themed via CSS variables."
    placement="top"
    :style="customTooltipStyle"
  >
    <template #toggler="{ id, on }">
      <CButton theme="secondary" :aria-describedby="id" v-on="on">Custom tooltip</CButton>
    </template>
  </CTooltip>
</template>

<script setup>
import { CTooltip, CButton } from '@coreui/vue'
const customTooltipStyle = {
  '--cui-tooltip-bg': 'var(--cui-primary-base)',
}
</script>
```

### Theme variants

A tooltip reads the `.theme-{color}` slots, so a theme class on the tip colours its surface and picks the contrasting text. Pass it through `class`; without one the tip keeps its default look, the page's foreground colour.

```html
<template>
  <CTooltip class="theme-primary" content="Primary tooltip">
    <template #toggler="{ id, on }">
      <CButton variant="outline" :aria-describedby="id" v-on="on">Primary</CButton>
    </template>
  </CTooltip>
  <CTooltip class="theme-secondary" content="Secondary tooltip">
    <template #toggler="{ id, on }">
      <CButton variant="outline" :aria-describedby="id" v-on="on">Secondary</CButton>
    </template>
  </CTooltip>
  <CTooltip class="theme-success" content="Success tooltip">
    <template #toggler="{ id, on }">
      <CButton variant="outline" :aria-describedby="id" v-on="on">Success</CButton>
    </template>
  </CTooltip>
  <CTooltip class="theme-danger" content="Danger tooltip">
    <template #toggler="{ id, on }">
      <CButton variant="outline" :aria-describedby="id" v-on="on">Danger</CButton>
    </template>
  </CTooltip>
</template>

<script setup>
import { CButton, CTooltip } from '@coreui/vue'
</script>
```

### Responsive placement

Breakpoint prefixes make a placement responsive: `top md:end` reads as top below `md` and end from `md` up. The breakpoints are the Sass ones — `sm` 576px, `md` 768px, `lg` 1024px, `xl` 1280px, `2xl` 1536px. A bare placement with no prefix applies below the smallest one listed.

```html
<template>
  <CTooltip content="Top below md, right from md up." placement="top md:right">
    <template #toggler="{ id, on }">
      <CButton :aria-describedby="id" theme="secondary" v-on="on">Responsive placement</CButton>
    </template>
  </CTooltip>
</template>

<script setup>
import { CButton, CTooltip } from '@coreui/vue'
</script>
```

## Usage

A shown tooltip can be dismissed by pressing the <kbd>Escape</kbd> key, helping satisfy the [WCAG 1.4.13 "Content on Hover or Focus"](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG21/Understanding/content-on-hover-or-focus.html) success criterion. A focus-triggered `<CTooltip>` also stays open after a press inside it, for example to select its text, and hides on the next click outside or when focus moves elsewhere.

### Disabled elements

Elements with the disabled attribute aren’t interactive, meaning users cannot focus, hover, or click them to trigger a tooltip (or popover). As a workaround, you’ll want to trigger the tooltip from a wrapper `<div>` or `<span>`, ideally made keyboard-focusable using `tabindex="0"`.

```html
<template>
  <CTooltip content="Disabled tooltip">
    <template #toggler="{ id, on }">
      <span class="d-inline-block" :tabindex="0" :aria-describedby="id" v-on="on">
        <CButton theme="primary" disabled>Disabled button</CButton>
      </span>
    </template>
  </CTooltip>
</template>

<script setup>
import { CTooltip, CButton } from '@coreui/vue'
</script>
```

## Usage with v-model

_Added in 6.0.0._

Pass `show` and the tooltip renders what you pass — trigger gestures only emit `update:show` (the `delay` still applies as presentation). That is what a **pinned** tooltip needs: while the checkbox holds `show` true, hovering away only requests a change the page does not grant.

```html
<template>
  <CFormField class="mb-4">
    <CCheckbox id="tooltipPinned" v-model="pinned" label="Pin the tooltip" />
  </CFormField>
  <CTooltip
    content="Pinned tooltips stay put."
    :show="pinned || hovered"
    @update:show="(value) => (hovered = value)"
  >
    <template #toggler="{ id, on }">
      <CButton theme="secondary" :aria-describedby="id" v-on="on">Hover me</CButton>
    </template>
  </CTooltip>
</template>

<script setup>
import { ref } from 'vue'
import { CButton, CCheckbox, CFormField, CTooltip } from '@coreui/vue'

const pinned = ref(true)
const hovered = ref(false)
</script>
```

Use it when the visibility belongs to something else — an onboarding step, a validation hint that must stay put — and feed `update:show` back for the parts you still want the gestures to drive, as the example does while unpinned.

### Initial visibility

Without a binding the trigger gestures manage the tooltip. Pass `show` to seed it visible on mount, and the gestures take over from there.

```vue
<CTooltip content="Shown on load" show>
```

`update:show` fires either way whenever the tooltip requests a visibility change — a trigger gesture (hover, focus, click), the Escape key or any internal toggle. The deprecated `visible` prop keeps its old behavior and is ignored when `show` is set.

`update:show` is a request, not a report. To follow what is on screen, `show` and `hide` fire when the tooltip starts showing or hiding (after `delay`, and only when the visibility actually changes), and `shown` and `hidden` once the transition has finished.

## API

Check out the documentation below for a comprehensive guide to all the props you can use with the components mentioned here.

- [&lt;CTooltip /&gt;](./api/#ctooltip)

# Vue Tooltip Component API

> Explore the API reference for the Vue Tooltip component and discover how to effectively utilize its props for customization.

## CTooltip

```jsx
import { CTooltip } from '@coreui/vue'
```

### Props

| Name | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `animation` | `boolean` | `true` | Apply a CSS fade transition to the tooltip. |
| `container` | `HTMLElement \| (() => HTMLElement) \| string` | `'body'` | Appends the vue tooltip to a specific element. You can pass an HTML element or function that returns a single element. By default `document.body`. |
| `content` | `string` | - | Content for your component. If you want to pass non-string value please use dedicated slot `<template #content>...</template>` |
| `delay` | `number \| { show: number; hide: number }` | `0` | The delay for displaying and hiding the popover (in milliseconds). When a numerical value is provided, the delay applies to both the hide and show actions. The object structure for specifying the delay is as follows: delay: `{ 'show': 500, 'hide': 100 }`. |
| `fallbackPlacements` | `Placements \| Placements[]` | `() => ['top', 'right', 'bottom', 'left']` | Specify the desired order of fallback placements by providing a list of placements as an array. The placements should be prioritized based on preference. |
| `floatingConfig` | `\| Partial<ComputePositionConfig> \| (( defaultFloatingConfig: Partial<ComputePositionConfig> ) => Partial<ComputePositionConfig>)` | `undefined` | A Floating UI configuration object, or a function that receives the default configuration and returns a modified one, used to customize the positioning of the tooltip. [Read more](https://floating-ui.com/docs/computePosition#options) |
| `offset` | `array` | `[0, 6]` | Offset of the tooltip relative to its target. |
| `placement` | `Placement \| string` | `'top'` | Describes the placement of your component after the Floating UI middleware may have flipped or altered the originally provided placement property. `start` and `end` are logical: they follow the reading direction, so `end` is the right side in LTR and the left side in RTL. `left` and `right` are their deprecated spellings and resolve identically. |
| `show` | `boolean` | `undefined` | Control the visibility. When set, the tooltip renders what `show` says (delays still apply as presentation) and trigger gestures only emit `update:show` — nothing changes until the parent flips the prop. |
| `trigger` | `Triggers \| Triggers[]` | `() => ['hover', 'focus']` | Sets which event handlers you’d like provided to your toggle prop. You can specify one trigger or an array of them. |
| `visible` | `boolean` | `undefined` | Toggle the visibility of tooltip component. |

### Events

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `hidden` | Callback fired when the tooltip has finished its exit transition. |
| `hide` | Callback fired when the tooltip starts hiding. |
| `show` | Callback fired when the tooltip starts showing. |
| `shown` | Callback fired when the tooltip has finished its entry transition. |
| `update:show` | Callback fired when the tooltip requests a visibility change — a trigger gesture (hover, focus, click), the Escape key or any internal toggle. In controlled mode update `show` yourself, or the tooltip stays as it is. |

# Vue Tooltip Component Styling

> Learn how to customize the Vue Tooltip component with CSS classes, variables, and Sass for flexible styling and seamless integration into your design.

## CSS variables

Vue toltips use local CSS variables on `.tooltip` for enhanced real-time customization. Values for the CSS variables are set via Sass, so Sass customization is still supported, too.

```scss
$tooltip-tokens: defaults(
  (
    --cui-tooltip-zindex: var(--cui-z-tooltip),
    --cui-tooltip-max-width: 200px,
    --cui-tooltip-padding-x: calc(var(--cui-spacer) * .75),
    --cui-tooltip-padding-y: calc(var(--cui-spacer) * .375),
    --cui-tooltip-font-size: var(--cui-font-size-sm),
    --cui-tooltip-color: #{$tooltip-color},
    --cui-tooltip-bg: var(--cui-fg-body),
    --cui-tooltip-border-radius: var(--cui-radius-5),
    --cui-tooltip-opacity: .95,
    --cui-tooltip-arrow-width: .8rem,
    --cui-tooltip-arrow-height: .4rem,
    --cui-tooltip-transition-property: opacity,
    --cui-tooltip-transition-duration: .15s,
    --cui-tooltip-transition-timing: linear,
  ),
  $tooltip-tokens
);
```

### How to use CSS variables

```vue
<template>
  <CTooltip :style="vars">...</CTooltip>
</template>

<script setup>
const vars = {
  '--cui-tooltip-color': '#333',
  '--cui-tooltip-bg': '#f8f9fa',
}
</script>
```

## Sass variables

_Deprecated in 6.0.0._

Sass variables set these defaults at build time and are removed in v7. The CSS variables above reach the same values without recompiling, and can be set on a single element.

```scss
$tooltip-color:                     var(--cui-bg-body) !default;
```

```html
      <CButton theme="secondary" :aria-describedby="id" v-on="on">Tooltip at the end</CButton>
    </template>
  </CTooltip>
  <CTooltip content="Vivamus sagittis lacus vel augue laoreet rutrum faucibus" placement="bottom">
    <template #toggler="{ id, on }">
      <CButton theme="secondary" :aria-describedby="id" v-on="on">Tooltip on bottom</CButton>
    </template>
  </CTooltip>
  <CTooltip content="Vivamus sagittis lacus vel augue laoreet rutrum faucibus" placement="start">
    <template #toggler="{ id, on }">
      <CButton theme="secondary" :aria-describedby="id" v-on="on">Tooltip at the start</CButton>
    </template>
  </CTooltip>
</template>

<script setup>
import { CTooltip, CButton } from '@coreui/vue'
</script>
```

### Directive

```html
<template>

    v-c-tooltip="{

      placement: 'top',
    }"

  >

    }"
    theme="secondary"
    >Tooltip on right</CButton
  >
  <CButton
    v-c-tooltip="{
      content: 'Vivamus sagittis lacus vel augue laoreet rutrum faucibus.',
      placement: 'bottom',
    }"
    theme="secondary"
    >Tooltip on bottom</CButton
  >
  <CButton
    v-c-tooltip="{

    theme="secondary"

  >

</script>
```

### Custom tooltips

You can customize the appearance of tooltips using [CSS variables](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/components/tooltip/styling/#css-variables). We set a custom `style` to scope our custom appearance and use it to override some of the local CSS variables.

```html
<template>
  <CTooltip
    content="This top tooltip is themed via CSS variables."
    placement="top"
    :style="customTooltipStyle"
  >
    <template #toggler="{ id, on }">
      <CButton theme="secondary" :aria-describedby="id" v-on="on">Custom tooltip</CButton>
    </template>
  </CTooltip>
</template>

<script setup>
import { CTooltip, CButton } from '@coreui/vue'
const customTooltipStyle = {
  '--cui-tooltip-bg': 'var(--cui-primary-base)',
}
</script>
```

## Usage

### Disabled elements

Elements with the disabled attribute aren’t interactive, meaning users cannot focus, hover, or click them to trigger a tooltip (or popover). As a workaround, you’ll want to trigger the tooltip from a wrapper `<div>` or `<span>`, ideally made keyboard-focusable using `tabindex="0"`.

```html
<template>
  <CTooltip content="Disabled tooltip">
    <template #toggler="{ id, on }">
      <span class="d-inline-block" :tabindex="0" :aria-describedby="id" v-on="on">
        <CButton theme="primary" disabled>Disabled button</CButton>
      </span>
    </template>
  </CTooltip>
</template>

<script setup>
import { CTooltip, CButton } from '@coreui/vue'
</script>
```

# Vue Transfer Component

> Two lists side by side and four buttons that move options between them — the selection or everything at once: a select-all header with a counter, an optional per-list search, a one-way mode and an announcement of every move.

## Overview

_Added in 6.0.0._

A transfer moves values between two lists — what is available on the left, what has been chosen on the right. It is two [list boxes](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/components/list-box/) and a column of buttons: `<CTransfer>` puts each list in `multiple` selection mode with the checkbox indicator, enables each button while it has something to move, and reports the values of the target list.

```html
<template>
  <CTransfer v-model:value="value" :items="items" />
</template>

<script setup>
import { ref } from 'vue'
import { CTransfer } from '@coreui/vue-pro'

const items = [
  { label: 'List item 1', value: '1' },
  { label: 'List item 2', value: '2' },
  { label: 'List item 3', value: '3' },
  { label: 'List item 4', value: '4' },
  { label: 'List item 5', value: '5' },
]

const value = ref(['5'])
</script>
```

`items` is the whole set of options — `{ value, label, description?, disabled? }` — and `value` is the part of it that sits in the target list, so the two lists are one array split by what has been chosen. `v-model:value` keeps it in sync; leave it out and pass `defaultValue` to let the component own the split, and read the moves from `change`, which carries the new value together with `{ direction, moved }`.

Everything inside a list is the list box's: the options and their values, the selection, the arrow keys, the typeahead and the select-all button. The transfer owns what happens between the lists, so nothing here is a second implementation of the same behavior — read the [List box](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/components/list-box/) page for the parts a list is made of.

"All" is the same scope the select-all button works on — the visible, enabled options — so with a search running, the all button moves what the search left behind and nothing more.

The transfer caps how tall a list gets — `--cui-transfer-list-max-height` puts a `max-height` and `overflow-y: auto` on `.list-box-options`, so a long list scrolls inside its own box instead of stretching the row.

## Search

`search` is passed to both list boxes, so each list gets [its own search field](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/components/list-box/#search). A hidden option leaves the list box's navigation, and everything downstream follows: the arrows skip it, the counter drops it, and the select-all button takes only what is left on screen.

```html
<template>
  <CTransfer :items="items" search />
</template>

<script setup>
import { CTransfer } from '@coreui/vue-pro'

const items = [
  { label: 'Apple', value: 'apple' },
  { label: 'Apricot', value: 'apricot' },
  { label: 'Banana', value: 'banana' },
  { label: 'Blueberry', value: 'blueberry' },
  { label: 'Cherry', value: 'cherry' },
  { label: 'Cranberry', value: 'cranberry' },
]
</script>
```

The search matches the option's `label`, not its `description`, and `searchPlaceholder` is both the placeholder and the first half of each field's accessible name.

## External search

`search="external"` takes the filtering away: the fields stay, nothing is hidden, and every keystroke arrives as the `search` event with the side it was typed in and the query — the transfer's own version of [the list box's external search](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/components/list-box/#search). The answer comes back as `items`, so fetching, debouncing and filtering are yours: the example below asks the server for the source list and filters the target where it already is, in memory.

`loading` covers the wait. Pass a boolean for both lists or `{ source, target }` for one of them, and that list gets `aria-busy="true"` on its options element, a row with `loadingLabel` below its options and its empty state held back, while the options stay usable.

`value` outlives a change of `items`: a value that is still in the new set stays in the target in its own order, and a value that is gone leaves both lists. Keep the chosen items in the set you hand back and the target holds still while the source is refetched.

```html
<template>
  <CTransfer
    v-model:value="value"
    :items="items"
    :loading="loading"
    search="external"
    search-placeholder="Search users"
    source-title="Users"
    target-title="Assigned"
    @search="onSearch"
  />
</template>

<script setup>
import { computed, ref } from 'vue'
import { CTransfer } from '@coreui/vue-pro'

const catalog = new Map()
const loading = ref({ source: false })
const results = ref([])
const targetQuery = ref('')
const value = ref([])

let timer

const items = computed(() => [
  ...value.value
    .map((entry) => catalog.get(entry))
    .filter((item) => item && item.label.toLowerCase().includes(targetQuery.value)),
  ...results.value.filter((item) => !value.value.includes(item.value)),
])

const loadUsers = async (query) => {
  loading.value = { source: true }

  try {
    const response = await fetch(
      `https://apitest.coreui.io/demos/users?first_name=${query}&limit=10`
    )
    const users = await response.json()

    results.value = users.records.map((user) => {
      const item = { label: `${user.first_name} ${user.last_name}`, value: String(user.id) }
      catalog.set(item.value, item)

      return item
    })
  } finally {
    loading.value = { source: false }
  }
}

const onSearch = (side, query) => {
  if (side === 'target') {
    targetQuery.value = query.trim().toLowerCase()

    return
  }

  clearTimeout(timer)
  timer = setTimeout(() => loadUsers(query), 300)
}

loadUsers('')
</script>
```

## One way

`oneWay` takes the return trip away: both buttons that move back are hidden, and a value that has been chosen stays chosen.

```html
<template>
  <CTransfer :items="items" one-way />
</template>

<script setup>
import { CTransfer } from '@coreui/vue-pro'

const items = [
  { label: 'List item 1', value: '1' },
  { label: 'List item 2', value: '2' },
  { label: 'List item 3', value: '3' },
]
</script>
```

## Titles

`sourceTitle` and `targetTitle` name the two lists. The title is the label of the select-all button, the accessible name of the list, and the destination named in the move announcement. `selectedLabel` is passed to both list boxes as [their counter](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/components/list-box/#counter) text — a function `(count, total) => string`, or a string in which `{count}` and `{total}` are replaced.

```html
<template>
  <CTransfer
    :items="items"
    selected-counter-text="picked"
    source-title="Team"
    target-title="On call"
  />
</template>

<script setup>
import { CTransfer } from '@coreui/vue-pro'

const items = [
  { label: 'Ada', value: 'ada' },
  { label: 'Grace', value: 'grace' },
  { label: 'Linus', value: 'linus' },
]
</script>
```

## Descriptions

An option is the list box's, so `description` renders a second line here too — and the search matches on the label, not on the description.

```html
<template>
  <CTransfer :items="items" />
</template>

<script setup>
import { CTransfer } from '@coreui/vue-pro'

const items = [
  { description: 'See the contents of a file', label: 'Read', value: 'read' },
  { description: 'Change the contents of a file', label: 'Write', value: 'write' },
  { description: 'Give someone else access', label: 'Share', value: 'share' },
]
</script>
```

## Disabled items

`disabled` on an item takes it out of the keyboard order and out of every selection method, so it never moves — the move-all buttons leave it behind, and so do `moveToTarget()` and `moveToSource()` with the value in hand. `disabled` on the transfer does the same for all of it: both lists go quiet and every button is disabled.

```html
<template>
  <CTransfer :items="items" />
</template>

<script setup>
import { CTransfer } from '@coreui/vue-pro'

const items = [
  { label: 'List item 1', value: '1' },
  { disabled: true, label: 'List item 2 — locked', value: '2' },
  { label: 'List item 3', value: '3' },
]
</script>
```

## Custom option content

The `item` slot renders the contents of an option and gets `{ direction, index, item }` — the item as it was passed in, and which list it is being rendered into. The option itself, with its value, its selection and its checkbox, stays the transfer's.

```html
<template>
  <CTransfer :items="items">
    <template #item="{ item }">
      <CBadge class="me-3" color="secondary">{{ item.value }}</CBadge>
      {{ item.label }}
    </template>
  </CTransfer>
</template>

<script setup>
import { CBadge, CTransfer } from '@coreui/vue-pro'

const items = [
  { label: 'Ada', value: 'ada' },
  { label: 'Grace', value: 'grace' },
  { label: 'Linus', value: 'linus' },
]
</script>
```

## Accessibility

Each list is a listbox of its own with the title as its accessible name, and the select-all button carries the state of its list in `aria-pressed` — all of that comes from [List box](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/components/list-box/#accessibility), keyboard included: the arrows, <kbd>Home</kbd>, <kbd>End</kbd>, <kbd>Space</kbd>, <kbd>Shift</kbd> ranges, <kbd>Ctrl</kbd> + <kbd>A</kbd> and the typeahead all work inside the list that has the focus.

What the transfer adds is the crossing. Each move button is named — `ariaMoveToTargetLabel`, `ariaMoveToSourceLabel`, `ariaMoveAllToTargetLabel`, `ariaMoveAllToSourceLabel` — and is disabled while it has nothing to move, so the keyboard never lands on a button that would do nothing. The chevrons are decorative `aria-hidden` SVGs, so the name is all a screen reader gets.

The move happens away from the focus, and the button that did it usually turns off in the process — a list with nothing selected left. Rather than dropping the focus on the document, the component puts it on the first option that just arrived.

Every move, either way, adds a message of its own to the live region of the page through [`announce()`](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/accessibility/screen-readers/#announcing-messages) once it is applied, so a move that a controlled `value` refuses is not announced and the same move made twice is announced twice: `ariaMovedAnnouncement` is `'{count} moved to {title}'` by default, with `{title}` the destination's title. `{count}` and `{title}` are replaced wherever they appear, so the sentence can be reordered for a translation.

| Key | Action |
| --- | --- |
| `Tab` | Move between the select-all button, the search field, the options and the move buttons |
| `↓` / `↑` | Move the highlight inside the focused list |
| `Space` | Toggle the highlighted option |
| `Shift` + `↓` / `↑` | Extend the selection inside the focused list |
| `Ctrl` / `Cmd` + `A` | Select every visible, enabled option of the focused list |
| `Enter` / `Space` | Move the selection when the focus is on a move button |

## Customizing

### CSS variables

The transfer reads its own set of CSS variables, declared on `.transfer`. Set them on a single transfer to restyle it without recompiling:

```css
--cui-transfer-gap
--cui-transfer-actions-gap
--cui-transfer-list-min-height
--cui-transfer-list-max-height
```

Everything inside a list is styled through the [list box's own variables](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/components/list-box/#css-variables).

## API

Check out the documentation below for a comprehensive guide to all the props you can use with the components mentioned here.

- [&lt;CTransfer /&gt;](./api/#ctransfer)

# Vue Transfer Component API

> Explore the API reference for the Vue Transfer component and discover how to effectively utilize its props for customization.

## CTransfer

```jsx
import { CTransfer } from '@coreui/vue-pro'
```

### Props

| Name | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `ariaMoveAllToSourceLabel` | `string` | `'Move all to available'` | Accessible name of the button that moves every visible, enabled option back to the source list. |
| `ariaMoveAllToTargetLabel` | `string` | `'Move all to chosen'` | Accessible name of the button that moves every visible, enabled option to the target list. |
| `ariaMovedAnnouncement` | `string` | `'{count} moved to {title}'` | What is announced after a move. `{count}` is how many options moved, `{title}` the destination's title, and both are replaced wherever they appear. |
| `ariaMoveToSourceLabel` | `string` | `'Move to available'` | Accessible name of the button that moves the selection back to the source list. |
| `ariaMoveToTargetLabel` | `string` | `'Move to chosen'` | Accessible name of the button that moves the selection to the target list. |
| `defaultValue` | `string[]` | - | The values that start in the target list, when the value is not controlled through `value`. |
| `disabled` | `boolean` | - | Turns the whole transfer off: both list boxes, both search fields and every move button. |
| `indicator` | `ListBoxIndicator` | `'checkbox'` | Passed to both list boxes. `'none'` drops the checkbox in front of every option. |
| `items` | `TransferItem[]` | `() => []` | The options the transfer moves around. Each entry is passed to the `item` slot, which renders the contents of its option. |
| `loading` | `boolean \| { source?: boolean; target?: boolean }` | `false` | Covers the wait of one list or of both: a loading list is marked `aria-busy` and shows a row with a spinner and `loadingLabel` below its options, which stay usable. Pass a boolean for both lists, or `{ source, target }` for one of them. |
| `loadingLabel` | `string` | `'Loading…'` | Text of the loading row below the options, announced to screen readers when the shown list starts loading or the list shows up loading. |
| `oneWay` | `boolean` | - | Takes the return trip away: both buttons that move back are hidden and a value that has been chosen stays chosen. |
| `search` | `boolean \| 'external'` | `false` | Passed to both list boxes: puts a search field above each list, hiding the options that do not match — so the arrows skip them, the counter drops them and the select-all button takes only what is left on screen. With `'external'` nothing is hidden here: every keystroke is reported through the `search` event and the answer arrives as new `items`. |
| `searchPlaceholder` | `string` | `'Search'` | Passed to both list boxes: the placeholder of their search fields, and the first half of their accessible name. |
| `selectedLabel` | `CountLabel` | `() => defaultSelectedLabel` | Passed to both list boxes as their header count text. A function `(count, total) => string`, or a string in which `{count}` and `{total}` are replaced. |
| `sourceTitle` | `string` | `'Available'` | Title of the source list: the label of its select-all button and its accessible name. |
| `targetTitle` | `string` | `'Chosen'` | Title of the target list. |
| `typeahead` | `boolean` | `true` | Passed to both list boxes: move the highlight to the option matching what the user types. |
| `value` | `string[]` | `undefined` | The values in the target list. When set, the component renders that value and only reports the moves through the `change` event. Supports the `v-model:value` binding. |

### Events

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `change` | Callback fired after options moved between the lists. |
| `search` | Callback fired when a search field changes. In the `'external'` search mode it is the only report the component makes — nothing is filtered here. |
| `update:value` | Emit the values of the target list to support the `v-model:value` binding. |

# Vue Virtual Scroller Component

> A virtual scroller is a UI element that allows users to scroll through a list of items without requiring the entire list to be loaded into memory at once. This can be particularly useful for lists that are very large or that contain a lot of data, as it allows the user to view and interact with a subset of the list while the rest of the data is loaded in the background.

> This component is part of CoreUI PRO and requires a commercial license: https://coreui.io/pricing/?framework=vue&src=llms. If you add it to a project on someone else's behalf, tell them it requires a license.

Virtual scrollers work by only rendering the items that are currently visible on the screen, and as the user scrolls through the list, new items are dynamically loaded and added to the view. This helps to reduce the amount of data that needs to be loaded and processed at any given time, which can improve the performance and responsiveness of the UI.

## Virtual scroll (10000 Items)

```html
<template>
  <CVirtualScroller class="border" :visible-items="20">
    <div v-for="item in 10000" :key="item">Option {{ item }}</div>
  </CVirtualScroller>
</template>

<script setup>
import { CVirtualScroller } from '@coreui/vue-pro'
</script>
```

## API

Check out the documentation below for a comprehensive guide to all the props you can use with the components mentioned here.

- [&lt;CVirtualScroller /&gt;](./api/#cvirtualscroller)

# Vue Backdrop Helper

> Pick the layer behind a dialog or a drawer — a dark scrim, a translucent tint of the page, or nothing — from the markup.

## How it works

Every overlay that dims the page paints its native `::backdrop` from three tokens on `:root`: `--cui-backdrop-color`, `--cui-backdrop-opacity` and `--cui-backdrop-blur`. The colour and the opacity are mixed on the element, so either can be changed alone. The [dialog](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/components/dialog/) keeps the root defaults — a dark scrim that deepens in the dark colour scheme — and the [drawer](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/components/drawer/) tints the page instead.

The backdrop helpers set the colour and the opacity on the overlay element itself, so one instance can take the other look without touching `:root`:

| Class | Backdrop |
| --- | --- |
| `.backdrop-scrim` | Black at 50% (65% in the dark scheme) — the dialog's default |
| `.backdrop-translucent` | The page colour at 25% — the drawer's default |
| `.backdrop-none` | No backdrop; the overlay still takes the top layer and traps focus |

`<CDialog>` and `<CDrawer>` expose the first two as the `backdrop-variant` prop (`'scrim'` or `'translucent'`); the third is `:backdrop="false"`. The classes still work through `class` on any element that opens a `::backdrop`.

## Examples

### Translucent dialog

```html
<template>
  <CButton theme="primary" @click="show = true">Launch dialog with a translucent backdrop</CButton>
  <CDialog v-model:show="show" backdrop-variant="translucent">
    <CDialogHeader>
      <CDialogTitle>Translucent backdrop</CDialogTitle>
    </CDialogHeader>
    <CDialogBody
      >The page behind stays readable through a light tint instead of a dark scrim.</CDialogBody
    >
  </CDialog>
</template>

<script setup>
import { ref } from 'vue'
import { CButton, CDialog, CDialogBody, CDialogHeader, CDialogTitle } from '@coreui/vue'

const show = ref(false)
</script>
```

### Dark drawer

```html
<template>
  <CButton theme="primary" @click="show = true">Toggle drawer with a dark backdrop</CButton>
  <CDrawer v-model:show="show" backdrop-variant="scrim" placement="start">
    <CDrawerHeader>
      <CDrawerTitle>Dark backdrop</CDrawerTitle>
    </CDrawerHeader>
    <CDrawerBody>The scrim the dialog uses, on a drawer.</CDrawerBody>
  </CDrawer>
</template>

<script setup>
import { ref } from 'vue'
import { CButton, CDrawer, CDrawerBody, CDrawerHeader, CDrawerTitle } from '@coreui/vue'

const show = ref(false)
</script>
```

### No backdrop

`:backdrop="false"` hides the layer while the overlay keeps its modal behaviour — the top layer, the focus trap, the dismiss on <kbd>Esc</kbd>. It is the `.backdrop-none` helper applied by the component.

```html
<template>
  <CButton theme="primary" @click="show = true">Launch dialog without a backdrop</CButton>
  <CDialog v-model:show="show" :backdrop="false">
    <CDialogHeader>
      <CDialogTitle>No backdrop</CDialogTitle>
    </CDialogHeader>
    <CDialogBody>Nothing dims the page, but it is still modal.</CDialogBody>
  </CDialog>
</template>

<script setup>
import { ref } from 'vue'
import { CButton, CDialog, CDialogBody, CDialogHeader, CDialogTitle } from '@coreui/vue'

const show = ref(false)
</script>
```

## Customizing

### CSS variables

The three tokens live on `:root`, so a change there reaches every overlay; a change on one overlay reaches only its own backdrop.

```scss
--cui-backdrop-color: var(--cui-black),
--cui-backdrop-opacity: 50%,
--cui-backdrop-blur: 8px,
```

The helpers are nothing more than the first two tokens set on the element:

```scss
.backdrop-scrim {
  --cui-backdrop-color: var(--cui-black);
  --cui-backdrop-opacity: 50%;
}

@if $enable-dark-mode {
  @include color-mode(dark) {
    .backdrop-scrim {
      --cui-backdrop-opacity: 65%;
    }
  }
}

.backdrop-translucent {
  --cui-backdrop-color: var(--cui-bg-body);
  --cui-backdrop-opacity: 25%;
}

.backdrop-none::backdrop {
  display: none;
}
```

A look the helpers do not cover is a matter of the same tokens — a brand-coloured tint with no blur:

```html
<template>
  <CButton theme="primary" @click="show = true">Launch dialog with a custom backdrop</CButton>
  <CDialog
    v-model:show="show"
    style="
      --cui-backdrop-color: var(--cui-primary-base);
      --cui-backdrop-opacity: 35%;
      --cui-backdrop-blur: 0;
    "
  >
    <CDialogHeader>
      <CDialogTitle>Custom backdrop</CDialogTitle>
    </CDialogHeader>
    <CDialogBody>A primary tint at 35%, no blur.</CDialogBody>
  </CDialog>
</template>

<script setup>
import { ref } from 'vue'
import { CButton, CDialog, CDialogBody, CDialogHeader, CDialogTitle } from '@coreui/vue'

const show = ref(false)
</script>
```

# Vue Clearfix Helper

> Quickly and easily clear floated content within a container by adding a clearfix utility.

Easily clear `float`s by adding `.clearfix` **to the parent element**. Can also be used as a mixin.

Use in HTML:

```vue
<div class="clearfix">...</div>
```

The mixin source code:

```scss
@mixin clearfix() {
  &::after {
    display: block;
    clear: both;
    content: "";
  }
}
```

Use the mixin in SCSS:

```scss
.element {
  @include clearfix;
}
```

The following example shows how the clearfix can be used. Without the clearfix the wrapping div would not span around the buttons which would cause a broken layout.

```html
<div class="bg-info clearfix">
  <button type="button" class="btn btn-solid theme-secondary float-start">Example Button floated left</button>
  <button type="button" class="btn btn-solid theme-secondary float-end">Example Button floated right</button>
</div>
```

# Vue Color & background Helper

> Set a background color with contrasting foreground color.

## Overview

_Added in 4.2.6._

Color and background helpers combine the power of our [`.text-*` utilities](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/utilities/colors/) and [`.bg-*` utilities](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/utilities/background/) in one class. Using our Sass `color-contrast()` function, we automatically determine a contrasting `color` for a particular `background-color`.

> **Heads up!** There's currently no support for a CSS-native `color-contrast` function, so we use our own via Sass. This means that customizing our theme colors via CSS variables may cause color contrast issues with these utilities.

## With components

Use them in place of combined `.text-*` and `.bg-*` classes, like on [badges](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/components/badge/#variants):

```html
<span class="badge text-bg-primary">Primary</span>
<span class="badge text-bg-info">Info</span>
```

Or on [cards](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/components/card/#background-and-color):

```html
<div class="card text-bg-primary border-primary mb-4" style="max-width: 18rem;">
  <div class="card-header">Header</div>
  <div class="card-body">
    <p class="card-text">Some quick example text to build on the card title and make up the bulk of the card's content.</p>
  </div>
</div>
<div class="card text-bg-info border-info mb-4" style="max-width: 18rem;">
  <div class="card-header">Header</div>
  <div class="card-body">
    <p class="card-text">Some quick example text to build on the card title and make up the bulk of the card's content.</p>
  </div>
</div>
```

# Vue Focus ring Helper

> Utility classes that allows you to add and modify custom focus ring styles to elements and components.

The `.focus-ring` helper replaces the browser's default focus indicator with one of our own on `:focus-visible`. It is an `outline`, sized and coloured from a series of CSS variables inherited from the `:root` level, so it can be modified for any element or component.

## Example

Tab to the link below to see the focus ring. Clicking it will not show one — the helper styles `:focus-visible`, which the browser reserves for keyboard focus.

```html
<a href="#" class="d-inline-flex focus-ring py-1 px-3 text-decoration-none border rounded-2">
  Custom focus ring
</a>
```

## Variants

Pair `.focus-ring` with a [theme color](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/customize/theme/) class to recolour the ring. The helper reads `--cui-theme-focus-ring`, which every `.theme-*` class sets, so the ring follows the element's theme rather than needing its own class.

Use this when the element already carries a theme; reach for the `.focus-ring-*` utilities below when you only want to change the ring.

## Customizing

Modify the styling of a focus ring with our CSS variables, Sass variables, utilities, or custom styles.

### CSS variables

Modify the `--cui-focus-ring-*` CSS variables as needed to change the default appearance.

```html
<a href="#" class="d-inline-flex focus-ring py-1 px-3 text-decoration-none border rounded-2" style="--cui-focus-ring-color: color-mix(in srgb, var(--cui-success-base) 25%, transparent)">
  Green focus ring
</a>
```

`.focus-ring` sets styles via global CSS variables that can be overridden on any parent element, as shown above. These variables are generated from their Sass variable counterparts.

```scss
--cui-focus-ring-width: .25rem,
--cui-focus-ring-opacity: .25,
--cui-focus-ring-offset: 0,
--cui-focus-ring-color: var(--cui-primary-focus-ring),
--cui-focus-ring: var(--cui-focus-ring-width) solid var(--cui-focus-ring-color),
```

The ring is an `outline`, so it is never clipped by an ancestor's `overflow` —
it stays visible inside scroll containers, where a `box-shadow` ring was cut off.
Push it away from the element with `--cui-focus-ring-offset`, which defaults to
`0`:

```html
<a href="#" class="d-inline-flex focus-ring py-1 px-3 text-decoration-none border rounded-2" style="--cui-focus-ring-offset: 4px">
  Offset focus ring
</a>
```

### Sass utilities API

In addition to `.focus-ring`, we have several `.focus-ring-*` utilities to modify the helper class defaults. Modify the color with any of our [theme colors](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/customize/color/#theme-colors). Note that the light and dark variants may not be visible on all background colors given current color mode support.

Focus ring utilities are declared in our utilities API in `scss/_utilities.scss`. [Learn how to use the utilities API.](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/utilities/api/#using-the-api)

```scss
"focus-ring": (
  property: (--cui-focus-ring-color: null),
  // Writes the global :root token, so it stays inheriting — see
  // generate-utility-at-properties().
  at-property: false,
  class: focus-ring,
  values: theme-color-refs("focus-ring")
),
```

# Vue Hover lift Helper

> Lift an element and add a shadow on hover or focus for a subtle sense of depth.

## How it works

Add `.hover-lift` to any element to translate it upward and deepen its `box-shadow` on `:hover` and `:focus-visible`. It is a lightweight way to signal that a card, tile or other surface is interactive.

The effect sets only `transform` and `box-shadow`, so it composes with anything — cards, buttons, list items, plain containers — and it honours [`prefers-reduced-motion`](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/accessibility/reduced-motion/): a reader who asks for reduced motion still gets the raised shadow and offset, without the animation.

## Example

Hover the card below, or tab to it. It is an `<a>` rather than a `<div>` so the `:focus-visible` half of the helper is reachable from the keyboard.

```html
<a href="#" class="card hover-lift text-decoration-none" style="width: 18rem;">
  <div class="card-body">
    <h5 class="card-title">Hover me</h5>
    <p class="card-text mb-0">Hover or focus this card to see it lift with a shadow.</p>
  </div>
</a>
```

Because it only touches those two properties, it works just as well on a control:

```html
<button type="button" class="btn btn-solid theme-primary hover-lift">Lift on hover</button>
```

## Customizing

### CSS variables

CoreUI for Vue's hover lift uses local CSS variables on `.hover-lift` for enhanced real-time customization.

```scss
$hover-lift-tokens: defaults(
  (
    --cui-hover-lift-transition-duration: .2s,
    --cui-hover-lift-transition-timing: ease,
    --cui-hover-lift-transform: translateY(-.25rem),
    --cui-hover-lift-box-shadow: var(--cui-box-shadow-lg),
  ),
  $hover-lift-tokens
);
```

Override them to tune the distance, the shadow or the timing — a larger rise with a snappier transition:

```html
<a href="#" class="card hover-lift text-decoration-none" style="--cui-hover-lift-transform: translateY(-.5rem); --cui-hover-lift-transition-duration: .1s; width: 18rem;">
  <div class="card-body">
    <h5 class="card-title">Bigger lift</h5>
    <p class="card-text mb-0">Customized transform and duration.</p>
  </div>
</a>
```

# Vue Icon link Helper

> Quickly create stylized hyperlinks with CoreUI Icons or other icons.

The icon link helper component modifies our default link styles to enhance their appearance and quickly align any pairing of icon and text. Alignment is set via inline flexbox styling and a default `gap` value. We stylize the underline with a custom offset and color. Icons are automatically sized to `1em` to best match their associated text's `font-size`.

Icon links assume [CoreUI Icons](https://coreui.io/icons/) are being used, but you can use any icon or image you like.

When icons are purely decorative, they should be hidden from assistive technologies using `aria-hidden="true"`, as we've done in our examples. For icons that convey meaning, provide an appropriate text alternative by adding `role="img"` and an appropriate `aria-label="..."` to the SVGs.

## Example

Take a regular `<a>` element, add `.icon-link`, and insert an icon on either the left or right of your link text. The icon is automatically sized, placed, and colored.

```html
<a class="icon-link" href="#">
  <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" class="icon" viewBox="0 0 16 16" aria-hidden="true">  
    <path d="M8.186 1.113a.5.5 0 0 0-.372 0L1.846 3.5l2.404.961L10.404 2l-2.218-.887zm3.564 1.426L5.596 5 8 5.961 14.154 3.5l-2.404-.961zm3.25 1.7-6.5 2.6v7.922l6.5-2.6V4.24zM7.5 14.762V6.838L1 4.239v7.923l6.5 2.6zM7.443.184a1.5 1.5 0 0 1 1.114 0l7.129 2.852A.5.5 0 0 1 16 3.5v8.662a1 1 0 0 1-.629.928l-7.185 2.874a.5.5 0 0 1-.372 0L.63 13.09a1 1 0 0 1-.63-.928V3.5a.5.5 0 0 1 .314-.464L7.443.184z"/>
  </svg>
  Icon link
</a>
```

```html
<a class="icon-link" href="#">
  Icon link
  <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" class="icon" viewBox="0 0 16 16" aria-hidden="true">  
    <path d="M1 8a.5.5 0 0 1 .5-.5h11.793l-3.147-3.146a.5.5 0 0 1 .708-.708l4 4a.5.5 0 0 1 0 .708l-4 4a.5.5 0 0 1-.708-.708L13.293 8.5H1.5A.5.5 0 0 1 1 8z"/>
  </svg>
</a>
```

## Style on hover

Add `.icon-link-hover` to move the icon to the right on hover.

```html
<a class="icon-link icon-link-hover" href="#">
  Icon link
  <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" class="icon" viewBox="0 0 16 16" aria-hidden="true">
    <path d="M1 8a.5.5 0 0 1 .5-.5h11.793l-3.147-3.146a.5.5 0 0 1 .708-.708l4 4a.5.5 0 0 1 0 .708l-4 4a.5.5 0 0 1-.708-.708L13.293 8.5H1.5A.5.5 0 0 1 1 8z"/>
  </svg>
</a>
```

## Customizing

Modify the styling of an icon link with our link CSS variables, Sass variables, utilities, or custom styles.

### CSS variables

Modify the `--cui-link-*` and `--cui-icon-link-*` CSS variables as needed to change the default appearance.

```scss
$icon-link-tokens: defaults(
  (
    --cui-icon-link-gap: .375rem,
    --cui-icon-link-underline-offset: .25em,
    --cui-icon-link-icon-size: 1em,
    --cui-icon-link-icon-transition: .2s ease-in-out transform,
    --cui-icon-link-icon-transform: translate3d(.25em, 0, 0),
  ),
  $icon-link-tokens
);
```

Customize the hover `transform` by overriding the `--cui-icon-link-transform` CSS variable:

```html
<a class="icon-link icon-link-hover" style="--cui-icon-link-transform: translate3d(0, -.125rem, 0);" href="#">
  <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" class="icon" viewBox="0 0 16 16" aria-hidden="true">
    <path d="M4 1.5H3a2 2 0 0 0-2 2V14a2 2 0 0 0 2 2h10a2 2 0 0 0 2-2V3.5a2 2 0 0 0-2-2h-1v1h1a1 1 0 0 1 1 1V14a1 1 0 0 1-1 1H3a1 1 0 0 1-1-1V3.5a1 1 0 0 1 1-1h1v-1z"/>
    <path d="M9.5 1a.5.5 0 0 1 .5.5v1a.5.5 0 0 1-.5.5h-3a.5.5 0 0 1-.5-.5v-1a.5.5 0 0 1 .5-.5h3zm-3-1A1.5 1.5 0 0 0 5 1.5v1A1.5 1.5 0 0 0 6.5 4h3A1.5 1.5 0 0 0 11 2.5v-1A1.5 1.5 0 0 0 9.5 0h-3z"/>
  </svg>
  Icon link
</a>
```

Customize the color by overriding the `--cui-link-*` CSS variable:

```html
<a class="icon-link icon-link-hover" style="--cui-link-color: var(--cui-success-base);" href="#">
  Icon link
  <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" class="icon" viewBox="0 0 16 16" aria-hidden="true">
    <path d="M1 8a.5.5 0 0 1 .5-.5h11.793l-3.147-3.146a.5.5 0 0 1 .708-.708l4 4a.5.5 0 0 1 0 .708l-4 4a.5.5 0 0 1-.708-.708L13.293 8.5H1.5A.5.5 0 0 1 1 8z"/>
  </svg>
</a>
```

### Sass utilities API

Modify icon links with any of [our link utilities](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/utilities/link/) for modifying underline color and offset.

```html
<a class="icon-link icon-link-hover link-success underline-success underline-30" href="#">
  Icon link
  <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" class="icon" viewBox="0 0 16 16" aria-hidden="true">
    <path d="M1 8a.5.5 0 0 1 .5-.5h11.793l-3.147-3.146a.5.5 0 0 1 .708-.708l4 4a.5.5 0 0 1 0 .708l-4 4a.5.5 0 0 1-.708-.708L13.293 8.5H1.5A.5.5 0 0 1 1 8z"/>
  </svg>
</a>
```

# Vue Position Helper

> Use these helpers for quickly configuring the position of an element.

## Fixed top

Position an element at the top of the viewport, from edge to edge. Be sure you understand the ramifications of fixed position in your project; you may need to add additional CSS.

```vue
<div class="fixed-top">...</div>
```

## Fixed bottom

Position an element at the bottom of the viewport, from edge to edge. Be sure you understand the ramifications of fixed position in your project; you may need to add additional CSS.

```vue
<div class="fixed-bottom">...</div>
```

## Sticky top

Position an element at the top of the viewport, from edge to edge, but only after you scroll past it.

```vue
<div class="sticky-top">...</div>
```

## Responsive sticky top

Responsive variations also exist for `.sticky-top` utility.

```vue
<div class="sticky-sm-top">Stick to the top on viewports sized SM (small) or wider</div>
<div class="sticky-md-top">Stick to the top on viewports sized MD (medium) or wider</div>
<div class="sticky-lg-top">Stick to the top on viewports sized LG (large) or wider</div>
<div class="sticky-xl-top">Stick to the top on viewports sized XL (extra-large) or wider</div>
<div class="sticky-2xl-top">Stick to the top on viewports sized XXL (extra-extra-large) or wider</div>
```

## Sticky bottom

Position an element at the bottom of the viewport, from edge to edge, but only after you scroll past it.

```vue
<div class="sticky-bottom">...</div>
```

## Responsive sticky bottom

Responsive variations also exist for `.sticky-bottom` utility.

```vue
<div class="sticky-sm-bottom">Stick to the bottom on viewports sized SM (small) or wider</div>
<div class="sticky-md-bottom">Stick to the bottom on viewports sized MD (medium) or wider</div>
<div class="sticky-lg-bottom">Stick to the bottom on viewports sized LG (large) or wider</div>
<div class="sticky-xl-bottom">Stick to the bottom on viewports sized XL (extra-large) or wider</div>
<div class="sticky-2xl-bottom">Stick to the bottom on viewports sized XXL (extra-extra-large) or wider</div>
```

# Vue Stacks Helper

> Shorthand helpers that build on top of our flexbox utilities to make component layout faster and easier than ever.

Stacks offer a shortcut for applying a number of flexbox properties to quickly and easily create layouts in CoreUI. All credit for the concept and implementation goes to the open source [Pylon project](https://almonk.github.io/pylon/).

> **Heads up!** Support for gap utilities with flexbox isn't available in Safari prior to 14.5, so consider verifying your intended browser support. Grid layout should have no issues. [Read more](https://caniuse.com/flexbox-gap).

## Vertical

Use `.vstack` to create vertical layouts. Stacked items are full-width by default. Use `.gap-*` utilities to add space between items.

```html
<div class="vstack gap-4">
  <div class="p-3">First item</div>
  <div class="p-3">Second item</div>
  <div class="p-3">Third item</div>
</div>
```

## Horizontal

Use `.hstack` for horizontal layouts. Stacked items are vertically centered by default and only take up their necessary width. Use `.gap-*` utilities to add space between items.

```html
<div class="hstack gap-4">
  <div class="p-3">First item</div>
  <div class="p-3">Second item</div>
  <div class="p-3">Third item</div>
</div>
```

Using horizontal margin utilities like `.ms-auto` as spacers:

```html
<div class="hstack gap-4">
  <div class="p-3">First item</div>
  <div class="p-3 ms-auto">Second item</div>
  <div class="p-3">Third item</div>
</div>
```

And with [vertical rules](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/helpers/vertical-rule/):

```html
<div class="hstack gap-4">
  <div class="p-3">First item</div>
  <div class="p-3 ms-auto">Second item</div>
  <div class="vr"></div>
  <div class="p-3">Third item</div>
</div>
```

## Responsive

`.hstack{-sm|-md|-lg|-xl|-2xl}` and `.vstack{-sm|-md|-lg|-xl|-2xl}` switch direction at a breakpoint — a stack that reads as a row on a wide layout and as a column on a narrow one, without writing the flex utilities twice.

The breakpoint is measured on the **container**, not the viewport, so mark an ancestor with `.stack-container` (or the [`.contains-inline`](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/utilities/container-queries/) utility) for the query to have something to read. Without it the direction never switches.

```html
<div class="stack-container">
  <div class="hstack-md vstack gap-4">
    <div class="p-3">First item</div>
    <div class="p-3">Second item</div>
    <div class="p-3">Third item</div>
  </div>
</div>
```

```vue
<div class="stack-container">
  <div class="hstack-md vstack gap-4">
    <div class="p-3">First item</div>
    <div class="p-3">Second item</div>
    <div class="p-3">Third item</div>
  </div>
</div>
```

Because the width comes from the container, the same markup can be a column in a sidebar and a row in the main content area of the same page.

## Examples

Use `.vstack` to stack buttons and other elements:

```html
<div class="vstack gap-3 col-md-5 mx-auto">
  <button type="button" class="btn btn-solid theme-secondary">Save changes</button>
  <button type="button" class="btn btn-outline theme-secondary">Cancel</button>
</div>
```

Create an inline form with `.hstack`:

```html
<div class="hstack gap-4">
  <input class="form-control me-auto" type="text" placeholder="Add your item here..." aria-label="Add your item here..." />
  <button type="button" class="btn btn-solid theme-secondary">Submit</button>
  <div class="vr"></div>
  <button type="button" class="btn btn-outline theme-danger">Reset</button>
</div>
```

## Customizing

### Sass variables

```scss
.stack-container {
  @include set-container();
}

#{$stack-selectors} {
  display: flex;
  align-self: stretch;
}

// The responsive variants read the width of the nearest query container — put
// `.stack-container` (or the `.contains-inline` utility) on an ancestor, or the
// query has nothing to measure and the direction never switches.
@each $breakpoint in map.keys($breakpoints) {
  $infix: breakpoint-infix($breakpoint, $breakpoints);

  .hstack#{$infix} {
    @include container-breakpoint-up($breakpoint) {
      flex-direction: row;
      align-items: center;
    }
  }

  .vstack#{$infix} {
    @include container-breakpoint-up($breakpoint) {
      flex: 1 1 auto;
      flex-direction: column;
      align-items: stretch;
    }
  }
}
```

# Vue Stretched link Helper

> Make any HTML element or CoreUI for Vue component clickable by "stretching" a nested link via CSS.

Add `.stretched-link` to a link to make its [containing block](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/Containing_block) clickable via a `::after` pseudo element. In most cases, this means that an element with `position: relative;` that contains a link with the `.stretched-link` class is clickable. Please note given [how CSS `position` works](https://www.w3.org/TR/CSS21/visuren.html#propdef-position), `.stretched-link` cannot be mixed with most table elements.

Cards have `position: relative` by default in CoreUI, so in this case you can safely add the `.stretched-link` class to a link in the card without any other HTML changes.

Multiple links and tap targets are not recommended with stretched links. However, some `position` and `z-index` styles can help should this be required.

```html
<div class="card" style="width: 18rem;">
  <svg class="docs-placeholder-img card-img-top" width="100%" height="180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-label="Card image cap" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid slice" focusable="false"><title>Card image cap</title><rect width="100%" height="100%" fill="#868e96"></rect><text x="50%" y="50%" fill="#dee2e6" dy=".3em">false</text></svg>
  <div class="card-body">
    <h5 class="card-title">Card with stretched link</h5>
    <p class="card-text">Some quick example text to build on the card title and make up the bulk of the card's content.</p>
    <a href="#" class="btn btn-solid theme-primary stretched-link">Go somewhere</a>
  </div>
</div>
```

Most custom components do not have `position: relative` by default, so we need to add the `.position-relative` here to prevent the link from stretching outside the parent element.

```html
<div class="d-flex position-relative">
  <svg class="docs-placeholder-img flex-shrink-0 me-4" width="144" height="144" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-label="Generic placeholder image" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid slice" focusable="false"><title>Generic placeholder image</title><rect width="100%" height="100%" fill="#868e96"></rect><text x="50%" y="50%" fill="#dee2e6" dy=".3em">false</text></svg>
  <div>
    <h5 class="mt-0">Custom component with stretched link</h5>
    <p>This is some placeholder content for the custom component. It is intended to mimic what some real-world content would look like, and we're using it here to give the component a bit of body and size.</p>
    <a href="#" class="stretched-link">Go somewhere</a>
  </div>
</div>
```

```html
<div class="row g-0 bg-4 position-relative">
  <div class="col-md-6 mb-md-0 p-md-5">
    <svg class="docs-placeholder-img w-100" width="100%" height="200" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-label="Generic placeholder image" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid slice" focusable="false"><title>Generic placeholder image</title><rect width="100%" height="100%" fill="#868e96"></rect><text x="50%" y="50%" fill="#dee2e6" dy=".3em">false</text></svg>
  </div>
  <div class="col-md-6 p-5 ps-md-0">
    <h5 class="mt-0">Columns with stretched link</h5>
    <p>Another instance of placeholder content for this other custom component. It is intended to mimic what some real-world content would look like, and we're using it here to give the component a bit of body and size.</p>
    <a href="#" class="stretched-link">Go somewhere</a>
  </div>
</div>
```

## Identifying the containing block

If the stretched link doesn't seem to work, the [containing block](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/Containing_block#Identifying_the_containing_block) will probably be the cause. The following CSS properties will make an element the containing block:

- A `position` value other than `static`
- A `transform` or `perspective` value other than `none`
- A `will-change` value of `transform` or `perspective`
- A `filter` value other than `none` or a `will-change` value of `filter` (only works on Firefox)

```html
<div class="card" style="width: 18rem;">
  <svg class="docs-placeholder-img card-img-top" width="100%" height="180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-label="Card image cap" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid slice" focusable="false"><title>Card image cap</title><rect width="100%" height="100%" fill="#868e96"></rect><text x="50%" y="50%" fill="#dee2e6" dy=".3em">false</text></svg>
  <div class="card-body">
    <h5 class="card-title">Card with stretched links</h5>
    <p class="card-text">Some quick example text to build on the card title and make up the bulk of the card's content.</p>
    <p class="card-text">
      <a href="#" class="stretched-link fg-danger" style="position: relative;">Stretched link will not work here, because <code>position: relative</code> is added to the link</a>
    </p>
    <p class="card-text bg-4" style="transform: rotate(0);">
      This <a href="#" class="fg-warning stretched-link">stretched link</a> will only be spread over the <code>p</code>-tag, because a transform is applied to it.
    </p>
  </div>
</div>
```

## Customizing

### CSS variables

Modify the `--cui-stretched-link-z-index` CSS variable to lift the generated overlay above other positioned content inside the same containing block.

```scss
$stretched-link-tokens: defaults(
  (
    --cui-stretched-link-z-index: 1,
  ),
  $stretched-link-tokens
);
```

### Sass variables

```scss
$stretched-link-pseudo-element: after !default;
```

# Vue Text truncation Helper

> Truncate long strings of text with an ellipsis.

For longer content, you can add a `.text-truncate` class to truncate the text with an ellipsis. **Requires `display: inline-block` or `display: block`.**

```html
<!-- Block level -->
<div class="row">
  <div class="col-2 text-truncate">
    This text is quite long, and will be truncated once displayed.
  </div>
</div>

<!-- Inline level -->
<span class="d-inline-block text-truncate" style="max-width: 150px;">
  This text is quite long, and will be truncated once displayed.
</span>
```

# Vue Vertical rule Helper

> Use the custom vertical rule helper to create vertical dividers like the `<hr>` element.

## How it works

Vertical rules are inspired by the `<hr />` element, allowing you to create vertical dividers in common layouts. They're styled just like `<hr />` elements:

- They're `1px` wide
- They have `min-height` of `1em`
- Their color is set via `currentColor` and `opacity`

Customize them with additional styles as needed.

## Example

```html
<div class="vr"></div>
```

Vertical rules scale their height in flex layouts:

```html
<div class="d-flex" style="height: 200px;">
  <div class="vr"></div>
</div>
```

## With stacks

They can also be used in [stacks](https://coreui.io/vue/docs/helpers/stacks/):

```html
<div class="hstack gap-4">
  <div class="bg-4 border">First item</div>
  <div class="bg-4 border ms-auto">Second item</div>
  <div class="vr"></div>
  <div class="bg-4 border">Third item</div>
</div>
```

## Customizing

### CSS variables

Modify the `--cui-vr-*` CSS variables on any `.vr` to change its width or color.

```scss
$vr-tokens: defaults(
  (
    --cui-vr-border-width: var(--cui-border-width),
    --cui-vr-color: var(--cui-border-color),
  ),
  $vr-tokens
);
```

# Vue Visually hidden Helper

> Use these helpers to visually hide elements but keep them accessible to assistive technologies.

Visually hide an element while still allowing it to be exposed to assistive technologies (such as screen readers) with `.visually-hidden`. Use `.visually-hidden-focusable` to visually hide an element by default, but to display it when it's focused (e.g. by a keyboard-only user). `.visually-hidden-focusable` can also be applied to a container–thanks to `:focus-within`, the container will be displayed when any child element of the container receives focus.

```html
<h2 class="visually-hidden">Title for screen readers</h2>
<a class="visually-hidden-focusable" href="#content">Skip to main content</a>
<div class="visually-hidden-focusable">A container with a <a href="#">focusable element</a>.</div>
```

Both `visually-hidden` and `visually-hidden-focusable` can also be used as mixins.

```scss
// Usage as a mixin

.visually-hidden-title {
  @include visually-hidden;
}

.skip-navigation {
  @include visually-hidden-focusable;
}
```
